8. Identical, less numerous lesions were also present on her hands and back.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

B: Hereditary progressive mucinous histiocytosis

2. She did not report trauma, changes in vision, or foreign travel and did not take any topical ophthalmic medications.
3. Her medical history was unremarkable.
4. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS.
5. Her pupils were round with no afferent pupillary defect, although the circular lesion did move in concert with the pupillary constriction and dilation.
6. The intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OU.
7. Extraocular movements were normal.
8. Slitlamp examination of the anterior segment showed a 2 mm × 2–mm circular iris lesion at the inferotemporal border of the iris.
9. The mass appeared to have a fluid-debris level (Figure 1A).

11. Its nasal surface appeared white with speckled-brown pigmentation, while the remainder of the lesion had brown pigment (Figure 1B).
12. The anterior segment of the left eye and posterior segment of both eyes were unremarkable.A, Slitlamp photograph of anterior segment showed an iris lesion with a fluid-debris level (black arrowhead) inferotemporal to the pupillary border (white arrowhead).
13. B, Gonioscopic view showed iris lesion (black arrowhead) emerging from pupillary border (white arrowhead).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observe at yearly intervals
B: Obtain high-frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy
C: Perform transcorneal biopsy of the lesion
D: Completely excise the lesion with pathological analysis

question:
1. A 66-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of fevers, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash on the extensor surfaces of his lower and upper extremities.
2. There were no other associated symptoms, including dyspnea, cough, urinary tract symptoms, or gastrointestinal symptoms.
3. His medical history was significant for hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis.
4. He was started on azathioprine for autoimmune hepatitis at a dose of 75 mg 10 days prior to his presentation after thiopurine methyltransferase activity was found to be normal.
5. His other regular medications include aspirin, metformin, verapamil, and pravastatin.
6. Examination was remarkable for a temperature of 38°C, an exquisitely tender erythematous papulonodular rash on the extensor surface of his lower and upper limbs, and bilaterally tender knees with a patellar tap (Figure 1).
7. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 10 500/μL (with neutrophil level elevated at 9900/μL [94%]) and elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein level, 76 mg/L [724 nmol/L]; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 69 mm/h).
8. Rheumatoid factor was slightly elevated at 16 IU/mL, but testing for anti–citrullinated protein antibody was negative.
9. Tests for double-stranded DNA, extractable nuclear antibodies, and anti-antistreptolysin O were negative.
10. Renal function was normal, and there were no leukocytes, nitrates, red cells, or casts noted in the urine.
11. Chest radiograph was also normal.
12. Synovial fluid analysis showed a noninflammatory picture with a leukocyte count of 700 cells/L; no bacteria or crystals were seen.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Check angiotensin-converting enzyme level
B: Stop azathioprine
C: Commence corticosteroids
D: Perform a punch skin biopsy

1. An 18-year-old man presented with an upper respiratory tract infection that persisted for a week without improvement.
2. Because of this infection, he went to an emergency department and was prescribed antibiotics for presumed sinusitis.
3. Five days later, he developed painless horizontal diplopia and returned to the emergency department.
4. Findings from a computed tomographic scan showed diffuse sinusitis that was procedurally drained by an otolaryngologist.
5. However, this treatment did not resolve the diplopia and he was subsequently referred to a neurologist.
6. Additional evaluation included a repeated computed tomographic scan that showed no infectious involvement of the orbits or petromastoid complexes (Figure).
7. Findings from magnetic resonance imaging of the patient’s brain and orbits did not reveal intracranial lesions or extraocular muscle myositis.
8. Results of lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid testing, including opening pressure, cell count, and glucose and protein levels, were in the reference range.
9. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels were also in the reference range.
10. Findings from neurologic examination did not reveal paresthesias, difficulty with gait, or abnormal tendon reflexes.A, A computed tomographic scan of the face and orbits in coronal sections demonstrating inflammatory changes in the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses without orbital involvement.
11. B, An axial computed tomographic scan does not show inflammatory involvement of the petrous apices (digitally processed image).
12. A indicates anterior.The patient was then referred for neuro-ophthalmic evaluation.
13. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU.
14. Positive findings were limited to a −2.5 bilateral abduction deficit.
15. Alternate cover testing revealed a 30 prism diopters (∆) esotropia on primary gaze that increased to 45∆ on lateral gaze.
16. His pupils, intraocular pressure, visual fields, and findings from external examination were normal.
17. Findings from anterior segment and dilated fundus examinations were also normal.
18. The angle of esotropia was not improved with a 30-minute sleep test.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform a serum test for autoantibodies
B: Perform a tensilon test
C: Perform magnetic resonance venography
D: Restart antibiotic treatment and arrange for an otorhinolaryngology follow-up examination

1. A woman in her 60s presented with a 1-month history of painless, blurred vision in the left eye.
2. Her medical history was significant for Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM), and recent laboratory test results showed active WM with bone marrow involvement.
3. Results of the eye examination showed best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS.
4. Anterior segment examination results showed a relatively shallow anterior chamber in the left eye.
5. Results of a dilated fundus examination showed a choroidal detachment in the left eye extending circumferentially from the 2-o’clock to the 5-o’clock position and extending posteriorly up to 3 to 4 disc diameters temporal to the macula (Figure, A).
6. There was vitreous hemorrhage with a poor view of the posterior pole (Figure, A).
7. A, Ultra-widefield fundus photograph of the left eye showing posterior vitreous hemorrhage (white arrowhead) and a choroidal detachment temporally (yellow arrowheads).
8. B, Anterior segment spectral domain optical coherence tomography of the left eye showing the narrow angle from suprachoroidal effusion.
9. Results of fundus fluorescein angiography of the left eye showed hypofluorescence corresponding to vitreous hemorrhage.
10. Tortuosity of the temporal vessels was prominent, with diffuse peripheral vascular leakage temporally.
11. Choroidal folds were observed 3 disc diameters temporal to the macula, extending to the periphery.
12. Peripheral capillary nonperfusion, vascular reorganization, neovascularization, and choroidal detachment were noted.
13. Anterior segment spectral domain optical coherence tomographic results showed a shallow anterior chamber and 360° narrow angles in the left eye (Figure, B).
14. Results of B-scan ultrasonography confirmed choroidal detachment in the left eye and revealed a small area of suprachoroidal effusion in the right eye in the superotemporal periphery.
15. Treat with combined systemic chemotherapy and pars plana vitrectomy

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observe the patient
B: Perform pars plana vitrectomy
C: Treat with systemic chemotherapy
D: Treat with combined systemic chemotherapy and pars plana vitrectomy

question:
1. In April 2010, a 19-year-old soccer player presented with a 4-week history of pain after a tap against his right knee.
2. Medical and family histories were unremarkable and no abnormalities were found on physical examination.
3. A radiograph of the right knee showed osteolytic lesions in the distal femur and the head of the tibia.
4. On magnetic resonance imaging, the epiphyseal lesions were visualized as cystic and nonsclerotic and extended to the articular surface of the distal femur and proximal tibia (Figure 1).
5. Soft tissue extension was suspected from the tibia.
6. Laboratory test results showed normal blood cell count, renal function, and concentration of C-reactive protein.
7. Aneurysmatic bone cysts were suspected and a biopsy was performed.
8. Histopathological examination detected spindle cell infiltrates with hemorrhages, fragmented trabecular bone, and numerous osteoclastic giant cells proliferating at a rate of 10% suggesting an aggressive giant cell lesion.
9. Since it was still not determined whether the lesions were malignant, flourodeoxyglucose F 18 positron emission tomography/computed tomography was performed and found additional lesions in the left distal femur and the left mandible.
10. Biopsy of the mandible showed the same type of tissue as seen in the right femur and tibia.

What Is the Diagnosis?

A: Malignant bone tumor
B: Aneurysmatic bone cyst
C: Primary hyperparathyroidism with multiple brown tumors
D: Giant cell tumor

1. A 13-year-old boy with a history of sports-related blunt trauma to the left eye was referred for evaluation of an asymptomatic, pigmented iris lesion in the left eye.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy with cytology and cytogenetics
B: Iodine 125 plaque radiotherapy
C: Observe with no additional testing or intervention
D: Cyst paracentesis with complete drainage

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Pretibial myxedema
B: Elephantiasis nostras verrucosa
C: Lobomycosis
D: Euthyroid pretibial mucinosis

1. An 81-year-old White woman noted decreased vision in her left eye for 6 months.
2. She was referred to the Ocular Oncology Service, Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for suspected choroidal melanoma.
3. She disclosed a history of macular degeneration in both eyes and retinal detachment in the left eye that was treated 35 years previously.
4. Medical history revealed cutaneous basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, both treated surgically.
5. On examination, visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/400 OS.
6. External examination showed posterior-chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes and conjunctival scarring in the left eye from circumferential scleral buckle surgery with no visible extraocular tumor.
7. Fundus evaluation showed macular drusen in the right eye and a pale optic disc with geographic macular atrophy in the left eye, explaining her visual acuity of 20/400 OS.
8. In addition, a shallow circumferential buckle effect and an inferotemporal mass measuring 15.0 × 10.0 mm in basal dimension and 9.1 mm in thickness (Figure, A) were seen in the left eye.
9. The mass appeared elevated, amelanotic with overlying retinal vasculature, and with chorioretinal atrophy.
10. No retinal detachment or breaks were seen.
11. By ultrasonography the mass was echolucent (Figure, A inset).
12. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a T1, T2-hypointense shallow circumferential band in the left eye.
13. In addition, there was an inferotemporal nodular mass in the left eye showing T1 (gadolinium) hypointense, T2-hyperintense features, underlying the encircling buckle, and with adjacent subtle delineation.
14. There was no enhancement with gadolinium (Figure, B).
15. Fundus photograph and magnetic resonance imaging of the left eye.
16. A, Fundus photograph of left eye showed a pale optic disc, geographic macular atrophy, and an inferotemporal amelanotic mass (white arrowhead); inset shows ultrasonography revealing an echolucent mass (white arrowhead).

B: Refer for strabismus surgery
C: Order genetic workup
D: Treat with clonazepam

question:
1. A 75-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) with isolated deletion 5q (del5q) presented with multiple nonhealing skin ulcers on the chest and upper extremities.
2. Four years earlier, he started taking lenalidomide, 10 mg/d (28-day cycle), to treat worsening anemia; after 2 cycles of treatment, he became transfusion independent.
3. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects.
4. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers.
5. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve.
6. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions.
7. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus hemolyticus.
8. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement.
9. Thus, he was transferred to our facility.
10. Physical examination showed multiple cutaneous ulcers with gray undermined borders and red papules of varying depths involving the chest, back, and upper extremity; lesions were as large as 9 × 15 cm.
11. A complete blood cell count showed a white blood cell count of 16.2 × 103/μL (to convert to 109/L, multiply by 1.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 12.7 × 103/μL, hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), and platelet count of 262 × 103/μL with no circulating blasts.
12. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative.
13. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively.
14. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A).
15. Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors.
16. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.A, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows polymorphonuclear neutrophils admixed with scattered histiocytes and vasculatures with a prominent endothelial lining.
17. B, Immunohistochemical staining shows myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils peripherally and in aggregates.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Leukemia cutis
B: Pyoderma gangrenosum
C: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
D: Lymphomatoid papulosis

1. A 61-year-old Black man with hypertension and diabetes presented with decreased vision 3 months after uneventful cataract surgery in his left eye.
2. He had undergone laser retinopexy for retinal tears in his right eye and a scleral buckle and vitrectomy for a retinal detachment in his left eye 1 year earlier.
3. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/40 OD and counting fingers OS.
4. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 14 mm Hg in the right eye and 44 mm Hg in the left eye.
5. Anterior segment examination of the right eye was unremarkable, while ophthalmoscopic examination showed vascular attenuation and treated retinal breaks.
6. In the left eye, microcystic corneal edema and Descemet membrane folds limited examination, but no residual lenticular fragments or neovascularization of the iris or angle were seen.
7. The patient was discharged taking timolol, dorzolamide, brimonidine, and prednisolone.
8. Twelve days later, the cornea had cleared and IOP in the left eye improved to 32 mm Hg.
9. Gonioscopy revealed 360° of anterior synechiae and complete angle closure, which was documented on ultrasound biomicroscopy (Figure 1).
10. The patient started treatment with 500 mg of acetazolamide daily and referred to the glaucoma service for surgical evaluation.
11. Ultrasound biomicroscopy of the left eye demonstrating angle closure (arrowheads).
12. When the patient returned for his glaucoma evaluation 3 days later, he was noted to have loss of appetite, drowsiness, nausea, and malaise.
13. The patient’s intraocular examination was stable bilaterally.
14. During this visit, the patient developed acute chest pain and respiratory insufficiency requiring immediate transfer to the emergency department.
15. He was found to have a hemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10.0) and a hematocrit level of 22.1% (to convert to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain blood cultures, perform vitreous tap, and inject antibiotics
B: Perform laser iridotomy
C: Observation
D: Perform hemoglobin electrophoresis

1. A 56-year-old woman presented at the clinic for follow-up of metastatic hormone receptor–positive, ERBB2-negative breast cancer.
2. She had locally advanced disease that was invading the skin overlying her right breast and metastatic disease to the thoracic and lumbar spine, liver, and mediastinal, axillary, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes.
3. Her disease had progressed after receiving first-line therapy with palbociclib and anastrozole.
4. Subsequent treatments with fulvestrant and paclitaxel were also followed by progressive disease.
5. She received treatment with capecitabine; after 6 weeks of treatment, she developed some redness on her hands and feet that resolved on its own.
6. She then presented to the clinic with pruritic, erythematous, scaly macules and papules on her forearms, faces, chest, and upper back (Figure).
7. The rash had been present for 3 weeks and had recently worsened.
8. Her palms and soles were spared.
9. The rash did not respond to treatment with topical clindamycin, oral solumedrol, or doxycycline.
10. She had a history of substantial sun exposure but no history of skin cancer.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Cutaneous deposits of metastatic breast cancer
B: Inflammation of actinic keratoses
C: Medication hypersensitivity reaction
D: Discoid lupus erythematosus

11. The punch biopsy of the skin showed a diffuse island of atypical cells in the dermis (Figure, B).

1. A 72-year-old man presented with mild proximal weakness developing into progressive camptocormia, head drop, and prominent dysphagia over a 2-year period.
2. He reported a 20-kg weight loss and numbness to the ankles.
3. His medical history was significant for thyroid cancer treated with total thyroidectomy resulting in a chronic left accessory nerve injury, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and gout.
4. His medications were metformin, allopurinol, perindopril, thyroxine, and rabeprazole.
5. He had no history of smoking and drank 3 glasses of wine per week.
6. His family history was unremarkable.
7. Examination revealed significant wasting of proximal and paraspinal muscles with a flexed spine posture in the upright position (Figure 1A).
8. He had symmetric Medical Research Council grade 4/5 weakness of neck flexion, shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and extension, and hip flexion and extension bilaterally.
9. He had weakness of left shoulder elevation and winging of the left scapula secondary to the accessory nerve injury.
10. His deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric.
11. Pinprick sensation was reduced in both feet.
12. Lateral profile of the patient (A) revealing a flexed spine posture (camptocormia) with marked generalized muscle atrophy.
13. B, A Gömöri trichrome stain of frozen left vastus muscle (original magnification ×400) reveals 3 atrophic muscle fibers with a patchy granular appearance (red arrowheads).
14. Metabolic, endocrine, autoimmune, and infectious screens had unremarkable findings.
15. Creatine kinase levels were normal.
16. A myositis panel demonstrated low-positive Mi2 antibodies.
17. Serum electrophoresis and immunofixation identified a small immunoglobulin G (IgG) κ paraprotein with normal findings on bone marrow biopsy.
18. A whole-body positron emission tomography scan was normal.
19. Nerve conduction studies revealed a mild axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
20. Concentric needle electromyography showed no spontaneous activity with widespread small, brief, polyphasic units, particularly in proximal and axial muscles, consistent with a myopathic process.
21. An initial deltoid muscle biopsy did not show evidence of myopathy.
22. Because the patient’s symptoms were worsening, a second muscle biopsy of vastus lateralis was performed.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Late-onset Pompe disease (glycogen-storage disease type 2)
B: Myasthenia gravis
C: Paraneoplastic myositis
D: Sporadic late-onset nemaline rod myopathy

2. She had no associated nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hematochezia, bloating, or anorexia.

4. Over the previous 2 years, the patient had experienced similar intermittent episodes of abdominal pain lasting approximately 1 week.
5. What Would You Do Next?

A: Administer gabapentin
B: Assess celiac artery flow
C: Inject a local anesthetic into the area of maximal tenderness
D: Measure urine porphobilinogen level

question:
1. A patient in their mid-60s was referred for evaluation of a left iris pigmented lesion.
2. The mass had been present for decades and multiple prior office visits with referring ophthalmologists, most recently 4 years prior, showed the mass remained stable in size.
3. The patient’s ocular history included cataract extraction with intraocular lens placement and retinal tear of the right eye and cataract of the left eye.
4. Review of systems was negative for any recent changes in health, weight loss, fever, or night sweats.
5. Visual acuity without correction was 20/20 OD and 20/25+ OS.
6. Intraocular pressures were normal.
7. Slitlamp examination of the right eye was unremarkable, and the left eye had a raised pigmented iris lesion without prominent internal vasculature and with mammillations on the surface (multiple small smooth dome-shaped protuberances on the surface of the tumor).
8. There were large pigment granules on the surface of the tumor and on the adjacent iris surrounding the mass (Figure 1A).
9. There was no ectropion uvea or iris neovascularization.
10. There were mild nuclear sclerotic changes across the lens in the left eye.
11. Ultrasound biomicroscopy showed a homogeneous intrinsic iris solid tumor with a height of 1.4 mm and basal diameter of 4.1 mm, without angle or ciliary body involvement (Figure 1B).
12. Color slitlamp photograph shows a pigmented iris mass (note both the mammillations [black arrowheads] as well as the pigment granules stuck on the tumor surface [white arrowheads]) (A); ultrasound biomicroscopy shows solid, echogenically homogeneous iris stromal tumor with high internal reflectivity (B).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observation
B: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy
C: Plaque brachytherapy
D: Iridectomy for excision of the lesion

4. His medical history was remarkable for mild anemia because of untreated hemorrhoids.

9. Quantification of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA showed high loads of virus in the peripheral blood (846 copies/mL in serum, 27 700 copies/mL in lymphocytes; normal range, <500 copies/mL).

1. A patient in their 70s presented to the emergency department (ED) with a unilateral painless right proptosis, first noticed 3 days prior.
2. There was no contributory medical history, recent trauma, or surgery.
3. Visual acuity (VA) was 20/32 OD and 20/20 OS.
4. Anterior-segment and fundus examination results were normal.
5. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits revealed a right retro-orbital hemorrhage.
6. No etiology could be identified on the image.
7. Systemic corticosteroid therapy (methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg per day) was prescribed for 48 hours.
8. The proptosis decreased, and the patient was discharged.
9. After 6 months, complete ophthalmologic examination was performed again; VA was 20/20 OU, and there was no remaining proptosis.
10. Two weeks later, the patient presented to the ED for another episode of acute, painless, right proptosis, and the VA had decreased to 20/40 OD.
11. MRI showed a right retrobulbar hemorrhage.
12. Systemic corticosteroid therapy was again prescribed for 48 hours with rapid resolution of the visual impairment but incomplete resolution of the proptosis.
13. One month later, the patient presented to our ophthalmology department.
14. The VA was 20/20 OU, with a persistent, mild, nonreducible, nonpulsatile proptosis unrelated to Valsalva maneuver but associated with extraocular movement limitation in upgaze.
15. A repeated MRI was performed, which showed the following images (Figure 1).
16. T2-weighted coronal (A) and axial (B) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveal an intraorbital lesion.
17. Additional imaging, including a computed tomography and positron emission tomography scan

What Would You Do Next?

A: Clinical follow-up for idiopathic recurrent retrobulbar hemorrhage
B: Transconjunctival orbital biopsy
C: Additional imaging, including a computed tomography and positron emission tomography scan
D: Arteriography to look for orbital vascular malformations

1. A 66-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B infection and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presented with subacute epigastric pain.
2. Three years prior, she was diagnosed with a solitary HCC and underwent surgical resection with curative intent.
3. Pathology revealed poorly differentiated HCC, 16 cm in largest dimension, with large vein involvement (T3bNXM0, R0 resection).
4. The patient underwent expectant observation.
5. One and a half years prior to the current presentation, laboratory results revealed an elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP), and cross-sectional imaging revealed multiple lung nodules consistent with metastases.
6. She was treated with nivolumab every other week and attained a biochemical (baseline, 212.2 ng/dL; best response, 3.3 ng/dL) and radiographic complete response.In the current presentation, the patient reported nonradiating epigastric pain of moderate intensity for 1 month.
7. Associated symptoms included nausea, anorexia, and water brash without emesis.
8. Review of systems was positive for unchanged chronic abdominal bloating and negative for other constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms.
9. Laboratory results, including liver function tests, amylase, lipase, and AFP, were within normal limits, and hepatitis B virus polymerase chain reaction was undetectable.
10. Computed tomography with multiphasic liver protocol showed new enlarged mesenteric nodes and diffuse thickening of the gastric body (Figure, A).
11. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) identified diffuse inflammation and ulcerations in the gastric body and antrum (Figure, B).
12. Biopsy specimens showed chronic and active mixed inflammatory infiltrate, including intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Figure, C).
13. No overt viral cytopathic effects were observed, and immunostaining results for Helicobacter pylori, cytomegalovirus, and adenovirus were negative.A, Coronal view of restaging computed tomography of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast.
14. The yellow circle notes borderline enlarged mesenteric nodes inferior to the stomach, and the yellow arrowheads show thickened gastric body wall.
15. B, Gross appearance of the gastric mucosa visualized via upper endoscopy, which showed diffuse inflammation and ulceration in the gastric body and antrum.
16. C, Biopsy of the gastric mucosa showed marked chronic and active intraepithelial infiltration of lymphocytes (blue arrowheads) and neutrophils (yellow arrowhead) and associated glandular epithelial injury with withered glands and gland dropout (red circle) (original magnification ×100).
What Is Your Diagnosis?



A: Portal hypertensive gastropathy
B: Immunotherapy-related gastritis
C: Infectious gastritis
D: Liver cancer progression

1. An 18-year-old woman presented to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of recurrent skin, nail, and oral mucosal abnormalities.

3. Approximately 6 months later, the oral plaques recurred, her toenails became thickened and yellowed, and red plaques appeared on both feet and lower legs.

5. Over the following years, she received intermittent 3- to 6-month courses of daily itraconazole for recurrent skin, nail, and oral mucosal abnormalities, which typically recurred within 6 to 12 months of discontinuing itraconazole.
6. Her last dose of itraconazole was approximately 2 years prior to presentation.
7. On physical examination, the patient had white, moist, nonadherent plaques in the oral mucosa and moist red fissures at bilateral oral commissures (Figure, left panel).

9. Results of complete blood cell count with differential were normal, as were results of measurement of serum IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE levels and analysis of CD3, CD4, and CD8 T-cell subsets.
10. Potassium hydroxide wet mount preparation of skin scrapings from the lower extremities demonstrated fungal elements.
11. Fungal culture of the skin scrapings grew Candida albicans.
12. Patient presentation.
13. Left, White plaques in the oral mucosa and angular cheilitis.
14. Right, Thickened, yellowed toenails and scaly erythematous plaques on both lower legs and feet.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Administer oral cefazolin
B: Prescribe hydrocortisone cream
C: Restart daily oral itraconazole
D: Treat with oral terbinafine

B: Upper eyelid gold weight implantation
C: Systemic steroid and antiviral therapy
D: Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit

question:
1. A 79-year-old female patient presented with a 2-year history of asymptomatic erythematous-infiltrated patches and plaques on the right side of her scalp and face.
2. The lesions gradually enlarged and coalesced into large plaques and nodules.
3. Mild erosions occurred occasionally on the surface of the lesions.
4. She denied having fever, fatigue, chills, night sweats, or weight loss.
5. Physical examination demonstrated ill-defined, indurated erythematous-violaceous patches, nodules, and plaques involving the surface of her head and face with sporadic erosion and brownish crusts (Figure, A).
6. The findings of systemic reviews were unremarkable, and there was no lymphadenopathy.
7. The complete blood cell count revealed normal white blood cell count.
8. The biopsy from an erythematous nodule displayed sheets of medium to large mononuclear cells infiltrated in the dermis, some of which filled and expanded apparent dermal blood vessels and had large, irregular, pleomorphic nuclei (Figure, B).
9. In addition, some neoplastic cells formed a balloon appearance.
10. No epidermotrophism was found.
11. The initial immunohistochemical stain revealed the tumor cells were positive for CD3 and negative for CD20, AE1/AE3, CK20, chromogranin A, and melan-A.
12. The Ki-67 labeling index was 70%.
13. A, Ill-defined, indurated erythematous-violaceous patches, nodules, and plaques on the head and face with sporadic erosion and brownish crusts.
14. B, The biopsy showed dilated vessels expanded by cohesive clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells (hematoxylin-eosin staining).
15. C, Immunohistochemical staining of D2-40 highlighted the exclusively lymphovascular location of the lymphoma.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Intravascular anaplastic large cell lymphoma
B: Large B-cell lymphoma
C: Metastatic carcinoma
D: Natural killer/T-cell lymphoma

1. A 2-year-old female toddler born to nonconsanguineous parents presented with multiple skin-colored subcutaneous nodules that developed 40 days after birth.
2. The lesions started on the left foot and subsequently progressed to involve the face, trunk, and extremities, with distal interphalangeal joint deformity of both hands (Figure, A).
3. The child had an older sibling with no skin ailments, and no other family members were affected.
4. Parents reported decreased oral intake, decreased activity, and delayed motor development.A, Nodules on the right hand and joint deformity.
5. B and C, Histopathological images show a granulomatous pattern, numerous foamy cells, marked collagen degeneration, and mucin deposition (hematoxylin-eosin stain).
6. D, Comma-shaped curvilinear tubular structures (yellow arrowhead).On examination, dozens of tough to hard subcutaneous skin-colored nodules ranging from 0.5 to 5 cm in diameter were observed on both sides of the nose and parts of both wrists, the knees, elbows, ankles and hips, and the trunk.
7. Symmetrical beaded subcutaneous nodules were observed in the bilateral auricles, while the mucous membrane was not involved.
8. The child weighed 8 kg (normal, 13-15 kg) and was 87 cm (normal, 91-95 cm) in length.
9. In addition, a physical examination revealed horizontal nystagmus and voice hoarseness.
10. The distal interphalangeal joints of both hands were stiff with limited extension.
11. The interphalangeal joints of the third through fifth distal segments of both feet were slightly bent.
12. A complete hematological and biochemical survey, including liver and renal function, C-reactive protein levels, thyroid function, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibodies, identified no abnormalities.
13. A magnetic resonance imaging study of the brain showed volume loss in the parietooccipital region.
14. Ultrasonographic evaluation of metacarpophalangeal joints showed multiple hypoechoic nodules on the skin of the hands.
15. Radiography showed deformities of the interphalangeal joints with soft tissue swelling.
16. A punch biopsy was obtained from 1 of the nodules (Figure, B-D).

A: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis
B: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis
C: Farber disease (disseminated lipogranuloma)
D: Rheumatoid nodules

1. An 88-year-old woman presented with persistent subretinal fluid (SRF) and enlarging pigment epithelial detachments (PEDs) in each eye following 32 near monthly injections of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
2. Ocular history included presumed exudative age-related macular degeneration.
3. Central serous chorioretinopathy was also suspected secondary to the presence of yellow subretinal deposits located within an inferior macular detachment in the right eye.
4. Visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/25 OS.
5. She had pseudophakia with an otherwise normal anterior segment examination in each eye.
6. Fundus examination was remarkable for macular PEDs and SRF in each eye.
7. There was an epiretinal membrane in the left eye.
8. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) in the right eye disclosed a central PED with SRF that extended beyond the inferior border of the PED (Figure, A).
9. Hyperreflective foci, suggestive of vitelliform material, were visible on the photoreceptors.
10. OCT in the left eye demonstrated 2 PEDs in the parafovea (Figure, B).
11. SRF was present with overlying thickening of the photoreceptors.
12. The choroid was thin in each eye.
13. Fluorescein angiography revealed punctate hyperfluorescent staining within the body of the PEDs in each eye.
14. There was no evidence of leakage in either eye.
15. Fundus autofluorescence displayed dispersed, speckled hyperautofluorescence corresponding to the potential vitelliform material and SRF in the right eye.
16. Review of the autofluorescence 3 years prior revealed boat-shaped hyperautofluorescence located in the most inferior aspect of the SRF in the right eye.
17. Optical coherence tomography with corresponding autofluorescence image is shown in each eye.
18. A, A 3000-μm-diameter pigment epithelial detachment with a 30-μm layer of subretinal fluid overlying the pigment epithelial detachment and a 140-μm layer of subretinal fluid inferior to the pigment epithelial detachment.

20. There are hyporeflective pockets within the pigment epithelial detachment possibly representing fluid.
21. B, Two 500-μm pigment epithelial detachments with subretinal fluid and thickening of the photoreceptors in the left eye.
22. An epiretinal membrane is visible.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Continue intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
B: Start photodynamic therapy
C: Perform an electrooculogram and molecular genetic testing
D: Obtain serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation test

2. Her medical history included neonatal seizures.
3. She was initially evaluated at an outside institution and was found to have bilateral symmetric vision loss with nyctalopia.
4. The onset of the symptoms was unknown.
5. At that time, her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/70 OU.
6. The patient did not receive any ophthalmological care until 2 years later, when she was seen for marked vision loss and was noted to have a BCVA of light perception in both eyes.

12. Color fundus photography showed optic disc pallor, attenuated retinal vasculature, prominent choroidal markings, and central retinal atrophy with diffusely mottled pigmentation (Figure 1B).
13. Optical coherence tomography displayed decreased retinal thickness, more prominent in the inner layers, and hyper-reflective dots in the outer retinal layers.
14. Family history included unilateral vision loss in her paternal grandmother in her late 20s.
15. Both parents were healthy and denied consanguinity.
16. The patient has 3 half sisters, all of whom are healthy.
17. A, Fundus autofluorescence discloses attenuated, narrow vasculature and diffuse peripheral patchy hypoautofluorescence.
18. B, Color fundus photograph displays optic disc pallor, attenuated retinal vasculature, prominent choroidal markings, and central retinal atrophy with diffusely mottled pigmentation.

A: Electroretinogram
B: Genetic testing

D: Muscle biopsy

1. A 50-year-old man was referred for ophthalmoplegia that developed immediately after an 8.5-hour robotic cystectomy for small cell cancer of the bladder.
2. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction.
3. He had a known enhancing central skull base lesion in sella turcica with compression of the optic chiasm and mild mass effect on the pons that was felt to be a pituitary macroadenoma (Figure).
4. His baseline examination before the cystectomy showed visual acuity of 20/20 OU with intact extraocular movements and unremarkable confrontational fields, although a mild bitemporal hemianopia was seen on automated visual fields.
5. T1-weighted coronal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast shows a 4.9 × 4.6 × 5.2-cm sellar/parasellar lobulated mass with homogenous enhancement before symptom onset (A), which became 5.3 × 5.1 × 5.3 cm and had loss of enhancement after symptom onset (B).
6. The mass caused superior displacement of the optic chiasm and had extension into the cavernous sinus bilaterally.
7. The mass also extended posteriorly and deformed the anterior aspect of the pons (not shown).
8. After symptom onset, the mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (not shown).
9. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis.
10. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing.
11. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally.
12. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark.
13. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation.
14. No exophthalmos was noted.
15. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.
16. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing.
17. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia.
18. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Orbital compartment syndrome
B: Ocular motor apraxia
C: Pituitary apoplexy
D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis

2. She denied experiencing pain, diplopia, muscle weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia, difficulty breathing, or other neurologic deficits.
3. On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, with normal color vision, visual fields, intraocular pressure, extraocular movements, alignment, and pupils.

D: Obtain orbital imaging with intravenous contrast

1. A 65-year-old woman was referred with a 6-week history of blurry vision, ocular pain, and subconjunctival yellow discoloration in the left eye.
2. Suspicious retinal detachment and intraocular mass were identified, which raised concerns for choroidal melanoma.
3. No symptoms or signs were reported in the right eye.
4. Her ocular history included bilateral cataract surgery 5 years prior.
5. Review of systems yielded negative results, including for ocular trauma, jaundice, and cutaneous melanoma.
6. She had no history of tobacco use.
7. On examination of the left eye, visual acuity was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 8 mm Hg.
8. The anterior segment showed diffuse conjunctival chemosis of yellow hue, low-grade aqueous reaction, and pseudophakia (Figure 1A).
9. On the fundus evaluation, large pockets of subretinal fluid suggested choroidal effusion based on marked fluid shifting with head position.
10. B-scan ultrasonography confirmed 4-quadrant choroidal hemorrhage and partially mobile serous retinal detachment.
11. B-scans also exhibited a solid lesion from the 6- to 10-o’clock meridians with irregular shape and variable internal reflectivity, measuring 5.8 mm in height.
12. Magnetic resonance imaging was requested to delineate the mass from the surrounding clot (Figure 1B).
13. In the interim, she received oral steroids aiming to contain the abundant exudation and topical atropine for pain, evolving with minimal clinical improvement on these features.
14. Coloration changes in the left eye associated with choroidal hemorrhage and an intraocular solid lesion.
15. B, The arrowhead indicates the lesion and the asterisk, the adjacent clot.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Investigate liver dysfunction and biliary tract obstruction
B: Drain the hemorrhage with scleral windows
C: Treat with plaque brachytherapy
D: Rule out an occult systemic neoplasm

1. An otherwise healthy man in his 20s presented to the dermatology department with thickening and swelling of hands after immersion in water, accompanied by burning pruritus for 3 years.
2. The lesions occurred as symmetrical white and transparent papules, white keratosis, excessive wrinkling on the dorsum of hands after water immersion and worsened in summer, and remitted in winter.
3. He was treated with topical tretinoin ointment intermittently per a diagnosis of chronic eczema at the local clinic with little improvement.
4. The lesions gradually aggravated, and the affected area dispersed to wrists and elbows during past the 1.5 years.
5. He attributed these changes to the need for washing hands frequently in the period of the COVID-19 epidemic.
6. He had no family history of similar skin problems and did not have a history of hyperhidrosis, cystic fibrosis, atopy, or trauma to the hands.
7. Physical examination showed some changes emerged on both hands after water immersion contrasting with any other condition (Figure, A and B).
8. We took a skin biopsy specimen from white papules on the right hand, and representative histopathologic features are shown in the Figure, C and D.
9. A and B, After immersing both hands in water for 10 mins, there were symmetrical white papules, white hyperkeratosis spots, and excessive wrinkling on the thenar eminence, wrist flexure of both hands, and dorsum of fingers and hands.
10. C and D, A skin biopsy taken from white papules after water immersion for 10 mins showed hyperkeratosis, dilated eccrine ducts in the epidermis and dermis, and hyperplasia of the eccrine sweat glanda (hematoxylin-eosin).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Eczema
B: Aquagenic syringeal acrokeratoderma
C: Hereditary papulotranslucent acrokeratoderma
D: Progressive symmetric erythrokeratoderma

question:
1. On the day of giving birth via a normal vaginal delivery, a healthy woman in her 20s developed painful swelling on her right thigh, at the site of a methergine injection administered 1 day prior.
2. Despite 3 days of treatment with an oral antibiotic (cefalexin), her thigh pain and swelling did not improve, and she was readmitted to the hospital and intravenous clindamycin was started.
3. Wound cultures and blood cultures obtained during incision and drainage performed on hospital day 1 were negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal organisms.
4. The following day, her temperature was 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), blood pressure was 86/42 mm Hg, and heart rate was 131/min.
5. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for presumed septic shock, and her antibiotics were changed to vancomycin and meropenem.
6. Surgical debridement of the right thigh was performed on hospital day 3.
7. On hospital day 4, a new purple dusky border developed along the wound edge, and the patent underwent a second surgical debridement.
8. After debridement on hospital day 5, her temperature was 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), and she required vasopressor infusion with norepinephrine for shock.
9. Her right thigh had a deep 9 × 8–cm ulcer with a dusky violaceous border extending 2 to 5 cm from the wound edge (Figure, left), with many 1- to 2-mm pustules (not visible in Figure).
10. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 30 000/μL (88% neutrophils); lactate level, 77.5 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L); and procalcitonin level, 16.1 ng/mL (reference, <0.1 ng/mL).
11. Histologic examination of the tissue obtained during the second surgical debridement revealed ulceration with extensive neutrophilic inflammation (Figure, right).
12. Stains for microorganisms, and tissue and blood cultures, remained negative.
13. Left, Patient’s right thigh showing characteristic violaceous border surrounding the surgical wound edge after multiple debridements.
14. Right, Histopathologic examination of excised tissue showing dense dermal neutrophilic infiltration (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Add intravenous amphotericin B
B: Further surgical debridement
C: Start hyperbaric oxygen therapy
D: Start intravenous glucocorticoids

1. A White woman in her 40s was referred to an outside ophthalmologist after developing nausea and a headache following a dilated eye examination.
2. She was found to have narrow angles in both eyes and a laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) was performed in her left eye.
3. Two weeks later she developed flickering photopsias and a temporal scotoma progressing to a “brown tint” of her vision in her left eye.
4. Her vision had decreased in her left eye and macular and optic nerve edema were noted and she was subsequently referred to us.
5. In our clinic, her visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/50 OS, and she had normal intraocular pressure, a shallow anterior chamber but open angle in both eyes, a patent LPI in the left eye, and clear crystalline lenses in both eyes.
6. The rest of her anterior segment was unremarkable.
7. The posterior examination was notable for shifting subretinal fluid with choroidal detachments without retinal breaks, inflammation, or optic nerve edema and leopard spotting, while her right eye was unremarkable (Figure, A).
8. Fluorescein angiography was unrevealing, while optical coherence tomography showed shallow subretinal fluid and an irregular and thickened choroid (Figure, B).
9. Ultrasonography showed an axial length of 20.0 mm, thickened sclera, anteriorly rotated ciliary body, and 360° of ciliochoroidal detachments in both eyes but worse in the left eye.
10. Results of a systemic laboratory evaluation for infectious and noninfectious disorders were unremarkable.
11. Systemic corticosteroids failed to resolve the subretinal fluid and her vision declined.Subretinal fluid and choroidal effusions following a laser peripheral iridotomy.
12. A, Fundus photography showed substantial choroidal effusions with overlying serous retinal detachments (asterisk).
13. B, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging identified choroidal congestion, thickening, and undulations as well as shallow subretinal fluid.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Repeat LPI in the left eye
B: Perform an LPI in the right eye
C: Sclerectomy in the left eye
D: Perform a clear lens exchange in the left eye

1. A white man in his early 80s with history of autoimmune pancreatitis, recurrent colon polyps, and benign prostatic hyperplasia developed rapid, painless vision loss of both eyes over a 2-week period 6 months after cataract surgery.
2. Vision was 20/250 OD and 20/60 OS.
3. The anterior segment was unremarkable in either eye, while the posterior segment examination noted 1+ vitreous cell, asteroid hyalosis, and a multilobulated, serous retinal detachment (RD) in the right eye and trace vitreous cell and a multilobulated, serous RD in the left eye.
4. Imaging included B-scan, optical coherence tomography, and fundus autofluorescence, which revealed diffuse choroidal and ciliary body thickening, multifocal pockets of subretinal fluid, and speckled hyperautofluorescence and hypoautofluorescence in both eyes (Figure 1).
5. No poliosis or skin changes were noted.
6. A review of systems was unremarkable, most notably a lack of any pulmonary symptoms.
7. A focused laboratory evaluation identified a significantly elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level and antinuclear antibody titer, but serum lysozyme, syphilis, and tuberculosis testing had negative results.
8. To better differentiate between Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome, a lymphoproliferative disorder, or sarcoidosis as the underlying cause of the vitreous inflammation and multilobulated, serous RD in both eyes, a computed tomographic scan was performed.
9. It showed marked lymphadenopathy throughout the mediastinum and diffuse scleral thickening in both eyes.
10. The institute’s radiologists believed these computed tomography findings were nonspecific and could be indicative of either sarcoidosis or intraocular lymphoma.Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome–like presentation of multilobulated pockets of subretinal fluid and choroidal thickening and undulations.
11. A, Serous retinal detachment (asterisk).
12. B, Substantial choroidal thickening (asterisk) and undulations and multilobulated subretinal fluid (arrowheads).

A: Perform a diagnostic vitrectomy in the right eye
B: Inject intravitreal antibiotics for endophthalmitis in both eyes
C: Perform ciliary body–choroidal biopsy in the right eye
D: Treat the patient with systemic steroids for presumed VKH syndrome

question:
1. A 55-year-old man with advanced primary open-angle glaucoma presented with 1 day of decreased vision and eye pain.
2. He had undergone trabeculectomy and 5-fluorouracil injection 1 month prior.
3. On initial examination, his visual acuity was 20/25.
4. He had diffuse conjunctival hyperemia without bleb purulence or leakage and more than 50 cells per high-power field of a 1 × 1-mm area of light on slitlamp biomicroscopy.
5. He was treated for blebitis with topical fortified antibiotics but subsequently developed vitritis.
6. He underwent vitreous tap and injection of vancomycin and amikacin followed by pars plana vitrectomy with bleb revision.
7. Separate vitreous samples from each procedure were sent for Gram stain and bacterial and fungal culture on chocolate and Sabouraud agar with no growth.
8. His eye pain worsened significantly, and ultrasound biomicroscopy showed scleral thickening (Figure 1A).
9. Lab workup for autoimmune scleritis including tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies was negative.
10. He was admitted to the hospital and started intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam treatment.
11. His vision continued to decline to counting fingers because of the development of a dense cataract with retrolenticular plaque (Figure 1B).
12. A, Episcleral and scleral thickening (yellow brackets) adjacent to normal tissue (white brackets) on ultrasound biomicroscopy.
13. B, Retrolenticular plaque (yellow arrowhead) and vitreous debris (white arrowhead) on inferotemporal longitudinal B-scan.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start topical and systemic steroids
B: Switch to intravenous meropenem
C: Repeat aqueous or vitreous sampling
D: Observe while receiving current therapy

1. A woman in her 40s with a medical history of multiple sclerosis consulted for the sudden development of 2 adjacent nodules on the left arm.
2. An excision with 1-cm margins of the left arm demonstrated desmoplastic melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1 mm, and a left axillary sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) had been performed 3 weeks before under general anesthesia.
3. The patient was also being treated with subcutaneous interferon beta 1a for the multiple sclerosis.
4. Physical examination revealed 2 indurated and mobile subcutaneous nodules on the anterior surface of the arm 5 cm distal to the surgical scar, the larger of them measuring 15 mm in diameter (Figure, A) and the smaller of them measuring 4 mm.
5. When the arm was abducted to 90°, the patient denied pain but described a subtle tightness sensation on the arm.
6. An excisional biopsy from the larger lesion was performed (Figure, B-D).
7. A, Clinical image showing indurated and mobile subcutaneous nodule on the anterior surface of the arm.
8. Arrowheads highlight a subtle linear plaque adjacent to the nodule.
9. B, Histopathologic image showing dilated and thrombosed lymphatic vessels in subcutaneous tissue with recanalization (hematoxylin-eosin).
10. C, Histopathologic image of partially thrombosed vessels.
11. D, Immunohistochemistry finding was positive for D2-40 (podoplanin).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia
B: Pseudo-aneurysmal metastasis of melanoma
C: Axillary web syndrome
D: Traumatic humeral pseudo-aneurysm

12. Otherwise, findings of his anterior examination and dilated fundoscopic examination were normal.External photographs show bilateral upper eyelid ecchymosis and edema, temporal subconjunctival hemorrhage of the right eye, and a right temple mass (asterisk).
13. Reassurance and treatment with cool compresses and artificial tears

A: Brain/orbital imaging
B: Reassurance and treatment with cool compresses and artificial tears

12. question:
1. A woman in her 20s was referred for evaluation of a 4-year history of recurrent pustular eruptions on her face, which initially presented while she was vacationing in Florida.
2. She noted mild associated pruritus but denied burning sensation.
3. The eruptions occurred intermittently, appearing as erythematous papules with prominent pustules, and were exacerbated by sunlight.
4. On average, her lesions would resolve in 3 to 4 days with only mild background erythema by 5 to 7 days.
5. Even mild sun exposure would induce the eruption, leading to frequent recurrences in summer months but long periods of remission in the fall through spring.
6. Trials with various broad-spectrum sunscreens in combination with topical and oral antibiotics and topical ivermectin did not prevent flares or mitigate severity of eruptions when they occurred.
7. She denied joint pain, fever, fatigue, changes in urine color, use of other topical or systemic medications, or presence of rashes elsewhere.
8. She was otherwise healthy without other medical history.
9. On physical examination, she was well appearing with numerous 1- to 2-mm monomorphous pustules over background erythema on the medial cheeks, chin, and nose (Figure, A).
10. No nail fold capillary changes or mucosal lesions were observed.
11. Serum analysis results for antinuclear, anti-SSA/Ro, and anti-SSB/La antibodies were negative.
12. A 4-mm punch biopsy was taken from a representative lesion along the right jawline (Figure, B-D).
13. A, Pustular eruption of the face characterized by monomorphous 1- to 2-mm pustules over background erythema on the cheeks, chin, and nose appearing less than 24 hours after sun exposure.
14. Punch biopsy of skin demonstrated intrafollicular (B and C) and subcorneal (B and D) pustule formation (hematoxylin-eosin).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Papulopustular rosacea
B: Pinpoint papular light eruption
C: Actinic folliculitis
D: Acute localized exanthematous pustulosis

2. She denied any history of fever, head trauma, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or cough.
3. She had traveled to northeastern Brazil 2 months before the onset of the neurological symptoms.
4. On examination, she had a mild right-side hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and hemiataxia.
5. She could walk unassisted but presented with a broad base.
6. There were no meningeal signs.
7. She did not present with hepatosplenomegaly of lymphadenopathy.
8. Her cranial magnetic resonance imaging showed a T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesion with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement in the pons (Figure).
9. There were no signs of diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging or hemorrhages on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
10. Sagittal gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and sagittal T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) (B) showing the extent of the lesion.
11. The laboratory test results showed a hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10.0), total leukocyte count of 10 390/uL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001), of which 1703 (16.4%) were eosinophils, and a platelet count of 284 000/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001).
12. The patient’s liver and kidney function test results were normal.
13. Computed tomography of the chest revealed bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates.
14. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 640 cells, of which 57% were lymphocytes, 26% were eosinophils, and 13% were monocytes; protein levels were 70 mg/dL, and glucose levels were 46 mg/dL.
15. Her blood cultures were found to be sterile.

A: Listeriosis
B: Neuroschistosomiasis

2. He had no fevers or night sweats.
3. Physical examination was notable for oral thrush and mild epigastric tenderness.
4. Results of a fourth-generation HIV Ab/Ag combination assay were positive, and subsequent testing showed a CD4 cell count of 16/mm3 and an HIV viral load greater than 10 million copies/mL.
5. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed thickening of the walls of the stomach, duodenum, and colon as well as multiple masses in the right hepatic lobe measuring up to 6.9 cm in diameter.
6. A core biopsy of one of the liver masses demonstrated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

9. Mesenteric computed tomography angiography demonstrated active extravasation in the jejunum from a branch of the superior mesenteric artery.
10. 11. Five weeks later, he developed blurred vision, and visual acuity testing revealed 20/50 vision in the left eye and 20/70 in the right eye.
12. A dilated retinal examination revealed extensive macular hemorrhage in the left eye, with peripapillary whitening and perivascular hemorrhage with whitening along the superior vascular arcade (Figure, right panel).

B: Perform vitreal sampling for cytology and flow cytometry

D: Begin azathioprine and infliximab

1. A 51-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of intense and worsening polyarthralgia and swelling of bilateral fingers and toes.
2. There was no history of alopecia, oral ulcers, rashes, or Raynaud phenomenon.
3. She did not report preceding fever, diarrhea, or dysuria.
4. There was no history of weight loss or anorexia.
5. Medical history included tertiary hyperparathyroidism related to end-stage kidney disease from chronic glomerulonephritis.
6. The patient had successfully received an ABO-incompatible kidney transplant 1 year ago, but this was complicated by invasive fungal (Volvariella volvacea) infection of the central nervous system.
7. Medications included tacrolimus (0.5 mg twice daily), prednisolone (10 mg daily), cinacalcet (12.5 mg daily), and voriconazole (500 mg daily).
8. On examination, her fingers and toes were symmetrically and diffusely swollen and tender.
9. There was no rash, enthesitis, psoriatic nail changes, clubbing, or lower limb edema.
10. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
11. Alkaline phosphatase level was elevated at 640 U/L (10.69 μkat/L) (reference range, 40-130 U/L [0.67-2.17 μkat/L]).
12. Corrected calcium and parathyroid hormone levels were 10.88 mg/dL (2.71 mmol/L) (reference range, 8.6-10.2 mg/dL [2.15-2.55 mmol/L]) and 23.7 pmol/L (reference range, 1.3-9.3), respectively.
13. Serum bilirubin, aspartate transferase, alanine transferase, creatinine, and phosphate levels were within reference ranges.
14. Free thyroxine and thyrotropin levels were normal.
15. Results of testing for rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated protein antibody were negative.
16. Her chest radiograph was unremarkable.
17. Radiography of her hands was performed

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain a positron emission computed tomography scan
B: Perform a bone biopsy
C: Schedule parathyroidectomy
D: Stop voriconazole

What Would You Do Next?

A: Measure C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
B: Measure blood glucose levels
C: Perform lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid contents
D: Perform magnetic resonance angiography of the head

9. Repeated MRI showed progression of the lesion with masslike expansion at the chiasm measuring 1.3 cm (anterior-posterior) × 1.5 cm (craniocaudal) × 1.1 cm (transverse).

2. Results of a previous intestinal biopsy had shown unspecific findings and absence of apoptosis.
3. He reported a 5-kg weight loss that he attributed to impaired intake owing to the oral lesions.
4. He was also being evaluated for a mediastinal mass detected in radiography of the chest performed for pneumonia.
5. Physical examination revealed whitish edematous lacy patches with erosions on the dorsal and lateral aspects of the tongue and buccal mucosa (Figure, A); skin and nails were not involved.
6. A lingual biopsy specimen was obtained for pathologic evaluation and direct immunofluorescence (DIF; Figure, B and C).
7. The result of indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) testing, using monkey esophagus, salt-skin split, and rat bladder as substrates, was negative.
8. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and immunoblot analysis did not detect any desmoglein-1 or -3, bullous pemphigoid-180 or -230, collagen VII, desmocollin-1 to -3, laminin-332, envoplakin, or periplakin antibodies.
9. Results were normal for liver function; negative for hepatitis B and C; indicative of hypogammaglobulinemia, with a decreased immunoglobulin (Ig) G serum level of 465 mg/dL (normal, 750-1600 g/L; for g/L, multiply by 0.01); and normal for IgA and IgM levels.
10. Positron emission tomography revealed a 10-cm hypercapturing extrapulmonary mass (Figure, D).
11. Surgical excision of the mediastinal mass was performed; its histopathologic features were consistent with a type AB thymoma, Masaoka-Koga stage 2A.A, Lacy, white erosive lesions on the tongue.
12. B, Epidermis with acanthosis, parakeratosis, necrotic keratinocytes, and dermal band lymphocytic infiltrate with effacement of the dermoepidermal junction (hematoxylin-eosin).
13. C, Fibrogen deposition along the basement membrane.

B: Thymoma-associated multiorgan autoimmunity
C: Good syndrome
D: Paraneoplastic lichen planus

B: Prescribe azithromycin
C: Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test
D: Treat with an oral antifungal medication

question:
1. An 80-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset bilateral horizontal diplopia accompanied by left-sided upper eyelid ptosis.
2. On further questioning, she reported a 1-week history of drooling when eating.
3. She had no other associated neurological or constitutional symptoms.
4. No anhidrosis was noted.
5. Her medical history was significant for a 2-year history of constant, dull, left-sided facial pain diagnosed as trigeminal neuralgia by her treating neurologist and moderately improved with gabapentin and nortriptyline.
6. Recent computed tomography (CT) of the brain, conducted as part of her headache workup, had been reported as normal.
7. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 OU.
8. Extraocular motility testing demonstrated no abduction of the left eye with corresponding large-angle incomitant esotropia increasing when looking to the left (Figure 1).
9. There was 2 mm of left upper eyelid ptosis with preserved levator function.
10. The left pupil was 1 mm smaller than the right in the light, with the difference increasing to 2 mm in the dark.
11. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect.
12. Cranial nerve examination demonstrated reduced sensation in the left V1-V3 distribution and mild flattening of the nasolabial fold.
13. Corneal sensation was slightly decreased on the left.
14. Intraocular examination, including dilated fundus examination, was normal in both eyes.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain CT angiography of head and neck
B: Perform lumbar puncture to analyze cellular composition of cerebrospinal fluid
C: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast
D: Order tests of inflammatory markers: erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and complete blood cell count

11. His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.

A: Discontinue apixaban
B: Discontinue minocycline

question:
1. A 47-year-old woman, with dyslipidemia, presented to the emergency department with sudden vision loss in the right eye.
2. Visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/20 OS.
3. Anterior segment, tonometry, and pupillary light reflex were unremarkable.
4. Ophthalmoscopy of the right eye showed discretely blurred optic disc margins, tortuous and dilated retinal veins, and intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants; the left eye was unremarkable.
5. An optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan showed a cystoid macular edema (CME) in the right eye; the left was unremarkable.
6. Retinal nerve fiber layer thickness was 133 μm OD and 82 μm OS (reference value, 95.4 ± 10.48 μm).
7. A fluorescein angiography was scheduled.
8. One week later, the patient returned to our department due to multiple episodes of amaurosis fugax in left eye.
9. By that time, ophthalmoscopy disclosed a mild optic disc swelling, tortuous venous vessels, and retinal hemorrhages bilaterally.
10. The OCT scan showed a CME spontaneous resolution in the right eye while the left eye was unremarkable.
11. Fluorescein angiography revealed a slight delay in venous filling but no capillary nonperfusion areas.
12. These features were compatible with bilateral nonischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), with spontaneous reperfusion in the right eye.
13. Fundus photography of the right and left eyes showing slightly elevated and blurred optic disc margins, mildly tortuous and dilated retinal vessels, and intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants in both eyes.
14. In the left eye, a superficial optic nerve drusen was noted.
15. A hypercoagulability and autoimmune workup—including peripheral blood smear, complete blood cell count, serum hyperviscosity, total protein level, protein electrophoresis, factor V Leiden, prothrombin, protein C and S, antithrombin, anticardiolipin, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies—gave normal results.
16. A brain angiomagnetic resonance imaging scan was performed, which excluded central thrombosis.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Initiate panretinal photocoagulation
B: Perform a thoracoabdominopelvic computed tomography scan
C: Follow-up without further intervention
D: Initiate acetylsalicylic acid and no further intervention

question:
1. A 42-year-old woman was referred for ophthalmologic evaluation after developing blurry vision in the right eye 30 days prior.
2. She had a history of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and migraine headaches.
3. Her medications included atorvastatin, carvedilol, and norethindrone.
4. Dilated-fundus examination of the right eye showed a single cotton-wool spot (indicating local retinal ischemia), with intraretinal hemorrhage in the inferotemporal quadrant.
5. Ultrawide-field imaging showed a cotton-wool spot on the left fundus (Figure 1A, right) and a peripheral arterial occlusion in the right eye (Figure 1A, left), and fluorescein angiographic study of the right eye demonstrated an area of blockage corresponding to intraretinal hemorrhage and venous hyperfluorescence (Figure 1B).
6. The patient was afebrile, with pulse 110 beats/min and blood pressure of 188/99 mm Hg.
7. Auscultation over the heart apex revealed a holosystolic ejection murmur (grade 2/6).
8. Laboratory testing showed normal complete blood cell count and thyrotropin level and negative results for autoantibodies against Sm, SSA, SSB, Scl-70, Jo-1, centromere, chromatin, ribonucleoprotein, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies.
9. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated (30 mm/h).
10. Results of testing for antinuclear antibodies were positive at low titer (1:40, homogenous pattern) with positive dsDNA (5.0 IU/mL; negative if <4.0 IU/mL).
11. Blood cultures were negative for bacterial or fungal growth after 5 days.
12. An echocardiogram revealed pedunculated and mobile aortic valve vegetations.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Administer intravenous antibiotics
B: Administer systemic corticosteroids
C: Administer anticoagulant therapy
D: Check antiphospholipid antibody levels

question:
1. A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertensive retinopathy presented with acute-onset, painless vision loss in his right eye accompanied by tinnitus and severe intermittent headaches.
2. His extraocular movements were full, and he had no other neurologic deficits.
3. His visual acuity was 20/400 OD and 20/30 OS, respectively, and his fundi were notable for bilateral optic nerve edema.
4. Results of recent computed tomography and angiography of the head and neck and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits were reportedly normal, and lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 26 cm H2O (normal range, 6 to 25 cm H2O) with elevated protein.
5. The patient was given acetazolamide and referred to neuro-ophthalmology.
6. On examination by neuro-ophthalmology 4 months later, his visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS.
7. He had an afferent pupillary defect in the right eye, and Humphrey visual fields (24-2) showed binasal inferior defects with a superior defect in the right eye that was considered an artifact of testing.
8. According to the Ishihara color plates test, color vision was full in both eyes.
9. Fundus examination was remarkable for pallor of both optic nerves, more notably in the right eye, without edema (Figure 1).
10. Findings of screening for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, angiotensin-converting enzyme, Bartonella, HIV, tuberculosis (Quantiferon), Treponema pallidum, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and a complete blood cell count were normal.
11. Color fundus photographs demonstrate optic nerve pallor, which was greater in the right eye than the left eye.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Advise tighter blood pressure control
B: Repeated lumbar puncture with serologies
C: Start high-dose corticosteroids
D: Continue acetazolamide and repeated Humphrey visual fields test and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer in 3 months

2. Four weeks following receipt of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab, he developed acute abdominal pain in the setting of a rapidly rising lactic acid dehydrogenase levels, prompting hospital admission.
3. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node).
4. Splenic infarct and portal/splenic vein thrombi were identified as etiologies of his acute pain and were presumed to be secondary to hypercoagulable state of malignancy.
5. Over the next 3 days, he had rising serum creatinine (sCr) levels (baseline, approximately 1 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]).
6. The initial workup included ultrasonography and urinalysis.
7. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis.
8. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis.
9. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued.
10. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed.
11. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis.
12. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure).
13. One week later, he received encorafenib, a BRAF inhibitor.
14. Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued.
15. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation.
16. Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).
17. Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced acute interstitial nephritis
B: Postinfectious glomerulonephritis
C: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to kidney melanoma metastasis
D: Drug-induced acute tubular necrosis

1. A woman in her 70s presented with a 3-month history of episodic fever and painless cutaneous lesions on her lower limbs.
2. The patient otherwise felt well and denied malaise, weight loss, or any other symptoms.
3. She did not have any known benign inflammatory conditions.
4. Physical examination showed indurated plaques with multiple telangiectasias (Figure, A and B) on almost all the surface of the legs.
5. Except for slightly elevated C-reactive protein levels, the results of other routine blood and urine tests were unremarkable.
6. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathology examination (Figure, C and D).
7. A, Indurated violaceous plaques with multiple telangiectasias on the lower limbs.
8. B, Prominent telangiectasia on the thigh.
9. C, Histopathologic analysis shows large round cells proliferating within dermal blood vessels (hematoxylin-eosin).
10. D, Round cells with scanty cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli filling a vessel (hematoxylin-eosin).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Intralymphatic histiocytosis
B: Reactive angioendotheliomatosis
C: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma
D: Intralymphatic proliferation of T-cell lymphoid blasts

question:
1. A school-aged boy experienced generalized erythematous rashes for 4 years.
2. Skin examination showed ichthyosiform brownish plaques on his lower extremities and multiple erythematous confluent papules and plaques on his trunk and face (Figure, A and B).
3. Topical steroid and pimecrolimus were administered, but their effects were limited.
4. In addition, painful distal and proximal interphalangeal joints were noted for 2 years, and the patient could not clench his fists.
5. Uveitis in both eyes was also diagnosed by an ophthalmologist.
6. Microscopic examination of his hair showed no trichorrhexis invaginata or trichorrhexis nodosa.
7. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained and submitted for further histopathologic analysis (Figure, C and D).
8. A, Diffuse erythematous papules and plaques with mild scaling and some confluence on the face, neck, and trunk.
9. B, Ichthyosiform rashes predominantly distributed over the lower extremities.
10. C, Tissue biopsy results revealed multiple circumscribed nests of granulomas that were infiltrating the dermis and subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin).
11. D, At higher magnification, histologic findings showed noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and neutrophil infiltration in the dermis and subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Ichthyosis vulgaris
B: Netherton syndrome
C: Pityriasis rubra pilaris
D: Blau syndrome

question:
1. A 71-year-old woman with non-Hodgkin lymphoma receiving maintenance obinutuzumab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) infusions underwent uneventful pars plana vitrectomy of the right eye for vitreomacular traction.
2. Diluted triamcinolone acetonide (TA) was used to stain the posterior hyaloid.
3. After removal of 25-gauge trocar cannulas, subconjunctival TA and ceftazidime was injected.
4. Owing to cystoid changes in the central macula, a short-acting gas tamponade with sulfur hexafluoride was used to tamponade any cystoid abnormalities that may have been unroofed.
5. Despite unremarkable postoperative day 1 (POD1) examination findings, the patient presented on postoperative week 3 with a painless central scotoma and worsening floaters.
6. Her visual acuity was 20/400 OD and intraocular pressure was normal.
7. There was no external hyperemia or chemosis, and the anterior chamber was deep and quiet with no cells or flare.
8. On dilated fundus examination, there were 15 to 20 cells per high-power field (using a 1 × 1-mm2 high-intensity incidental slit beam) and a white macular lesion with disc edema and scattered intraretinal and peripapillary hemorrhages and mixed venous and arterial sheathing.
9. Optical coherence tomography of the macula showed atrophy, full-thickness hyperreflectivity, and a residual epiretinal membrane (Figure).
10. Color fundus photograph (A) of the right eye demonstrating white macular lesion and optic disc edema with scattered intraretinal and peripapillary hemorrhages and vascular sheathing (white arrowheads).
11. The dashed yellow line shows the location of spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) (B), which shows full-thickness hyperreflectivity and atrophy, epiretinal membrane (yellow arrowheads), and vitreous cells and debris (red arrowheads).
12. Perform vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal antibiotics Review medical records to see if gentamicin was given intraoperatively Urgently refer patient to emergency department for embolic stroke workup Begin valganciclovir hydrochloride therapy and sample intraocular fluid for polymerase chain reaction testing

A: Perform vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal antibiotics
B: Review medical records to see if gentamicin was given intraoperatively
