question:
1. An 82-year-old man with an ocular history significant for bilateral nuclear sclerotic cataracts presented to the Cornea Service at Bascom Palmer Eye Institute, Miami, Florida, with a history of blurred vision in the right eye after phacoemulsification cataract extraction 8 weeks earlier.
2. Current ophthalmic medications included topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, in the right eye 6 times per day.
3. The patient reported no improvement with the treatment.
4. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS.
5. Pupils were reactive without relative afferent pupillary defect, and intraocular pressures were 18 mm Hg in the right eye and 11 mm Hg in the left eye.
6. A slitlamp biomicroscopic examination of the right eye revealed grade 2 to 3 diffuse central corneal edema and folds (Figure 1).
7. The anterior chamber was deep and the posterior chamber intraocular lens was in good position within the capsular bag.
8. Although the view to the posterior pole of the right eye was hazy owing to corneal edema, dilated fundus examination findings were unremarkable.
9. Examination of the left eye revealed a few guttate.
10. The central corneal thickness by ultrasound pachymetry was 957 μm in the right eye and 547 μm in the left eye.Slitlamp biomicroscopic photographs of the right eye show central corneal edema with diffuse illumination (A) and with slitbeam illumination (B).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform penetrating keratoplasty
B: Provide medical management with topical corticosteroids and hypertonic saline solution for an additional 3 months
C: Obtain an anterior-segment optical coherence tomogram
D: Perform an endothelial keratoplasty (Descemet stripping and endothelial keratoplasty or Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty)

question:
1. A 49-year-old African American man who was hospitalized with hypervolemia due to supraventricular tachycardia presented with acute unilateral painless vision loss.
2. His active medical problems included atrial flutter on anticoagulation, antisynthetase syndrome (which was diagnosed based on the presence of autoantibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase), fever with negative infectious workup results, and interstitial lung disease that was managed with azathioprine.
3. Two weeks before the onset of sudden vision loss, the patient developed a rapidly evolving purpuric rash on his hands and feet that progressed to digital ischemia (Figure 1A).
4. He was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, which was completed 3 days before the onset of loss of vision and transitioned to treatment with azathioprine, 150 mg, and prednisone, 80 mg, that he was taking at the time of his vision loss.Cutaneous and retinal vasculitis.
5. A, Purpuric rash involving the left foot.
6. B, Montage fundus photograph of the left eye shows frosted branch angiitis with preretinal hemorrhages over the disc (arrowhead) and macula (arrowhead), intraretinal hemorrhages, perivenular exudates, and sheathing.On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was 20/20 OD and hand motions OS (baseline from 2 weeks prior was 20/20 OU), with a briskly reactive right pupil and a left afferent pupillary defect.
7. Left eye examination revealed 2 or more anterior chamber cells, preretinal hemorrhage, frosted branch angiitis with diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages, and perivascular exudates (Figure 1B).
8. Fluorescein angiography results revealed extensive vascular nonperfusion and late perivenular leakage.
9. The right eye was normal.Laboratory workup results revealed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 85 mm per hour, C-reactive protein levels of 2.53 mg/dL (to convert to milligrams per liter, multiply by 10), negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies test result, antinuclear antibodies, cryoglobulins, syphilis serology, tuberculosis testing, and transthoracic echocardiogram.
10. Skin biopsy results showed medium vessel vasculitis.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Escalate systemic immunosuppression
B: Diagnostic anterior chamber paracentesis and intravitreal foscarnet
C: Peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry
D: Whole-body positron emission tomography–computed tomography

4. One month before presentation, she was hospitalized for acute cellular transplant rejection managed with systemic corticosteroids, belatacept, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus therapies.

12. Total body skin examination was notable for 1- and 3-cm tender, round perianal ulcers with a clean base.
13. Another 4-mm round ulcer was present at the superior intergluteal cleft (Figure, A).
14. There were no ocular or oral ulcers.

21. Abdominal computed tomography revealed no abnormalities.

B: Check for fecal ova and parasites

question:
1. A 50-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, heroin use, and alcohol use disorder presented with a new epithelial defect in the setting of a healing right corneal ulcer.
2. Six days prior, he had presented with an inferior stromal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect, diffuse corneal edema, and a small hypopyon with no hemorrhage in the anterior chamber (Figure 1A).
3. He also had patchy iris hemorrhages with no transillumination defects and areas of conjunctival ulceration nasally and temporally.
4. He denied contact lens use.
5. Given these findings, a presumed herpes zoster sine herpete1 with secondary bacterial infection was suspected.
6. Treatment with hourly topical vancomycin at 14 mg/mL and tobramycin at 25 mg/mL, as well as 1000 mg of oral valacyclovir 3 times a day, was initiated.
7. Corneal cultures grew Streptococcus pneumonia.
8. He initially responded well with improvement of the stromal infiltrate and overlying epithelial defect.
9. However, on day 6 of treatment, he had a new larger epithelial defect and subepithelial bullae in an adjacent location but no infiltrate.
10. While evaluating the new defect, the patient was also noted to have dull conjunctival reflexes and bulbar conjunctival lesions in both eyes (Figure 1B).
11. Additionally, both eyes had patchy interpalpebral results on lissamine green staining of the conjunctiva and clinically significant punctate epithelial erosions of the cornea with fluorescein staining.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Continue treatment with current topical antibiotics.
B: Repeat the corneal cultures with Lowenstein-Jensen medium.
C: Obtain serum anti-Ro and anti-La tests.
D: Obtain serum vitamin levels.

2. Her medical history was significant for hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine, as well as 2 forms of hematologic malignancy: retroperitoneal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma and indolent-phase T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.
3. She had received no treatment for her hematologic malignancies, as she had been asymptomatic since her diagnoses 6 years prior.
4. Ophthalmological examination revealed 27 mm of bilateral proptosis, conjunctival injection, chemosis, and bilateral lower eyelid retraction (Figure 1A).
5. Visual acuity, color vision, and pupillary responses were normal.
6. Extraocular motility was full in all positions of gaze, and there was no associated pain.
7. Upper eyelid retraction was minimal.
8. Von Graefe sign (delayed descent of the upper eyelid with initiation of downgaze) and lagophthalmos were absent.
9. Results of slitlamp examination and dilated fundus examination were normal, including the appearance of both optic nerves.
10. A, Clinical photograph at presentation; bilateral proptosis, lower eyelid retraction, chemosis, and conjunctival injection are present.
11. There is mild temporal retraction of both upper eyelids.
12. B, Radiographic images documenting marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles bilaterally.
13. The lateral rectus is especially enlarged on both sides.
14. Using a measurement technique described by Dagi and colleagues, the maximal diameter of each extraocular muscle in this patient was as follows: right inferior rectus, 8.0 mm; right medial rectus, 9.1 mm; right superior muscle group, 9.7 mm; right lateral rectus, 9.3 mm; left inferior rectus, 8.1 mm; left medial rectus, 9.5 mm; left superior muscle group, 10.0 mm; and left lateral rectus, 9.6 mm.
15. There is sparing of anterior tendinous insertions (arrowheads) of each medial rectus (MR) and lateral rectus (LR).
16. However, the anterior portion of the muscle belly (brackets) appears uninvolved compared with the posterior portion, causing an acute taper of the muscle that is similar in shape to an amphora (inset).
17. An orbital computed tomography scan revealed marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles (Figure 1B).
18. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, and thyroid peroxidase antibody levels were normal.
19. Test results for autoimmune diseases, including sarcoidosis, Sjogren syndrome, granulomatous polyangiitis, IgG4 disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, and vasculitis, were negative.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Prescribe high-dose intravenous steroids
B: Perform staged bilateral orbital decompressions
C: Perform extraocular muscle biopsy
D: Refer for bilateral orbital external beam radiation

question:
1. A 16-year-old boy with acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage developed tender, 1- to 2-cm erythematous plaques and nodules during treatment with chemotherapy.
2. Previously, he had been well, with morphological remission found on a recent bone marrow biopsy.
3. The patient had no significant dermatological history, except an allergy to cashew nuts and a prior episode (6 mo) of urticaria during a platelet transfusion that had resolved with 1 dose of oral antihistamine.
4. The patient’s medications included ondansetron, aprepitant, prednisolone, and oxycodone (supportive care initiated with chemotherapy), and long-term posaconazole and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole treatment.
5. Lesions were noted on day 2 of the fourth cycle of a chemotherapy regimen comprising fludarabine, cytarabine, and filgrastim (G-CSF).
6. Initially present over the distal limbs, palms, and soles, the lesions progressed to the proximal limbs and lower trunk during 24 hours (Figure, A and B).
7. The patient developed a fever, which we extensively investigated.
8. Intravenous cefotaxime was commenced, but because no infectious source was identified, the fever was thought to be secondary to cytarabine.
9. A and B, Clinical images showing erythematous plaques and nodules on patient’s palm and forearm.
10. C, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained specimen showing leukocytoclastic neutrophilic infiltrate in deeper dermis, around appendage structures and coiled eccrine glands, and into the interstitium.
11. The results of a complete examination of blood drawn at lesion onset demonstrated a total white cell count of 6330/μL (to convert to 109/L multiply by 0.001) with absolute neutrophil count of 6140/μL, more than the previous day’s counts of 3210/μL and 1720/μL, respectively.
12. The blood film demonstrated increased neutrophil granulation with a left shift.
13. A punch biopsy from the upper arm was performed.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Sweet syndrome
B: Urticaria
C: Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis
D: Leukemia cutis

1. A 48-year-old man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and obstructive sleep apnea presented with a rash over his right foot accompanied by 1 week of episodic fever, diaphoresis, and headaches.
2. Six weeks prior, he fell from a ladder and had right nondisplaced medial malleolar and comminuted talar fractures.
3. The fractures were managed nonsurgically in a controlled ankle movement boot, with resolution of swelling and bruising.
4. On current presentation, his temperature was 38.2 °C (100.8 °F); heart rate, 88/min; respiratory rate, 18/min; and blood pressure, 102/65 mm Hg.
5. He was well appearing with normal cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations.
6. There was trace right lower extremity edema localized to the ankle and normal pedal pulses.
7. Erythema without warmth was present over the right ankle and dorsomedial foot, along with nontender, nonpalpable purpura over the dorsum of the foot and scattered petechiae over the right lower leg (Figure).
8. question:
1. A 64-year-old man presented with concern about an abnormal genetic test result for apolipoprotein E (APOE) obtained through his primary care physician.
2. He reported forgetfulness and word-finding difficulties for 3 years but performed all activities of daily living independently and was generally healthy.
3. His father and maternal great aunt developed dementia in their 70s.
4. Physical (including neurologic) examination, basic laboratory studies, and brain magnetic resonance imaging results were normal.
5. The Short Test of Mental Status (STMS) score was 33 (maximal attainable score of 38 indicates best performance).
6. Neuropsychological assessment showed average to above-average performance in all cognitive domains, accounting for age and education.
7. Results of his genetic testing for APOE were reported as follows: “This individual possesses an apolipoprotein E genotype (3 and 4) that indicates, with high specificity, that Alzheimer’s disease is the cause of or a contributor to the observed dementia.”

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain a brain fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan.
B: Order cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing for Alzheimer disease biomarkers.
C: Reassure and address patient’s concerns and follow up in 1 year.
D: Refer for genetic counseling.

1. An 18-year-old man with unremarkable medical history was referred to the oculoplastics service for evaluation of progressive gradual-onset ptosis and ophthalmoplegia in both eyes in the past 2 years (Figure).
2. He had emigrated from Ghana 2 years before but denied any illness there.
3. His visual acuity without correction was 20/20 OD and 20/20 OS, although he had to manually elevate his eyelids to see the Snellen chart.
4. He had no movement of the right eye past midline in elevation, adduction, depression, and abduction and no movement of the left eye past midline in elevation, depression, and abduction, with 50% deficit of adduction.
5. His external examination results were notable for a margin reflex distance 1 of −4 mm OU and a levator function of 0 OU.
6. On funduscopic examination, his optic nerves were sharp and pink without atrophy, maculae and retinal vasculature were normal, and peripheral retina appeared normal without pigment abnormalities.
7. A review of systems was negative for fatigue, generalized muscle weakness, or neurologic deficits.
8. Clinical photograph of the patient, who presented with severe bilateral ptosis.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform surgical repair of ptosis with frontalis sling
B: Order neuroimaging with magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits with and without contrast
C: Order an electrocardiogram
D: Investigate for thyroid eye disease

question:
1. A 35-year-old man presented after experiencing a 5-minute episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days earlier.
2. No other accompanying symptoms were reported.
3. He had experienced painless decrease of vision in both eyes for 6 years but did not seek medical care.
4. He had had hypertension for 3 years, with amlodipine taken regularly.
5. A sibling developed uremia in their 30s.
6. A parent died of kidney failure in their 40s.
7. On results of an ophthalmic examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/40 OS, without visual field defects, dyschromatopsia, or relative afferent pupillary defect.
8. Extraocular movements were intact.
9. Neurologic examination findings were unremarkable except for mild cognitive impairment.
10. Fundus fluorescein angiography showed retinal vasculitis (Figure, A).
11. Enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed diffuse white matter hyperintensities—leukoencephalopathy—with multiple ring-enhancing lesions (Figure, B).
12. Results of routine blood tests were significant for kidney insufficiency (proteinuria, 3.47 g of protein in 24 hours; estimated glomerular filtration rate, 38.5 mL/min).
13. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level and serum tumor marker findings were normal.
14. Infection panel screenings for hepatitis, HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis, and parasites were negative.
15. Antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative.
16. Whole-body positron emission tomographic/computed tomographic (PET/CT) imaging detected no hypermetabolic changes.
17. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiling, including cytologic analysis, was normal.
18. Culture of the CSF and blood was negative for bacteria and fungus.Representative ophthalmic and neuroimaging results.
19. A, Fundus fluorescein angiography findings in the right eye.
20. The arrowheads indicate perivascular fluorescein leakage and hyperfluorescence of the vessel walls; the asterisk indicates the nonperfusion area.
21. B, This enhanced magnetic resonance image (MRI) shows the ring-enhancing lesions (arrowheads).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Brain or kidney biopsy
B: Genetic sequencing
C: Second CSF culture
D: Aqueous humor paracentesis

1. A 42-year-old woman presented with clinical features of microcephaly, short stature, intellectual disability, severe degree of scoliosis, gait abnormality, and encephalopathy (Figure, A and B).
2. She was born in 1973 at 38th week of gestation followed by a normal delivery (weight, 3.15 kg and head circumference, 42 cm) to nonconsanguineous parents.
3. The head size was normal at birth, and no other abnormalities were seen during her infancy.
4. At age 2 years, her parents noticed that she had delayed motor and language milestones.
5. She experienced a progressive developmental delay such as reduction of head growth, loss of acquired communication, and loss of motor functions between ages 9 and 12 years.
6. The severity of scoliosis increased with age, and she became a wheelchair user at age 18 years.
7. She was referred to us at age 40 years with the characteristic features of growth deceleration (height, 142 cm; weight, 22 kg; body mass index, 11 [calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared]), apraxia, left-sided hemiplegia, spasticity, sleep apnea, constipation, osteoporosis, hypoalgesia, and repetitive hand tapping (Video).

10. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with T wave inversion (V3-V6), and echocardiography showed mild cardiomegaly.
11. The brain magnetic resonance imaging studies showed a diffuse reduction in the corpus callosum involving splenium and enlarged right ventricle, resulting in cerebral lateral ventricular asymmetry (Figure, C).
12. A, Characteristic features of a 42-year-old woman with microcephaly.

A: Turner syndrome
B: Fragile X syndrome
C: Rett syndrome
D: Cerebral palsy

1. A 19-month-old boy presented for evaluation of widespread edema and acute dermatitis.
2. Following an upper respiratory tract infection 1 month prior, he developed disseminated red, scaly patches and a progressive eruption of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented patches of skin.
3. He had occasional nonbloody loose stools but no fevers or vomiting.
4. Although he was otherwise well, his growth had fallen from the 75th to the 25th percentile for height and weight over the preceding 9 months, and he could speak only 2 words.
5. His medical history was notable for atopic dermatitis and diarrhea in infancy that prompted allergy testing at age 6 months; he was subsequently diagnosed with milk, egg, and peanut allergies.
6. His parents avoided feeding him these foods, providing him only soy-based milk and formula, with improvement of dermatitis, until age 1 year.
7. Since then his diet had consisted of multiple rice milk feeds daily, supplemented only with pureed fruits and vegetables, pasta, snack puffs, and sunflower butter.
8. The patient had no history of meconium ileus or family history of cystic fibrosis.
9. There was no recent travel and no changes to the home environment.
10. On presentation, the patient was irritable, with normal vital signs.
11. He displayed prominent scrotal swelling and pitting edema of the legs bilaterally.
12. Skin examination was notable for erythematous, denuded patches with peeling scale and reticulate hyperpigmentation, accentuated on the abdomen, back, diaper area, and extensor extremities (Figure; left panel).
13. Notably, his skin also demonstrated widespread patches of hypopigmentation, with an accompanying band of hypopigmentation proximally at the site of newest hair growth (Figure; right panel).
14. Physical examination findings at presentation.
15. Left, Right abdomen, back, buttock, and thigh.
16. Right, Site of newest scalp hair growth.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Check levels of serum protein, albumin, prealbumin, and other nutritional laboratory measures
B: Check urinalysis and urine microscopy to evaluate for protein in urine
C: Perform a skin biopsy
D: Treat with topical steroids

1. A well-appearing 14-month-old girl was referred for the evaluation of recurrent left subconjunctival hemorrhage with increasing frequency since 7 months of age.
2. Multiple prior office visits with referring ophthalmologists during which eyes were dilated showed normal results.
3. Clinical examination revealed 180° of left interior subconjunctival hemorrhage with overlying conjunctival elevation and mild fullness of the left lower eyelid (Figure 1A).
4. Fixation was central, steady, and maintained bilaterally, with full ocular motility and absence of appreciable proptosis.
5. Penlight anterior segment examination demonstrated normally formed anterior segment structures without inflammation or hyphema in either eye, although the left eye exhibited a small intraocular lightly pigmented lesion at the 5-o'clock limbus.
6. Examination under anesthesia (EUA) was deemed appropriate and further demonstrated normal intraocular pressures bilaterally.
7. Handheld slitlamp examination localized the left eye 2-mm limbal lesion on the posterior corneal surface.
8. The surrounding corneal and iris structures were normal appearing without evidence of vascularization.
9. Ultrasound biomicroscopy was used to further evaluate both the intraocular lesion and better characterize the left lower eyelid fullness.
10. This demonstrated no iris, angle, or ciliary body involvement by the intraocular lesion.
11. A 10-MHz contact B-scan examination showed a large inferior orbital lesion measuring more than 17 mm in the anterior-to-posterior dimension (Figure 1B).
12. Doppler ultrasonography did not demonstrate significant flow to suggest a vascular cause.
13. Clinical photograph of a subconjunctival hemorrhage of the left eye (A) and B-scan image of an orbital mass (B).

1. A woman in her late 40s presented with rapidly progressive redness and stiffness of both hands, accompanied by 2 months of multiple finger joint and right shoulder pain.
2. Results of autoimmune serology, including antinuclear antibody, C3 and C4, rheumatoid factor, and Scl-70 antibody tests, were negative.
3. Raynaud phenomenon was not seen.
4. There was an absence of nailfold capillary changes and distal digital pitting.
5. The patient was treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, systemic steroid therapy, and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (ie, hydroxychloroquine), but symptoms persisted.
6. Two weeks after treatment initiation, multiple tender nodules developed over the palms and interphalangeal joints, and flexion contractures continued (Figure, A).
7. Incisional skin biopsy of the palmar nodules (Figure, B and C) and computed tomography (CT) were performed.
8. Results of the CT demonstrated bilateral ovarian tumors with highly suspect peritoneal metastases.
9. A, Clinical image of erythematous and edematous changes of bilateral hands and multiple nodules on palms and interphalangeal joints.
10. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained specimen showing increased fibroblasts with fibrosis from dermis to subcutis.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Dupuytren contracture
B: Fibroblastic rheumatism
C: Palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome
D: Scleroderma

C: Hobnail hemangioma
D: Low-grade angiosarcoma

2. Following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, low anterior resection, and 6 cycles of adjuvant FOLFOX therapy (fluorouracil, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin), he had developed a lung metastasis (KRAS wild type) 1 year later.
3. He subsequently developed multiple lung metastases treated with palliative local interventions (lobectomy, radiofrequency ablation) and 4 lines of chemotherapy.
4. Owing to symptomatic lung disease, he was enrolled in a clinical trial (NCT03502733) following informed consent and achieved a confirmed partial response.
5. After 9 months, contrast computed tomography restaging scans noted a new, 1-cm posterior subglottic lesion of unclear origin (Figure, A).
6. He had no shortness of breath or noisy breathing, dysphagia, voice change, or hemoptysis.
7. A partial response was maintained without evidence of progression of lung disease.A, An axial computed tomographic image reveals a new posterior subglottic lesion (pink arrowhead) of unclear etiology.
8. B, In the operating room, the larynx was exposed with a Lindholm laryngoscope, and a Hopkins rod-lens endoscope was used to photograph the lesion under apneic conditions.
9. C, Photomicrograph (original magnification ×20) of a section of the mass stained for CDX2 via standard immunohistochemical techniques.Otolaryngology was consulted to assess the lesion.
10. The differential diagnosis based on imaging included a mass vs inspissated mucus.
11. Examination using distal-chip flexible laryngoscopy revealed a 1-cm, broad-based, exophytic mass along the posterior wall of the subglottis with prominent vasculature.
12. No other anatomic abnormalities in the upper aerodigestive tract or cervical lymphadenopathy were noted.
13. The decision was made to proceed to the operating room for definitive endoscopic biopsy under general anesthesia (Figure, B).
14. Examination revealed a subglottic mass that did not extend inferiorly beyond the caudal aspect of the cricoid cartilage.
15. The mass was debulked and sent to pathology for analysis, including hematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemical staining (Figure, C).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Tracheal granuloma
B: Metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma
C: Subglottic squamous cell carcinoma
D: Subglottic papilloma

15. D, Monomorphic cells in a syncytial configuration surrounding collagen bundles (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400).

A: Chondroid syringoma
B: Cutaneous meningeal heterotopia
C: Scalp metastasis

7. A: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

question:
1. A previously healthy 27-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 2 weeks of headache, photophobia, vomiting, and confusion.
2. She denied fevers or chills.
3. She was born in Guatemala and had immigrated to the US approximately 1 year ago, without subsequent international travel.
4. She took no medications.
5. On examination, she was afebrile (36.8 °C) and hemodynamically stable, with heart rate 70/min and blood pressure 95/53 mm Hg.
6. She was somnolent and confused without focal neurologic deficits.
7. Serum white blood cell count was elevated to 14.9 ×109/L (86% segmented neutrophils, 9% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, 0% basophils/eosinophils).
8. A computed tomography scan of her brain was notable for diffuse ventriculomegaly and sulcal effacement consistent with hydrocephalus and cerebral edema.
9. Given her diminished level of consciousness, a ventriculostomy was placed emergently.
10. Laboratory analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) obtained from the ventriculostomy was notable for 40 red blood cells/mm3; 3 nucleated cells/mm3; protein level, 11 mg/dL; and glucose level, 73 mg/dL.
11. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with and without contrast demonstrated ventriculomegaly of the lateral and third ventricles, with a 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.6–cm nonenhancing lesion obstructing the aqueduct of Sylvius (Figure 1A).
12. No abnormal meningeal enhancement or parenchymal lesion was identified.
13. On hospital day 5, in the midst of an ongoing infectious diseases workup, the measured intracranial pressure and rate of CSF drainage from the ventriculostomy suddenly decreased.
14. Repeat MRI demonstrated resolved hydrocephalus, a patent aqueduct of Sylvius, and the aforementioned nonenhancing lesion now located in the fourth ventricle (Figure 1B).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observe the patient without intervention
B: Initiate anthelminthic therapy with adjuvant steroids
C: Extract the lesion surgically
D: Divert cerebrospinal fluid via ventriculoperitoneal shunt

10. Targeted biopsies were obtained (Figure, C).

B: Capecitabine-induced terminal ileitis
C: Ileal metastasis
D: Small bowel carcinoid tumor

1. A 72-year-old White woman, who was experiencing episodes of nontraumatic transient vision loss for 2 weeks, was evaluated by an ophthalmologist.
2. On examination, visual acuity was 20/30 OU.
3. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 16 mm Hg OD and 41 mm Hg OS.
4. The anterior segment was normal in the right eye.
5. Anterior examination of the left eye revealed 10% hyphema.
6. The patient was prescribed cyclopentolate, 1%, and prednisolone acetate, 1%, to reduce inflammation and lower the IOP in the left eye.
7. Two days later, IOP was 16 mm Hg OD and 10 mm Hg OS.
8. Slitlamp biomicroscopy revealed resolved hyphema and abnormal blood vessels at the superotemporal pupillary margin of the iris, prompting referral for further evaluation.
9. On further examination, visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/50 OS, and IOP was 15 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS.
10. Slitlamp examination results in the right eye appeared normal, whereas the left eye demonstrated subtle, multifocal ectatic vascular channels arranged circumferentially at the pupillary margin.
11. On fluorescein angiography (FA), both the right and left irises displayed multifocal, pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence at the pupillary margin and was more noticeable on the left iris.
12. The remainder of the eye examination was unremarkable, and there was no sign of neovascularization of the retina or disc.
13. Photocoagulate lesions with argon laser at slitlamp evaluation

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observe until repeated incident
B: Photocoagulate lesions with argon laser at slitlamp evaluation
C: Administer intravitreal bevacizumab injections
D: Perform iridocyclectomy to excise the lesions

B: Aqueous tap
C: Sickle cell testing
D: Genetic testing

D: Refer for surgical consultation

2. Her symptoms started 1 day after she rubbed her left eye with her hands after handling the milky latex (a fluid found in 10% of flowering plants) of a plant in her garden.
3. She had no recent history of recent eye surgery, eye trauma, cold sores, or new illnesses.
4. On presentation, her visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/200 OS.

10. The fellow eye had no corneal edema and was pseudophakic, with prior panretinal photocoagulation scars in the peripheral retina.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Intrastromal injection of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor
B: Start topical corticosteroid eyedrops
C: Begin oral and/or topical antiviral medications
D: Perform an endothelial keratoplasty

question:
1. An 81-year-old woman with systemic hypertension and atrial fibrillation underwent Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) for visual acuity of counting fingers because of postphacoemulsification bullous keratopathy with no prior episodes of inflammatory eye disease (Figure 1A).
2. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) improved to 20/40 two weeks later, limited because of a preexisting corneal scar.A, Pre–Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) photograph of edema and bullous keratopathy, and superficial scar.
3. Central corneal thickness was 758 μm.
4. B, Cytomegalovirus endotheliitis–associated coin-shaped lesion (arrowhead) superior to an F-stamp of the DMEK graft.Five weeks later, there was a painless decrease in BCVA to 20/80.
5. Small keratic precipitates (KPs) were noted.
6. Because the patient admitted to inconsistent adherence to the topical steroid regimen, rejection was suspected.
7. Prednisolone acetate, 1%, was increased from 4 times to 8 times daily.
8. Five days later the KP resolved and a slow taper of the prednisolone was initiated.
9. Six weeks later, while taking prednisolone 6 times daily, the patient developed new KPs in coin-shaped aggregates (Figure 1B) along with new anterior chamber (AC) inflammation.
10. Her intraocular pressure (IOP) increased to 25 mm Hg.
11. No vitritis or infiltrates were in the graft-host interface or capsular bag.
12. Donor rim culture results were negative for mycobacteria, fungus, and bacteria, including Propionibacterium acnes.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Increase frequency or potency of steroids
B: Obtain polymerase chain reaction of aqueous humor for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA
C: Perform a vitreous tap with intravitreal antibiotic injection
D: Initiate empirical treatment with acyclovir

2. His medical history was significant for Crohn disease controlled with monthly injections of ustekinumab (Stelara; Janssen Biotech Inc).
3. Symptoms of fever, headache, and myalgia began 1 week prior following a tick bite.
4. He was prescribed oral doxycycline hyclate for suspected Lyme disease.
5. Owing to persistent fever while receiving oral doxycycline hyclate, he was admitted for intravenous administration of doxycycline hyclate, and the fever resolved.
6. He was found to be anemic (hemoglobin concentration, 6.7 g/dL; normal concentration, 13.5-17.5 g/dL) (to convert hemoglobin concentration to g/L, multiply by 10), requiring transfusion.

8. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit and brain with and without contrast was unremarkable.

10. Rheumatologic serology test results for antinuclear antibodies, including Sjögren anti-Ro and anti-La, anti-DNA, and anti-Smith, were also negative.
11. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing revealed elevated proteinase 3 antibody level.
12. In the setting of anemia, infectious-disease consultants raised concern for babesiosis.
13. Peripheral blood smear and polymerase chain reaction were performed; empirical therapy of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, plus atovaquone, 750 mg twice daily, was initiated.
14. Polymerase chain reaction results for babesiosis later returned as negative.Ocular examination revealed uncorrected distance acuity of 20/50 OD and 20/60 OS.
15. Intraocular pressure values were normal, and there was no afferent pupillary defect.
16. Slitlamp evaluation showed bilateral rare anterior vitreous cell.
17. Dilated fundus examination revealed bilateral reddened foveal lesions and irregular macular pigmentation.
What Would You Do Next?



A: Obtain indocyanine green angiography
B: Discontinue immunosuppression therapy
C: Order optical coherence tomography
D: Repeat neuroimaging

1. An African American woman in her 30s presented with a 6-month history of 1-cm to 2-cm erythematous and scaly plaques on her lower legs associated with 30-kg weight loss.
2. The plaques began around her ankles and spread proximally, reaching the upper thighs by the time of presentation.
3. She also noted new lesions on her arms and abdomen in the preceding weeks.
4. The eruption was asymptomatic, and the plaques were preceded by lower extremity edema and weakness, resulting in difficulty ambulating and frequent falls.
5. The patient also reported allodynia, tingling, and numbness in her lower legs.

7. She was a schoolteacher and had not traveled outside of the country in the past 10 years.

10. Sensation to light touch and proprioception were diminished below the knee.
11. Two punch biopsies were performed for histologic review (Figure, C and D).
12. A, Dark brown, coarse, ichthyosiform scale on the bilateral lower legs.
13. B, Firm pink plaques with overlying coarse scale.
14. C, Granulomatous inflammation throughout the dermis with mild hyperparakeratosis around a hair follicle (hematoxylin-eosin).
15. D, Well-formed, epithelioid granulomas (hematoxylin-eosin).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Plaque and ichthyosiform sarcoidosis
B: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis
C: Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis
D: Cutaneous tuberculosis

D: Observe

question:
1. A 46-year-old healthy Hispanic woman presented with 2 days of photophobia in her right eye.
2. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/30 + 2 OD and 20/20 OS.
3. Her intraocular pressure, extraocular motility, and pupillary light reactions were normal.
4. An examination demonstrated trace anterior cells in the right eye; otherwise, the examination had normal results.
5. No vitreous cells were present.
6. Topical prednisolone was started for presumed acute anterior uveitis.
7. One week later, the photophobia had improved.
8. However, unnoticed by the patient, her BCVA had worsened to 20/200 OD and 20/40 OS.
9. An examination demonstrated new subretinal fluid in the macula in the right eye (Figure 1A).
10. Fluorescein angiography showed peripapillary speckled pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence in the right eye.
11. Indocyanine green showed early choroidal vessel hyperfluorescence and several posterior focal hypofluorescent spots in the midphase in both eyes.
12. Autofluorescence showed patchy hyperautofluorescence in both eyes.
13. Tuberculosis and syphilis testing had negative results.
14. A complete blood cell count was unremarkable.
15. A diagnosis of central serous retinopathy (CSR) was made.
16. The topical prednisolone was stopped.
17. Findings on presentation and follow-up.
18. A, Optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrates posterior vitreous cells (white arrowheads), subretinal fluid, and choroidal corrugation (yellow arrowheads).
19. B, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrates multifocal, demarcated exudative retinal detachments, including in the macula.
20. Similar findings were present in the left eye.
21. One week later, the BCVA worsened to E at 3 feet OD and 20/200 OS.
22. An examination now revealed 2+ vitreous cells and extensive exudative retinal detachments in both eyes (Figure 1B).
23. No retinal tears were seen on a depressed examination.
24. Retinal detachment repair with vitrectomy and/or scleral buckle

What Would You Do Next?

A: Initiate immunosuppressive therapy
B: Monitor for resolution of subretinal fluid
C: Retinal detachment repair with vitrectomy and/or scleral buckle
D: Surgery to create scleral windows

question:
1. A preschool-age girl presented for evaluation of an asymptomatic plaque on the right lower extremity that had been present for 1 year.
2. Prior treatments included triamcinolone ointment and frankincense with no improvement.
3. A potassium hydroxide preparation had negative results for fungal elements.
4. Her medical history and family history were unremarkable.

10. Periodic acid–Schiff stained sections failed to show fungal or yeast elements.
11. Immunohistochemical staining was markedly positive for CD3, CD5, and CD8 (Figure, D); CD4 reactivity was less robust and mainly restricted to dermal lymphocytes.
12. Also, CD20 was present in 5% of dermal lymphocytes, and CD30 showed variable staining of 5% of lymphocytes.A, Image of a solitary plaque on the right lateral lower leg.
13. B, Scanning view with hyperkeratosis, epidermal hyperplasia, and a lichenoid-like lymphoid infiltrate (hematoxylin-eosin).
14. C, Biopsy results with marked epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes (hematoxylin-eosin).
15. D, Biopsy results with robust CD8 signal (magnification ×100).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Langerhans cell histiocytosis
B: Lymphomatoid contact dermatitis
C: Mycosis fungoides
D: Pagetoid reticulosis

1. A 77-year-old man was referred to the cornea service for bilateral corneal verticillata noted first by his general ophthalmologist.
2. One year prior to presentation, the patient had undergone coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).
3. He was discharged with amiodarone and used the medication for 6 weeks.

5. Prior to his CABG procedure, the patient only used a low dose of lisinopril until he began experiencing progressive dyspnea and fatigue.

8. He denied any other symptoms, including headache, rash, joint pain, or chest pain.

13. His pupils were round and equally reactive, and the remainder of the slitlamp examination and dilated fundus examination were within normal limits.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Provide reassurance, because the patient is no longer taking amiodarone
B: Obtain genetic testing
C: Initiate corneal scraping and culture
D: Initiate laboratory testing for immunoglobulins

question:
1. An African American woman in her 20s presented to an outside hospital with progressive vision loss in both eyes, photophobia, and nausea, which had developed over weeks.
2. Her home medications were hydrocodone and ibuprofen.
3. Bilateral disc edema was noted on examination, and neuroimaging was obtained.
4. Noncontrast head computed tomography (CT) and CT angiogram were remarkable only for bilateral optic nerve head abnormalities.
5. Magnetic resonance imaging was concerning for prominent optic nerves (Figure, A).
6. There was no evidence of intracranial masses, hydrocephalus, or bleed.
7. Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure of 40 cm of water.
8. Cerebrospinal fluid protein, glucose, IgG, and oligoclonal band levels were within normal limits.
9. Renal function was normal.
10. The patient started receiving oral acetazolamide, 500 mg, twice daily for presumed idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) and transferred to our institution.
11. On admission, she was noted to have near-complete vision loss in both eyes, severe postural headaches, and nausea with vomiting.
12. Visual acuity was hand motion OD and no light perception OS.
13. Fundoscopic examination revealed severe papilledema (Frisen grade 4-5 OD; grade 5 OS).
14. A magnetic resonance venography was performed and revealed bilateral filling defect of the transverse sinuses, suggestive of bilateral nonocclusive dural venous sinus thromboses (DVST) (Figure, B).
15. The patient continued receiving acetazolamide, 500 mg, twice daily, which was dose escalated to 2000 mg twice daily over 24 hours.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Begin intravenous anticoagulation
B: Serial lumbar punctures
C: Immediate optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF)
D: Consult neurosurgery for consideration of drain or shunt placement

question:
1. A 58-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of severe and progressive action tremor in his dominant hand when writing.
2. When questioned, he described subtle balance problems without falls developing over the past 3 years.
3. With the exception of profound difficulties with handwriting, motor symptoms did not affect livelihood or activities of daily living.
4. There was no tremor reported in the nondominant hand or other limbs or symptoms of autonomic dysfunction.
5. Neither he nor his wife reported any changes in cognitive function.
6. His medical history comprised surgeries of the hand (laceration repair), leg (fracture repair), knee (reconstruction), and ear (stapedectomy); these were not related to the presenting symptoms.
7. He had a family history of ischemic heart disease (both parents) but no family history of neurological disorder.
8. He exercised regularly (5 times per week) and consumed 2 to 4 standard drinks per week.
9. He was a former smoker with a 2-year pack history and denied any illicit drug use.
10. Cognitive testing revealed deficits in executive function and speed of information processing.
11. Examination of eye movements and speech revealed jerky eye pursuit, saccadic dysmetria, and moderate slurring of speech.
12. Additional motor signs included abnormal handwriting (Figure 1A), bilateral intention tremor, mild rigidity (upper extremities), and moderately impaired heel tapping.
13. Facial expression was normal.
14. There was no head or resting tremor.
15. He demonstrated moderate body sway while standing, was unable to stand on 1 foot for more than 10 seconds, and had impaired tandem walking.
16. Gait, posture, and walking capacities during a timed 6-m walk were normal.
17. A, Handwriting task from the motor examination showing abnormal handwriting.
18. B, T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery image from brain magnetic resonance imaging showing white matter hyperintensities in the middle cerebellar peduncles.
19. Routine blood test results were normal.
20. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed moderate volume loss in the cerebral hemispheres bilaterally as well as the cerebellum and brainstem.
21. Abnormal signal intensity was noted in the cerebral hemispheric white matter bilaterally, the middle cerebellar peduncles (Figure 1B), the cerebellar white matter, and the pons.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Multiple system atrophy
B: Vascular dementia
C: Fragile X–associated tremor ataxia syndrome
D: Essential tremor

2. Despite taking omeprazole (20 mg once daily) 30 minutes before breakfast, avoiding foods that precipitated symptoms, and sleeping with his head elevated, heartburn and regurgitation while supine continued.
3. He reported intermittent solid-food dysphagia for 2 years but no weight loss (254-lb [115 kg] body weight); physical examination results were unremarkable.
4. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed normal esophageal mucosa and normal biopsies.
5. Given his persisting symptoms, an esophageal high-resolution manometry (HRM) study was performed (Table 1; eFigure in the Supplement).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform 360-degree (Nissen) fundoplication.
B: Perform esophageal (Heller) myotomy and partial fundoplication.
C: Increase omeprazole dosing to twice daily.
D: Replace omeprazole with nortriptyline.

question:
1. A woman in her mid-60s with a history of breast cancer (status post lumpectomy 7 years earlier [N0, M0]) and benign thyroid nodules presented for evaluation of right-sided proptosis.
2. Bulging of the right eye was first noted 6 months earlier elsewhere when she reported progressive proptosis, worsening vision, and tearing in the right eye.
3. She did not report any pain or diplopia.
4. Visual acuity was 20/150 OD (no improvement with pinhole) and 20/20 OS.
5. Pupillary reaction and confrontational visual fields were normal.
6. External examination was notable for proptosis of 7 mm, hypoglobus, and resistance to retropulsion.
7. A firm, nontender mass was palpable in the right superotemporal orbit.
8. The palpebral lobe of the right lacrimal gland was erythematous and prominent compared with the normal-appearing left lacrimal gland.
9. Ocular motility showed −2 abduction deficit, right eye.
10. Slitlamp examination revealed pseudophakia and posterior capsular opacification (right > left), but was otherwise normal.
11. Sensation was normal in the V1, V2 distribution, and there was no preauricular, submandibular, or anterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
12. Computed tomographic scan of the orbits without contrast from an outside facility revealed a spherical mass of unclear cause in the area of the right lacrimal gland.
13. No lytic bone changes or bone remodeling could be seen (Figure 1).
14. Computed tomographic imaging from outside facility revealed a 1.9 × 2.3 × 1.8-cm mass of an unclear cause within the anterolateral right orbit, exerting mass effect on the globe.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Arrange 6-month follow-up
B: Obtain additional imaging
C: Perform an incisional biopsy
D: Perform an excisional biopsy

1. A man in his 20s presented with a 2-month history of itchy skin lesions on his trunk, arms, and groin.
2. He was otherwise healthy, with no other underlying conditions, and he was taking no medications.
3. He had no history of atopic dermatitis or other eczematous dermatoses.
4. There were no associated extracutaneous symptoms.
5. His family medical history was relevant only in that his mother had systemic lupus erythematosus.
6. On physical examination, there were several erythematous annular patches on the abdomen (flanks and periumbilical region), lower back, groin, wrists, and legs (Figure, A).
7. The lesions showed slightly raised red-brown borders and a clear center in some patches with no visible scaling, hypopigmentation, induration, or atrophy.
8. Results of laboratory studies including complete blood cell count, biochemical analysis, complement levels, antinuclear antibodies, anti-Ro, anti-La, anti-ribonucleoprotein, anti-Smith, and anti-dsDNA antibodies, as well as serologic testing for syphilis and hepatitis B and C virus, were all normal or negative.
9. A punch biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic evaluation (Figure, B and C).
10. A, Clinical image shows several erythematous annular patches on the flanks and periumbilical region.
11. B, Histopathologic analysis of a punch biopsy sample from the abdomen showing superficial lymphocytic infiltrates in the papillary and superficial reticular dermis.
12. C, There are also prominent vacuolar changes at the dermoepidermal junction, and in some areas mild lymphocytic exocytosis.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Pigmented purpuric dermatosis
B: Mycosis fungoides
C: Annular lichenoid dermatitis of youth
D: Secondary syphilis

question:
1. A healthy adolescent Latino man with juvenile open-angle glaucoma underwent Ahmed valve placement in the left eye via uncomplicated surgery.
2. Preoperative Snellen visual acuity was 20/40 and intraocular pressure (IOP) was 36 mm Hg; on postoperative day 1, IOP was 10 mm Hg and visual acuity fell to count fingers.
3. Slitlamp examination of the left eye revealed an elevated bleb over the Ahmed plate with no leakage.
4. The cornea was clear and compact, and there was a well-positioned tube overlying the iris superotemporally.
5. The anterior chamber was deep with trace inflammation.
6. Dilated fundus examination revealed disc edema, peripapillary hemorrhages, and diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages throughout the posterior pole and periphery (Figure 1).
7. Spontaneous venous pulsations were not appreciated.
8. Slitlamp examination of the right eye revealed a normal anterior and posterior segment, with no retinal vascular abnormality or hemorrhage.
9. The fundus of the left eye showed peripapillary hemorrhages, nasal disc edema, and diffuse retinal and preretinal hemorrhages throughout the posterior pole and periphery; a white-centered hemorrhage is found within the superior macula.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Order a complete blood cell count and coagulation testing
B: Oral and topical corticosteroids
C: Plasmapheresis for hyperviscosity syndrome
D: Fluorescein angiography

question:
1. A woman in her 40s presented to the dermatology clinic with a 10-year history of progressive skin thickening and subcutaneous enlargement of the right side of her nose and right cheek.
2. She had been seen by several dermatologists and otolaryngologists and had undergone nondiagnostic skin biopsies.
3. She underwent a septorhinoplasty 6 months prior to presentation because of collapse of her right nasal ala.
4. During the surgical procedure, the surgeon noted a significant amount of submucosal tissue in the right nasal cavity, which was removed; histopathological analysis was performed, and the results were reported as fibroadipose tissue and vascular proliferation.
5. A skin biopsy was performed at the time of the surgical procedure and was interpreted as sebaceous hyperplasia.
6. The patient initially had improvement in her skin, but she again noticed enlargement of the soft tissue with thickening of the overlying skin on her right cheek and right side of her nose several months later.
7. Clinical examination revealed slightly hyperplastic soft tissue with dilated patulous follicles involving the right medial malar cheek and right nasal ala in addition to deviation of the nasal tip (Figure, A).
8. The surgical pathology specimens from her septorhinoplasty were obtained and reviewed.
9. A, Clinical image shows facial asymmetry with deviation of the nasal tip.
10. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of an interstitial proliferation of spindle cells within mature adipocytes that extends between bundles of skeletal muscle.
11. C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of mature adipocytes that are separated by a proliferation of spindle cells associated with fragments of thickened collagen.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Lupus panniculitis (subcutaneous lupus erythematosus)
B: Spindle cell lipoma
C: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
D: Diffuse pattern neurofibroma

question:
1. A man in his 50s presented with weakness in the distal right hand and leg and paresthesias of the right hand.
2. Four days before presentation, he experienced sudden, severe neck pain that swiftly progressed to neck stiffness and bilateral shoulder pain.
3. The next day, he noticed weakness in the right arm and leg.
4. The day before hospitalization, the weakness progressed, and he lost the ability to ambulate.
5. Until 18 months ago, he had worked as a clerk, but he retired because of a history of hypertension and diabetes.
6. His family history revealed no neurological disorders, except for a brother who had a brain lesion excised.
7. On examination, he was afebrile, and his vital signs were normal.
8. He was fully alert but had weakness in the right distal arm (medical research council [MRC] grade 3/5) and the right leg (MRC grade 4/5) with sensory impairment to pinprick and temperature in the left leg.
9. Laboratory values revealed an elevated γ-glutamyltransferase level of 615 U/L (reference range, 10-71 U/L).
10. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid indicated xanthochromia; normal white blood cell count, 1 cell/µL; red blood cell count, 2.19 × 10/μL; increased glucose level at 133 mg/dL (reference range, 40-80 mg/dL); increased total protein level at 0.10 g/dL (reference range, 0.03-0.05 mg/dL); and increased lactate level at 28.8 mg/dL (reference range, 9.9-21.6 mg/dL).
11. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and the entire spinal cord revealed patency of the intracranial vessels and multiple abnormal signals throughout the brain on T1-, T2-, and susceptibility-weighted sequences (SWIs) and 1 lesion at the level of the fifth cervical vertebra (Figure).A, Susceptibility-weighted magnetic resonance image (MRI) showing numerous intraparenchymal hypointensities (red arrowheads).
12. B, T1-weighted MRI at the level of the fifth cervical vertebra showing hyperintensity in the right ventral portion of the spinal cord (red arrowhead).
13. C, T2-weighted MRI showing central hypointensity of the spinal cord between the levels of the fifth cervical and seventh thoracic vertebrae (not shown) (red arrowheads).Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Amyloid angiopathy
B: Multiple cavernous malformations
C: Metastatic melanoma
D: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy

question:
1. A 35-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 4 days of fever (temperature up to 39°C), extreme weakness, fatigue, and 1 to 2 days of progressive confusion.
2. He was born in the United States but had traveled to Sierra Leone for a period of 3 weeks and had returned 1 week prior to presentation.
3. He did not take any form of malaria prophylaxis, nor did he use insect repellent while traveling.
4. He previously received the yellow fever vaccine but not hepatitis A or typhoid vaccination.
5. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 39.3°C, heart rate of 120/min, blood pressure of 119/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 32/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.
6. The patient was jaundiced, with scleral icterus, and was alert and oriented, although he had a fluctuating attention span and was unable to complete basic tasks.
7. He was able to localize painful stimuli.
8. No retinal lesions were present on dilated ophthalmologic examination.
9. Laboratory tests were notable for a white blood cell count of 5000/μL with 88% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 1% bands, 5% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, and 0% eosinophils; hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL, and platelet count of 25 ×103/μL.
10. Sodium level was 132 mEq/L; potassium, 4.0 mEq/L; chloride, 100 mEq/L; carbon dioxide, 15 mEq/L; blood urea nitrogen, 40 mg/dL; and creatinine, 1.5 mg/dL.
11. Total bilirubin level was 23.9 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase, 252 U/L; and alanine aminotransferase, 100 U/L.
12. Venous lactate level was 49.6 mg/dL.
13. A computed tomography scan of the head was unremarkable.
14. A thin preparation blood smear was obtained (Figure).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start artemether-lumefantrine
B: Start chloroquine
C: Start intravenous quinidine gluconate and doxycycline
D: Perform an exchange transfusion

1. A 30-year-old man presented to the emergency department with palpitations and tachycardia.
2. He had been experiencing sore throat, fevers, and myalgias for the past day.
3. He became alarmed when he awoke from sleep with strong palpitations and a heart rate greater than 200/min documented on his smartwatch.
4. He had similar symptoms 1 year ago and was diagnosed with and treated for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).
5. A subsequent outpatient echocardiogram revealed a structurally normal heart; results of a follow-up electrocardiogram (ECG) were also normal (Figure 1, top).
6. Patient’s baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram (top) and on presentation (bottom).
7. On presentation to the emergency department, the patient’s temperature was 38.2°C; blood pressure, 125/67 mm Hg; and pulse, 241/min.
8. Physical examination was notable for an erythematous oropharynx, tonsillar exudates, a tachycardic, regular heart rhythm, and clear lungs.
9. An ECG was obtained (Figure 1, bottom).
10. A modified Valsalva maneuver failed to convert the rhythm.
11. He was subsequently given a series of doses of intravenous adenosine (6 mg, 12 mg, 12 mg), followed by direct current cardioversion at 200 J, which converted the rhythm to sinus for approximately 3 minutes.
12. Intravenous metoprolol and intravenous diltiazem bolus and drip were then administered, which slowed the heart rate but did not terminate the arrhythmia.
13. A rapid strep test result was positive, and he was given ampicillin.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Stop diltiazem drip and administer intravenous amiodarone
B: Repeat synchronized direct current cardioversion at 200 J
C: Switch to intravenous esmolol drip
D: Stop diltiazem drip and administer intravenous verapamil

10. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×20); C, α-smooth muscle actin immunostain (original magnification ×40); D, CD117 immunostain (original magnification ×40); and D, CD34 immunostain (original magnification ×40).

A: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasia of the pancreas
B: Atypical mucinous cystic neoplasia of the pancreas
C: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
D: Pancreatic pseudocyst

1. A woman in her 30s noticed a painless left neck mass.
2. She had no history of dysphagia, dyspnea, recent upper respiratory tract infection, injury, or surgery.
3. She also had no weight loss, pain, or fever and had no history of tobacco or alcohol use, radiation exposure, family history of thyroid cancer, and no previous thyroid dysfunction.
4. Thyroid function test results were normal.
5. Physical examination revealed a palpable nontender, firm mass and no cervical lymphadenopathy.
6. She had a medical history of high-grade osteosarcoma with areas of leimyosarcoma of the tibia which had been treated with right above-knee amputation and chemotherapy 4 years prior to presentation.
7. She was followed up in the oncology clinic without any recurrence or metastases.
8. Her last visit was 6 months earlier.
9. She was also diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix 2 months earlier and was awaiting surgery.
10. Computed tomography (CT) of the neck revealed a 6.0 × 3.4 × 4.4-cm calcified left thyroid lobe mass (Figure, A).
11. Positron emission tomography–computed tomographic (PET-CT) imaging showed increased uptake in the left thyroid gland.
12. She underwent a left thyroid lobectomy.
13. The neoplastic cells were positive for p53, vimentin, and smooth muscle actin, and negative for S-100, thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), and CD34 (Figure, B).
14. A, Computed tomographic image reveals a calcified mass (blue arrowhead).
15. B; Left, negative immunostain results for S-100; right, positive immunostain results for vimentin (original magnification ×100).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Thyroid lymphoma
B: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
C: Osteosarcoma metastasis
D: Squamous cell carcinoma metastasis

1. A patient in her 50s with a history of type 2 diabetes and mild bilateral nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy presented with new-onset floaters in both eyes but no blurry vision, eye pain, or photopsia.
2. This patient was recently discharged from the hospital for West Nile virus (WNV) encephalitis (confirmed seropositive for IgM and IgG antibodies against WNV).
3. Polymerase chain reaction analyses detected no DNA for Epstein-Barr virus, BK virus, cytomegalovirus, or herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2.
4. Neither HIV antibody nor antigen was detected.
5. Cerebrospinal fluid culture analysis findings were normal.
6. She received supportive treatment and made a full recovery.
7. The patient’s corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU, and her intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OU.
8. Anterior segment examination findings were unremarkable for both eyes.
9. Dilated fundus examination revealed microaneurysms, a dot-blot hemorrhage, and scattered, deep, white, chorioretinal lesions in the posterior pole and periphery that were more numerous in the right than left eye (Figure 1A).
10. Vitritis was absent.
11. Fluorescein angiography showed chorioretinal lesions with central hypofluorescence and peripheral hyperfluorescence (Figure 1B).
12. A, Deep, white, creamy lesions (arrowheads) are observed in the posterior pole of the right eye.
13. The dot-blot hemorrhage inferior to the fovea is secondary to nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy.
14. B, Fluorescein angiogram of the posterior pole of the right eye showing lesions (arrowheads) with a hypofluorescent center and surrounding hyperfluorescence.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Order vitreous biopsy
B: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
C: Order biopsy of chorioretinal lesion
D: Observe

question:
1. A woman in her 20s was referred to the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Neuro-Ophthalmology Service with a 2-month complaint of frequent headaches and 1 week of blurry vision in her left eye.
2. Her ocular history was significant only for refractive error.
3. Her medical history revealed systemic hypertension, depression, and obesity.
4. Her current medications included hydrochlorothiazide and fluoxetine.
5. On review of systems, she endorsed nausea as well as paresthesia in her hands.
6. Neuro-ophthalmic examination revealed visual acuities of 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS, with no pinhole improvement.
7. Color vision (Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plates) was within normal limits bilaterally, although it was noted to be slightly slower in the left eye.
8. With the Amsler grid, she reported significant metamorphopsia in the left eye.
9. Pupils were symmetric with slow responses bilaterally but without afferent defects.
10. Applanation tonometry revealed pressures of 16 mm Hg OD and 17 mm Hg OS.
11. Slitlamp examination revealed no cells in the anterior chamber or the anterior vitreous in either eye.
12. Automated (Humphrey) visual field testing revealed enlargement of the blind spot in the right eye (mean deviation, −2.91 dB) and generalized, nonspecific depression in the left eye (mean deviation, −3.41 dB).
13. Examination of her fundus was notable for bilateral optic disc swelling (Frisén grade 2 in each eye) as well as unilateral macular exudates, subretinal fluid, and subretinal hemorrhages in the left eye (Figure 1).
14. Results from brain magnetic resonance imaging with magnetic resonance venography with and without contrast were normal.
15. A, Color fundus photograph demonstrating Frisén grade 2 optic disc edema.
16. B, Color fundus photograph demonstrating Frisén grade 2 optic disc edema associated with subretinal fluid, exudate, and retinal hemorrhages.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observe the patient and treat headaches conservatively
B: Consult surgery for immediate surgical intervention
C: Perform a lumbar puncture with opening pressure, routine chemistry, and cell count analysis
D: Begin treatment with high-dose corticosteroids

2. The tender area was beneath an adhesive bandage placed where she had received DTaP (diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis) and polio vaccinations 3 weeks earlier.
3. Otherwise, she appeared remarkably well, and her vital signs were normal.
4. Removing the bandage revealed a tender indurated gray-violet plaque (Figure, A).
5. White blood cell and neutrophil counts were low at 0.4 K/μL (normal range, 4.86-13.18 K/μL) and 0.18 K/μL (normal range, 1.60-8.29 K/μL), respectively.
6. Blood culture findings were negative.
7. Punch biopsy specimens were obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B) and fungal culture (Figure, C).
8. A, Gray-violet plaque on posterior upper arm at site of adhesive portion of bandage.
9. B, Broad nonseptate hyphae surrounding and infiltrating dermal blood vessels (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×400).
10. Of note, occasional septae are seen in this specimen, consistent with the characteristic finding that mucormycetes are pauciseptate, rather than aseptate, molds.
11. C, Nonseptate hyphae with round terminal sporangia and free spores (lactophenol cotton blue mount; original magnification ×400).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Mucormycosis
B: Cutaneous diphtheria
C: Pseudomonal ecthyma gangrenosum
D: Aspergillosis

1. A 43-year-old man with generally good health presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of cramps and abdominal pain.
2. For the past year, the patient had been investigated for hypochromic microcytic anemia.
3. As part of the investigation, he underwent an esophagogastroduodenoscopy and a colonoscopy, which revealed a normal-looking bowel with no obvious source of bleeding visualized.
4. Further investigation involved capsule endoscopy, which was ingested 3 days prior to his emergency department admission.
5. The patient claimed not to have passed a bowel movement containing the capsule.
6. Physical examination results were normal except for a nontender distended and tympanic abdomen.
7. Results of routine laboratory testing were essentially normal except for a low level of hemoglobin (8.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]), with no leukocytosis noted.

9. An intraluminal hypodense mass was demonstrated in this area and appeared to be the cause of the obstruction.
10. Adjacent to this area, the capsule was clearly demonstrated in a dilated proximal loop of the small bowel (Figure 1).Computed tomographic scan showing an intraluminal hypodense mass (pink arrowhead) causing a small-bowel obstruction.
11. Adjacent to this area, the endoscopic capsule (asterisk) is demonstrated in a proximal dilated loop of the small bowel.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Small-bowel adenocarcinoma
B: Lymphoma of the small bowel
C: Carcinoid tumor
D: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the small bowel

1. A Caucasian male in his 40s was referred by his primary care doctor for evaluation after experiencing blurry vision associated with frontal headaches for a week.
2. Despite his headaches, he denied having eye pain.
3. He was otherwise healthy, with no past medical or ocular history.
4. Prior to referral, his symptoms prompted magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, orbits, and cervical spine which were unremarkable.
5. Laboratory test results for the presence of Lyme disease, rapid plasma reagin, antinuclear antibodies, angiotensin-converting enzymes, and erythrocyte sedimentation rates were normal.
6. The best corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye.
7. Motility, intraocular pressures, and pupillary light reflexes were normal.
8. The anterior segment examination results were normal, and the lenses were clear bilaterally.
9. A fundus examination showed vitreous cells in both eyes, but the optic nerve and retinal vessels were visualized clearly.
10. Also, both eyes had optic nerve hyperemia and multiple shallow serous retinal detachments.
11. The fluorescein angiography of both eyes demonstrated optic disc leakage, multiple pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence, and fluorescein pooling in the areas of serous detachment (Figure).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Surgical decompression of vortex veins
B: Perform B-scan ultrasonography
C: Start prednisone at 80 mg daily with a slow taper
D: Check blood pressure

1. A woman in her 70s and of Korean descent reported difficulty seeing in dimly lit settings for the past 6 years and was referred for evaluation.
2. Her medical history was remarkable for long-standing hypertension, diabetes, and mixed connective tissue disease.
3. On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/25 OS.
4. Slitlamp examination showed prominent nuclear sclerosis and a posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye and a well-positioned intraocular lens in the left eye.
5. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed bilateral pigment mottling with extensive peripheral depigmentation of the retinal pigment epithelium, sparing the central fovea bilaterally.
6. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography showed complete loss of photoreceptors outside the fovea, with retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, irregular proliferation, and some remodeling (Figure, A).
7. Fundus autofluorescence showed a ring of parafoveal hypofluorescence and hyperfluorescence, with speckled hypofluorescence peripherally (Figure, B).
8. Goldmann perimetry of both eyes (Figure, C) revealed significant constriction of the V-4-e isopter with an extensive ring scotoma between approximately 10° and 30° eccentricity.
9. Central vision with the I-4-e isopter was constricted to 5° to 7°.
10. A multifocal electroretinogram (ERG) showed profound signal attenuation throughout the examined area.
11. The full-field electroretinogram was nonrecordable under both scotopic and photopic conditions.A, Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) reveals extensive and diffuse retinal thinning (arrowhead) beyond the fovea, with loss of photoreceptors and pigment migration into the retina.
12. B, Fundus autofluorescence of the left eye shows a perimacular ring of hypofluorescence (blue asterisk) and hyperfluorescence (black asterisk) in a bull’s-eye configuration with diffuse scattered granular areas.
13. C, Goldmann visual field of the left eye shows an evolving ring scotoma (asterisk) and a small preserved central island of vision (arrowhead).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform genetic testing
B: Order antiretinal antibodies
C: Perform systemic evaluation for malignancy
D: Review medications

2. The lesions started spontaneously as erythematous tender papules with white purulent discharge.
3. He recently failed a course of amoxicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethaxazole initiated by his primary care physician.

5. The patient denied any recent changes to his medications or recent travel.
6. No other household members were affected.

12. A punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the edge of the lesion (Figure, C and D).
13. A, Left pretibia on initial visit.
14. B, Left pretibia at 7-day follow-up.
15. C, Periodic acid–Schiff stain (original magnification ×4).
16. D, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×20).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Blastomycosis
B: Pyoderma gangrenosum
C: Atypical mycobacterial infection
D: Ecthyma gangrenosum

1. A 43-year-old healthy human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B27–positive man was referred to the retina clinic with progressively worsening blurry vision in both of his eyes.
2. His right eye had experienced an episode of blurry vision 4 months previously that had spontaneously improved over a few weeks.
3. Two weeks before presentation, he experienced blurry vision in his left eye and received a diagnosis of vasculitis based on fluorescein angiography (FA) findings.
4. He was referred to a rheumatologist and received high-dose oral prednisone therapy for presumed autoimmune vasculitis.
5. Over the next 2 weeks, he experienced a rapid worsening of vision in both eyes and presented to the Illinois Eye and Ear Infirmary.
6. During an interview, he noted that the laboratory workup results had recently come back as notable for a mildly reactive fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test.
7. In the absence of other signs or symptoms of syphilis, he was scheduled to undergo a lumbar puncture later that day.
8. On presentation, his visual acuity was counting fingers OD and 20/300 OS, with manifest refraction to 20/60 OS only.
9. He had no afferent pupillary defect and his intraocular pressures were healthy.
10. The anterior segment examination yielded normal results without evidence of anterior chamber inflammation.
11. A dilated fundus examination was notable for mild vitritis of both eyes, mild hyperemia of the right optic nerve, and a large white lesion that encompassed the nerve and macula of both eyes.
12. Fluorescein angiography results revealed multiple hyperfluorescent lesions in late frames (Figure 1).
13. A, Color fundus photograph of the left eye shows a large placoid lesion in the macula.
14. B, Late fluorescein angiography showing multiple areas of hyperfluorescence in the macula and periphery with peripheral vascular leakage.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform bilateral posterior sub-Tenon triamcinolone injections
B: Increase the dose of oral prednisone
C: Initiate antiviral therapy
D: Initiate intravenous penicillin therapy

question:
1. A 4-week-old male infant presented to the pediatric ophthalmology clinic with bilateral congenital corneal opacities.
2. The pregnancy was full-term and uncomplicated, and he was delivered spontaneously without the use of forceps.
3. His corneal abnormalities were noted by the neonatologists on the first day of life.
4. A systemic survey revealed no other dysmorphic findings.
5. He was referred to the clinic for further evaluation and management.
6. Examination under anesthesia revealed bilateral corneal opacities with peripheral clearing and absent red reflexes.
7. The white-to-white corneal diameters were 10 mm horizontally and vertically in both eyes, and B-scan ultrasonography revealed unremarkable posterior segments.
8. Ultrasound biomicroscopy confirmed the diagnosis of Peters anomaly type I with iridocorneal adhesions and no apparent lens involvement.
9. At the same session, a large iridectomy with lysis of iridocorneal adhesions was performed in both eyes to establish a clear, noncentral optical axis.
10. Shallowing of the anterior chamber was observed immediately after the iridectomy.
11. However, the patient’s corneal opacity precluded an accurate assessment of the chamber depth and stability (Figure 1).
12. A temporal iridectomy was present, but the anterior chamber depth could not be assessed accurately owing to corneal opacity.
13. Inflate the anterior chamber with ophthalmic viscosurgical device.
14. Tilt the microscope for better visualization of the anterior chamber.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Apply fibrin glue to all surgical wounds.
B: Inflate the anterior chamber with ophthalmic viscosurgical device.
C: Inject a sterile air bubble.
D: Tilt the microscope for better visualization of the anterior chamber.

A: Observe

D: Perform vitreous biopsy

question:
1. A 21-year-old man was admitted to the hospital owing to recurrent, transient episodes of dysarthria, dysphagia, and limb weakness over the course of 3 days.
2. Although these symptoms had resolved after 3 hours’ rest, they recurred 2 hours prior to hospital admission.
3. In addition, the patient had begun to experience weakness and numbness of his limbs, with more severe symptoms on the right side.
4. The symptoms began to gradually resolve 2 hours following admission, and normal function had returned within 2 days.
5. No significant history of illness was noted in the patient or among family members.
6. Neurological examination on admission revealed normal mental status, and the results of cranial nerve examination were normal.
7. Although the patient had cavus feet, no atrophy was observed in the distal lower limbs (Figure, A).
8. Muscle strength was classified as grade 4 for the left limbs and grade 3 for the right limbs, according to Medical Research Council criteria, and muscle tone was diminished.
9. The sensory examination was unremarkable.
10. Deep reflexes were diminished or absent.
11. However, bilateral positive Babinski signs were observed.
12. Results from laboratory examinations, including blood electrolytes, cerebrospinal fluid, and lactate, were normal.
13. Oligonucleotide bands and aquaporin 4 detection were negative.
14. Craniocervical computed tomographic angiography results were normal.
15. Cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed abnormal bilateral increases in T2 signal and diffusion restriction in the periventricular areas and the splenium of corpus callosum (Figure, B).
16. Interestingly, a significant reduction of the abnormal signal was noted on MRI 3 months later.
17. Electrophysiological examination of peripheral nerves revealed extensive bilateral nerve conduction abnormalities.
18. Significantly reduced motor nerve conduction velocity was also observed in the median nerves (38.3 m per second in the left and 36.5 m per second in the right).
19. A, Image shows patient’s pes cavus.
20. B, Patient’s brain axial diffusion-weighted image at admission.
21. Demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis)

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Transient ischemic attack
B: Demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis)
C: Periodic paralysis
D: X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease 1
