question:
1. A man in his late 60s with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes for more than 10 years that was complicated by neuropathy and retinopathy presented with persistent chorea in the left upper extremity for about 1 month despite aggressive correction with insulin.
2. He was alert and oriented with healthy vital signs.
3. No evidence of cognitive impairments was present on bedside testing results.
4. The patient denied any recent infections and risk for human immunodefiency virus (HIV) infection.
5. Neurological examination results were significant for choreiform and hemiballistic movements involving the left upper extremity.
6. His home medications were carefully reviewed to rule out any medications that could cause chorea.
7. A review of his previous records indicated an admission to an outside facility 3 weeks beforehand with severe hyperglycemia and a hemoglobin A1c level of 14.1% (to convert to the proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01).
8. Despite an aggressive correction of blood glucose levels and metabolic correction, his choreiform movements had remained unresolved.
9. On admission, a complete electrolyte and toxicology panel, including calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, yielded normal results.
10. The patient’s serum glucose level was 159 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555) and his hemoglobin A1c was 10.9% without ketoacidosis.
11. Test results for antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulants, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.
12. Serum thyrotropin levels, liver function test results, and parathyroid hormone levels were healthy.
13. Copper studies, a peripheral smear, and a routine electroencephalogram yielded normal results.
14. A general screening for cancers yielded negative results.
15. The patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure), which showed a T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion.
16. Oral administration of olanzapine, 2.5 mg daily, in divided doses with careful monitoring of blood glucose levels resulted in the complete resolution of chorea.
17. Magnetic resonance imaging shows T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head (A) and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion (B).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Postinfectious/autoimmune chorea
B: Paraneoplastic chorea
C: Diabetic striatopathy
D: Acute stroke

1. A healthy 29-year-old pregnant woman, with 34 weeks’ gestational age, presented to the emergency department with diffused acute abdominal pain and vomiting.
2. The pain was located in the periumbilical region and intensified within a few hours.
3. The patient felt normal fetal movements during this time.
4. An initial surgical evaluation was done, and the cause for the abdominal pain was assumed to be not of surgical condition.
5. Next, the patient was evaluated by an obstetrician-gynecologist, and although the gynecologic examination, ultrasonography, and monitoring were all normal, the patient was admitted for further supervision in the obstetrics department.
6. The next day, when the abdominal pain and vomiting persisted and an elevated leukocyte blood count of 14 200/mL was noted (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001), a second surgical consultation was done.
7. The physical examination was significant for diffuse abdominal tenderness.
8. Although the patient was pregnant, and owing to nonavailability of magnetic resonance imaging at that time, a contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic computed tomography was performed (Figure 1).
9. Coronal computed tomographic image showing an edematous small intestinal loop on the left abdomen, with uterus and head of fetus in the pelvis.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Crohn ileitis
B: Foreign body ingestion
C: Ileo-colic intussusception
D: Adenocarcinoma of small intestine

question:
1. A 65-year-old white man was referred to the clinic with a pigmented conjunctival lesion in the left eye.
2. The referring physician suspected primary acquired melanosis (PAM).
3. His ocular history was notable for occupational exposure to sunlight and occasional smoking.
4. There was no personal or family history of cancer, and he denied ocular surgery or trauma.
5. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD/OS, and intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 18 mm Hg OS.
6. A slitlamp examination of the right eye showed no conjunctival pigmentation.
7. Examination of the left eye revealed a pigmented lesion at the temporal limbus from 3 to 4 o’clock with a 2-mm extension into the cornea (Figure 1A).
8. Some opalescence underlied the pigment on the cornea.
9. In addition, there was an adjacent small area of flat, superficial, mobile bulbar conjunctival pigmentation.
10. The anterior segment high-resolution optical coherence tomography (HR-OCT) of the 4-o’clock corneolimbal lesion of the left eye demonstrated thickened hyperreflective corneal epithelium with an abrupt transition from normal to abnormal (Figure 1B).
11. A, Slitlamp photography of the left eye shows a pigmented limbal lesion at 3 to 4 o’clock; another small area of bulbar conjunctival pigmentation is noted (arrowhead).
12. B, High-resolution optical coherence tomography of the left eye through the area of the pigmented conjunctival lesion (inset with red line in area of scan), showing epithelial hyperreflectivity and thickening with an abrupt change from normal to mildly thickened epithelium (arrowhead).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Refer to an oncologist for metastatic workup
B: Biopsy the conjunctival and corneal lesion
C: Perform cryotherapy over the lesion
D: Start oral doxycycline

question:
1. A man in his 20s with panhypopituitarism, septo-optic dysplasia, developmental delay, duodenal stricture, and a history of pancreatitis presented with a painful eruption on his bilateral lower legs.
2. The patient was well until 2 days prior to hospitalization when he developed bilateral lower extremity edema.
3. The day prior to admission, he developed painful pink lesions on both legs.
4. He had not applied any topical medications to his legs or had recent exposure to hot tubs or fish tanks at the home.
5. He had a history of keratosis pilaris on the lower legs and was otherwise well with no fevers, recent upper respiratory infections, abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea.
6. Physical examination showed a man in no apparent distress.
7. On the bilateral anterior legs were scattered tender, pink to purple nodules, and plaques (Figure, A).
8. There was also a background of pinpoint folliculocentric papules on leg and thighs consistent with keratosis pilaris.
9. There was 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities.
10. A punch biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathology and microbiology cultures (Figure, B-D).
11. Routine complete blood cell count and complete metabolic panel had results within normal limits.
12. A, Clinical photograph shows scattered pink to purple nodules and plaques on the bilateral lower extremities.
13. B, C, and D, Histopathologic images of a biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
14. B, Subcutaneous tissue with superficial and deep, dermal and perivascular inflammation, fibrosis, and fat necrosis.
15. C, Lobular panniculitis.
16. D, Dense neutrophilic infiltration of subcutaneous fat associated with fat necrosis and deposition of granular basophilic material (arrowhead).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Erythema nodosum
B: Pancreatic panniculitis
C: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency panniculitis
D: Polyarteritis nodosa

question:
1. A 65-year-old man was referred for evaluation of uveitis in the left eye.
2. Several days after YAG capsulotomy for posterior capsule opacification, his left eye had become red and painful and his visual acuity had declined to counting fingers.
3. Inflammation improved but persisted after vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal vancomycin hydrochloride (1.0 mg) and ceftazidime (2.25 mg) followed by intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide.
4. Vitreous cultures yielded no growth.
5. Six months after the patient’s symptoms began, he presented to our clinic.
6. His visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/160 OS improving to 20/120 OS with pinhole.
7. His intraocular pressure was 32 mm Hg OD and 20 mm Hg OS.
8. The results of ophthalmic examination of the left eye were notable for pigmented keratic precipitates, a rare anterior chamber cell, 2+ (ie, 16-25 cells per field) anterior vitreous cells, epiretinal membrane, and cystoid macular edema.
9. Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, syphilis, and HLA-B27 laboratory test results were negative.
10. The macular edema improved with 4 times daily topical prednisolone acetate and ketorolac tromethamine.
11. After 2 months, the patient reported recurrent pain, redness, and decreased visual acuity.
12. At that time, the visual acuity in the left eye was 20/200E at 2 ft, and there were 4+ (ie, >50 cells per field) anterior chamber cells, a layered hypopyon and 2+ anterior vitreous cells.
13. A subsequent vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal vancomycin hydrochloride (1.0 mg) and ceftazidime (2.25 mg) were performed.
14. Cultures yielded 1+ Propionibacterium acnes.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Prescribe topical moxifloxacin and consult an infectious diseases specialist
B: Perform another vitreous tap and intravitreal vancomycin injection
C: Perform intraocular lens explantation, capsulectomy, and intravitreal vancomycin injection
D: Inject intravitreal vancomycin and administer systemic vancomycin and prednisone

11. 12. Only c-ANCA testing revealed positive results.

11. Optical coherence tomography showed macular edema that involved the center of the macula in both eyes (Figure, inset).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain a fluorescein angiogram
B: Determine blood glucose level and perform glycated hemoglobin test
C: Measure heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure
D: Perform immediate computed tomography of the head

1. An 11-year-old previously healthy boy was referred to the pediatric department with impaired vision after an episode of fever and vomiting.
2. Ophthalmologic examination revealed bilateral mydriasis, with a reduced pupillary response to light and accommodation (Figure).
3. Diluted norepinephrine (0.1%) was instilled in both eyes, which elicited supersensitive dilatation of the pupils bilaterally owing to reinnervation and upregulation of the postsynaptic receptors, consistent with tonic pupils.
4. Uncorrected Snellen visual acuity was 20/32 OU for distance and 20/200 OU for near.
5. Ocular motility was normal.
6. Results of slitlamp examination and ophthalmoscopy showed no abnormalities.
7. Bilateral mydriasis with a reduced pupillary response to light and accommodation in an 11-year-old boy.
8. Results of complete blood cell counts, serum chemistry examination, cerebrospinal fluid examination, and virologic studies of blood and stool performed for exclusion of infection were all negative.
9. Tumor, aneurysm, or traumatic lesion were excluded by cranial magnetic resonance imaging.
10. Serum GQ1b ganglioside IgG antibodies associated with internal ophthalmoplegia in Fisher syndrome were not detected.
11. Within the following 2 weeks, progressive generalized autonomic dysfunction developed including reduced food intake and weight loss, constipation, urinary retention, anhidrosis, xerostomia, and xerophthalmia.
12. Ophthalmologic reexamination showed unaltered pupillary abnormality.
13. Results of Schirmer test without topical anesthesia showed 0 mm of tear production.
14. Lissamine green staining of the exposed interpalpebral areas showed moderate changes of the conjunctiva.
15. Mild corneal staining was evaluated with cobalt blue illumination after fluorescein instillation.
16. Artificial tears and ointment were initiated to treat the aqueous tear deficiency.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Prescribe phototropic variofocal glasses
B: Start pilocarpine eyedrops
C: Obtain blood sample to investigate for autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy
D: Recommend genetic testing

1. A 30-year-old man was referred with progressive quadriplegia for 2 months.
2. The muscle weakness started from the right lower limb and gradually spread to the upper limb and contralateral side.
3. Urinary retention developed 1 month later.

5. The symptoms ameliorated in the first week but thereafter deteriorated with fever.
6. He had no history of central nervous system injury or drug overuse.
7. He was a construction supervisor and had daily contact with moist earth.
8. No relevant family history was reported.
9. On physical examination, he was alert and well oriented.
10. The cranial nerve was intact, but he had quadriplegia with a Medical Research Council muscle scale grade of 0 of 5 power, decreased tendon reflexes, and bilateral positive Babinski sign.
11. Pinprick and vibration sensation were markedly impaired below the nipples.
12. Multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes could be palpitated.
13. The skin was extraordinarily dry, and a pigmentation of 10 mm in diameter at the T2 vertebrae, just on the midline of the back, was noticed.
14. Total blood T-cell count (CD3+) was 1643/uL (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001), and the patient had a CD4+/CD8+ ratio of 0.89.
15. Results of blood testing for human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, and tuberculosis were negative.
16. Cerebrospinal fluid testing revealed pleocytosis (72 cells/uL; mononuclear cells, 59 of 72), elevated protein concentration (200 mg/dL), and a decreased glucose level (36.0 mg/dL [to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555]), but no organisms were identified on Gram stain or on stain for acid-fast bacilli.
17. Pulmonary computed tomography showed enlarged lymph nodes in mediastinum and axillary regions.
18. Results from magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were normal, while magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine revealed multiple intramedullary lesions with enhancement (Figure 1).Magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine.

20. A, Lateral view of the cervical cord.

D: Central nervous system lymphoma

question:
1. A 58-year-old woman with a history of cervical spondylosis and hypothyroidism presented with a 2-week history of joint pain.
2. She noted pain and swelling in her right knee, which migrated to the right ankle and then affected the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of her fingers.
3. About 2 weeks before her symptoms began, her 5-year-old grandson had a febrile illness characterized by headaches, body aches, malaise, and rash on the cheeks, trunk, and extremities but no arthritis.
4. Ten days later, her 10-month-old granddaughter developed a similar febrile illness.
5. Eight days ago, her 25-year-old daughter developed headaches, malaise, and significant arthralgias affecting her wrists and knees but no rash or fever.
6. Manifestations in all of the family members resolved spontaneously within 1 week.
7. On examination, the patient was afebrile with normal vital signs.
8. A malar rash was present (Figure), but there was no rash on the trunk or extremities.
9. She had swelling and tenderness of the MCP and PIP joints and had difficulty making a fist and fully extending her fingers.
10. Laboratory studies revealed a mild normochromic normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL, normal white blood cell and platelet counts, and normal results for a comprehensive metabolic panel.
11. She had a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) result (1:160 [homogeneous pattern; negative <1:80 serum dilution]).
12. Testing for rheumatoid factor was negative; levels of inflammatory markers were normal.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Check for anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies
B: Schedule bilateral hand radiographs
C: Order serologic testing for parvovirus
D: Order testing for anticyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody

question:
1. A 26-year-old white man presented for evaluation of blurry vision over the past year.
2. He had no back or joint pain or skin rashes.
3. Five years ago he had a black ink tattoo placed on his left arm, and 3 years ago a second tattoo was placed on his right arm.
4. Two years after the right arm tattoo was placed, he noticed tattoo elevation on the left arm and onset of decreased vision.
5. He had recurrent episodes of ocular redness and blurred vision, coincident with inflammation of the skin surrounding both tattoos.
6. Two months before presentation, bilateral peripheral iridotomies (iris laser procedures) were performed because of inflammation-induced adhesions between the iris and the lens (Figure, panel A).
7. A, Slitlamp photograph of left eye.
8. B, Tattooed skin on left arm.
9. C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of skin biopsy sample (original magnification ×100).
10. At presentation, best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left.
11. Intraocular pressure was 34 mm Hg in the right eye (upper limit of normal, 21 mm Hg) and 11 mm Hg in the left.
12. On anterior segment slitlamp examination, there were no visible inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber of the right eye, but there were more than 26 cells per 1-mm field in the left.
13. The left arm tattoo was elevated, with nodular elevation most prominent at the superior aspect of the tattoo (Figure, panel B).
14. Punch biopsy of the tattooed skin revealed epithelioid histiocytes with macrophages containing coarse black granular pigment (Figure, panel C).
15. Results of testing for syphilis, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis were negative.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Initiate topical steroid eyedrop therapy
B: Recommend removal of tattoos
C: Refer immediately to rheumatology
D: Perform surgical implantation of glaucoma drainage device

1. A 69-year-old white man presented to the emergency department after a tractor-on-tree collision.
2. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated an incidental right infrarenal, retroperitoneal mass measuring 9.7 × 7.7 × 9.1 cm (Figure 1A), with dilated tortuous supply from a lumbar artery branch and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.
3. He denied any history of systemic symptoms, pain, urinary symptoms, or abnormal bowel function but described 6 years of decreased appetite.
4. Laboratory evaluation of plasma-free metanephrine levels showed a slight elevation in normetanephrine levels (1.21 nmol/L).
5. Given the dramatic arterial enhancement and hypertrophied perivascular plexus, biopsy was not performed, and preoperative arterial embolization was deemed appropriate to minimize intraoperative blood loss.A, Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan demonstrating an incidental right infrarenal, retroperitoneal mass measuring 9.7 × 7.7 × 9.1 cm, with dilated tortuous supply from a lumbar artery branch.
6. B, Flush aortogram outlining supply to the mass from a hypertrophied lumbar artery (blue arrowhead) and from a branch of the internal iliac artery (red arrowhead).At preoperative embolization, initial aortography identified the predominant lumbar artery branch and also demonstrated supply from a branch of the internal iliac artery (Figure 1B).
7. These branches were embolized and the mass was devascularized.
8. Twenty-four hours following embolization, surgical exploration was performed through a periumbilical midline incision.
9. With no evidence of distant metastasis (peritoneal or liver), the mass was resected with partial resection of the iliopsoas muscle to achieve negative margins in conjunction with aortocaval lymphadenectomy of the enlarged lymph nodes.
10. The mass was running parallel to the right ureter, which was meticulously dissected, and the right kidney was successfully saved.
11. There were no complications, and the postoperative course was uneventful.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Angiosarcoma
B: Leiomyosarcoma
C: Pheochromocytoma
D: Unicentric Castleman disease

2. The double vision occurred every day, multiple times throughout the day, and was provoked after looking to the right.

4. She had no history of strabismus, eye patching, or ocular surgery.
5. Her medical history was notable for a growth hormone–producing pituitary macroadenoma for which she underwent surgical resection 2.5 years prior to presentation, followed by γ-knife radiosurgery (50 Gy) 6 months after the initial surgical procedure.

14. However, on returning to a primary gaze from a sustained right-gaze position, a large angle exotropia was present, and on attempted left gaze, there was a limitation of adduction of the right eye (Figure).
15. After 10 to 15 seconds, the exotropia resolved, and eye movements returned to normal.

B: Perform bilateral lateral rectus recessions

5. On day 2 of her hospitalization, she complained of left-eye blurred vision.
6. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/70 OS.
7. Both eyes had normal pupillary responses, color vision, and intraocular pressures.
8. The results of an anterior chamber examination were unremarkable in each eye.

3. He had no history of contact lens use, ocular trauma, or ocular surgery.

B: Observe with serial examinations

1. A 63-year-old man with a history of well-controlled hypertension, lumbar stenosis, and hip arthroplasty with revisions presented with bilateral loss of vision and hearing for several weeks.
2. He also reported a history of painful paresthesias at his feet beginning about 1 year prior.
3. On examination, his visual acuity was initially 20/80 OD and 20/200 OS; it deteriorated over the next 2 months to finger counting bilaterally.
4. The Weber test gave a nonlateralizing result, and bone conduction hearing was absent bilaterally.
5. There was length-dependent loss of vibratory sensation and absent reflexes at both lower extremities.
6. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated abnormal enhancement of bilateral optic nerves (Figure, A).
7. Optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiogram were normal.
8. Nerve conduction studies showed mild sensory axonal polyneuropathy.
9. Laboratory tests were notable for elevated thyrotropin (63 mlU/ml), low levels of free thyroxine (T4) (0.2 ng/dL), and elevated levels of cerebrospinal fluid protein (94 mg/dL).
10. Cerebrospinal fluid IgG index, oligoclonal bands, aquaporin 4 antibody, paraneoplastic panel, and protein electrophoresis test results were all normal.
11. He was treated empirically with high-dose steroids and plasmapheresis, with no improvement in symptoms.
12. A, Axial postgadolinium, fat-suppressed, T-1–weighted magnetic resonance image of the orbits, demonstrating left greater than right enhancement of the optic nerves (arrowheads).
13. The enhancement is centrally located within the optic nerves on coronal sections (not shown).
14. No other lesions were seen in the brain.
15. B, Axial T-2–weighted magnetic resonance image of the right hip, demonstrating susceptibility artifact of orthopedic hardware, as well as soft tissue heterotopic ossification (corroborated by plain-film radiographs), consistent with pseudotumor of metallosis with decompression into the right hip joint space (blue asterisk), the subiliac bursa (red asterisk), greater trochanter bursa (yellow asterisk) extending into the gluteus maximus muscle (arrowheads), and into a potential space between the tensor fascia lata and the rectus femoris (black asterisk).
16. Four months after initial presentation, the patient reported new symptoms of chest tightness and dyspnea on exertion.
17. An echocardiogram showed a left ventricle ejection fraction of 20% to 25%, which had been 55% to 60% at the last test 2 years prior.
18. At 5 months after initial presentation, the patient developed acute worsening of dyspnea and was admitted for respiratory distress.
19. He was found to have nonischemic cardiomyopathy and died on hospital day 13.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic disease)
B: Amyloidosis
C: Susac syndrome
D: Cobalt toxicity

4. A mouth guard prescribed by her dentist for temporomandibular joint disease had provided substantial relief over the past 2 months.
5. She denied any history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, or human immunodeficiency virus exposure but had a 20 pack/year cigarette smoking history.
6. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 OU.
7. Automated perimetry revealed a small paracentral relative scotoma in the left eye.
8. Superficial temporal artery pulses were palpable without tenderness, and anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes.

10. No intra-arterial plaques were noted.

12. Fluorescein angiography revealed normal choroidal and retinal arterial perfusion.

14. A, Fundus photograph shows a normal left optic disc with an adjacent arc-shaped patch of retinal whitening and no other macular pathology.
15. B, Optical coherence tomography through the retinal lesion reveals abnormal thickening and hyperreflectivity of the retinal nerve fiber and ganglion cell layers (arrowhead), producing shadowing over an otherwise normal outer retina.
16. Perform diagnostic vitreous paracentesis and intravitreal antibiotic injection Start systemic corticosteroids and biopsy the superficial temporal artery

8. She had been treated with naproxen during these flares, which improved her joint pain but not her cutaneous symptoms.

10. Titers for parvovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and antistreptolysin O were also negative.A, Approximately 1-cm, oval-shaped, salmon-pink macules on the right lower abdomen and right lateral thigh.
11. B, 3- to 4-mm pink urticarial-appearing papules on the dorsal hand.
12. C, Flagellate arrays of nonblanching 1- to 2-mm petechial macules on the upper medial arm.

A: Systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis
B: Cystic fibrosis-associated episodic arthritis
C: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
D: Serum sickness-like reaction

1. A man in his late 30s with a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy presented for evaluation of sudden-onset painless blurry vision of the right eye.
2. His ocular history included nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage in the right eye requiring pars plana vitrectomy, panretinal photocoagulation, multiple treatments with intravitreous bevacizumab, and cataract extraction with placement of an intraocular lens (IOL) into the capsular bag approximately 4 years ago.
3. At his routine follow-up visit 2 weeks prior, the proliferative diabetic retinopathy was quiescent, and his Snellen visual acuity was 20/20 OD with manifest refraction of −1.50 + 0.25 × 180.
4. Examination of the anterior segment at that time was unremarkable.
5. At his current visit, visual acuity with the previous correction had been reduced to 20/150.
6. Repeated manifest refraction of the right eye was −4.00 + 1.50 × 166, resulting in a visual acuity of 20/25.
7. Intraocular pressure of the right eye was 10 mm Hg by Goldmann applanation tonometry.
8. Evaluation of the posterior segment, including dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula, showed stability compared with previous results.
9. Imaging of the anterior segment with OCT is shown in Figure 1.
10. The anterior chamber did not appear shallow, and there was no cell or flare.
11. Slitlamp photograph of the anterior segment (A) and optical coherence tomographic imaging of the lens–capsular bag complex (B) obtained at initial presentation (arrowheads show hyperdistention of the capsular bag with turbid fluid).
12. Perform posterior capsulotomy as part of pars plana vitrectomy

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform posterior capsulotomy as part of pars plana vitrectomy
B: Perform posterior capsulotomy with Nd:YAG laser
C: Exchange the IOL
D: Observe the patient

1. A man in his early 60s received his initial zoledronic acid (Aclasta, Novartis, Sydney) intravenous infusion (5 mg in 100 mL of solution) for the management of biochemically and radiologically diagnosed Paget disease of the bone.
2. Within 24 hours he developed prodromal flu like myalgias and malaise.
3. After 48 hours, the patient experienced severe bilateral photophobia, conjunctival injection, lacrimation, and blurred vision.
4. His photophobia peaked at 72 hours but had significantly improved by the time of his initial ophthalmic review 4 days after the infusion.
5. His uncorrected visual acuities were 6/5 bilaterally.
6. His intraocular pressures were within normal limits.
7. An anterior segment examination demonstrated symmetric bilateral nasal sectoral subconjunctival hemorrhages (Figure).
8. The corneas were clear.
9. Examination of his anterior chambers revealed a 2+ cell count and 2+ flare count in both eyes without hypopyon or synechiae.
10. The posterior segment was unremarkable, with no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or macular edema.
11. Routine investigations returned results of an elevated alkaline phosphatase level (230 U/L) and mild-positive (1:160) antinuclear antibody speckled pattern.
12. The complete blood cell count and coagulation profile were normal.
13. The results for extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, antidouble-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid, rheumatoid factor, human leukocyte antigen B27, QuantiFERON-TB Gold (Quest Diagnostics), syphilis serology, elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, and a chest radiography were all negative.
14. Topical dexamethasone, 0.1%, and homatropine, 2%, were commenced, with complete resolution of uveitic signs within 2 weeks.
15. Dexamethasone frequency was initially once hourly for 3 days and was followed by a standard weekly tapering course.
16. The homatropine frequency was twice daily.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Advise the patient’s endocrinologist to request an alternative to a bisphosphonate
B: Rechallenge the patient in 12 months with zoledronic acid and manage reactively if uveitis recurs
C: Preemptively treat the patient before his next dose of zoledronic acid
D: Treat the problem as an unrelated idiopathic uveitis

1. A 5-year-old girl was referred for evaluation of blepharoptosis of the left eye present since birth (Figure).
2. Her mother reported that, since infancy, the child’s left eye has twitched during feeding and mealtimes.
3. The patient was born at term; had an unremarkable delivery; and had no history of developmental delay, trauma, or systemic illness.
4. Her ocular history was significant only for bilateral mixed astigmatism (−0.25 + 0.75 × 145 OD and −0.25 + 1.00 × 005 OS).

6. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/40 OS.
7. Pupils were reactive to light bilaterally, and there was neither an afferent pupillary defect nor anisocoria.
8. Extraocular motility was full.
9. There was notable asymmetry in the following eyelid measurements: palpebral fissure height (10 mm OD; 5-6 mm OS) and margin reflex distance 1 (3.5 mm OD; 0.5-1.5 mm OS).
10. In addition, elevation of the left upper eyelid was observed with lateral jaw thrust but not with anterior-posterior jaw movements or with mouth opening and closing.
11. The levator function was 14 mm OU, and the margin crease distances were 5 mm OD and 6 mm OS.
12. The remainder of the anterior and posterior segment slitlamp examination was unremarkable.External photographs of blepharoptosis of the left eye in the neutral jaw position (A) and the left upper eyelid elevated with rightward jaw thrust (B).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Conduct genetic testing
B: Perform urgent neuroimaging
C: Start oral corticosteroids
D: Discuss carefully observing vs surgical repair of the ptosis

1. A 71-year-old man presented with 4 weeks of a diffuse rash along with 1 week of bilateral elbow and knee pain.
2. For the past year, he had recurrent episodes of diverticulitis complicated by colovesical fistula.
3. Six weeks ago, he underwent sigmoid colon resection with fistula repair.
4. He had no fever, abdominal pain, dysuria, or urinary frequency.
5. He was prescribed prednisone when the rash first presented (starting at 30 mg/d and decreased by 10 mg every 4 days).
6. The rash improved initially but recurred at the 10-mg/d prednisone dosing.
7. Medical history included glaucoma, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteoarthritis.
8. His home medications included lansoprazole, probiotics, vitamin B12, folic acid, vitamin D3, prednisone (10 mg/d), and timolol eye gel.
9. He had no sick contacts or recent travel and reported no alcohol or tobacco use.
10. On examination, the patient was afebrile and normotensive, with a pulse of 88/min.
11. He had an erythematous rash, characterized by a combination of palpable purpura and petechiae extending from the axilla to the lower abdomen, back, and lower extremities (Figure 1A).
12. The face, neck, chest, upper extremities, and oral and nasal mucosa were spared.
13. The abdomen was nontender, with a healed postoperative scar.
14. Cardiopulmonary and musculoskeletal examination results were unremarkable.
15. Left, Cutaneous findings on physical examination.

18. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria (6-10 red blood cells) and 1+ proteinuria.
19. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio on morning void was 1.17 mg/mg creatinine.
20. A punch biopsy of the rash on the lower abdomen was performed (Figure 1B).
21. Check serologies for hepatitis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), parvovirus, and streptococcal infections.
22. Perform direct immunofluorescence (DIF) evaluation of the skin biopsy.
23. Prescribe steroids with a slow and prolonged tapering regimen

1. A neonate in her second week of life was brought to our hospital for evaluation of a scalp lesion initially thought to be an open abscess.
2. She was born full term to a primigravid mother, who had an uncomplicated pregnancy.
3. At parturition, the baby presented in occiput posterior position and remained partly crowned for more than 24 hours of maternal labor.
4. Finally, due to failure to progress, the baby was delivered by urgent cesarean delivery.
5. Birth weight was 3.13 kg (15th percentile), head circumference was 31 cm (<1 percentile), and Apgar score was 9 of 9.
6. The baby’s head had a markedly elongate vertex, which the neonatal intensive care unit team diagnosed as cephalohematoma.
7. On day 5 of life, her serum total bilirubin and conjugated bilirubin were 20.5 mg/dL (>95 percentile) and 0.3 mg/dL (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 17.104), respectively.
8. The girl was hospitalized for 1 day of phototherapy before being discharged home weighing 2.95 kg (−5.75%).
9. She was exclusively breastfed.
10. She was admitted to our hospital for evaluation of the scalp.
11. Wound culture samples were sent for analysis, and she was given empirical intravenous clindamycin hydrochloride.
12. Dermatology was consulted.
13. On examination, the baby was alert and healthy appearing, although her sclerae were icteric.
14. The vertex of her scalp was uniformly boggy, soft, and edematous, extending beyond suture lines, consistent with a diagnosis of caput succedaneum.
15. On the right occiput, there was a mat of hair and thick serosanguineous crust adhering to the scalp (Figure 1A).
16. Beneath the mat and extending laterally in both directions was a deep, 8 × 1-cm, trenchlike ulcer with no drainage (Figure 1B).
17. It was nontender to palpation.
18. A, Serosanguineous crust adhering to occipital scalp of a neonate.
19. Prior to removing this crust it was being treated as an open ulcer.
20. B, Trenchlike linear ulcer revealed after removal of the crust.
21. It was 8 × 1 cm in size, was nontender to palpation, and did not appear to be infected.
22. Cellulitis and abscess associated with neonatal group B streptococcal infection

A: Aplasia cutis congenita

D: Halo scalp ring (pressure necrosis)

14. Intraocular pressure was 10 mm Hg OU.
15. There was ecchymosis of the right upper eyelid.
16. Results of dilated eye examination were unremarkable. 24-2 Humphrey visual fields were normal in both eyes.
17. Magnetic resonance angiography of the head showed no vascular abnormalities.
18. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits showed a fusiform heterogeneous peripherally enhancing extraconal mass within the superior orbit on the right, resulting in proptosis with downward displacement of the right globe (Figure).

D: Perform a surgical drainage of the collection

1. A postmenopausal woman in her mid-50s (gravida 2, aborta 2) with a known history of endometriosis and adenomyosis presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain that she rated 10 of 10 in intensity and which had developed suddenly 5 days before presentation.

3. On examination, the patient was afebrile and her abdomen was soft and nondistended without guarding or rebound but tender in the left lower quadrant.
4. The patient had a palpable nodule in the posterior vaginal fornix and fullness in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen on bimanual examination.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Rupture of an infected endometriotic implant
B: Inflamed diverticulum
C: Perforation by foreign bodies
D: Malignant growth with unknown primary tumor

1. An adolescent boy presented with cognitive and behavioral changes, headaches, and progressively worsening weakness of the left arm and leg.
2. The patient was subsequently admitted to our hospital for further evaluation.
3. Sixteen months earlier, the patient was admitted to a hospital for weakness of the left fingers and mild spasticity of the left lower extremity.
4. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at the time revealed a suspicious lesion in the right basal ganglia (Figure, A).
5. In addition, carotid and intracranial angiography revealed no abnormalities (not shown).
6. Slight weakness in the left lower extremity was detected 3 months later.
7. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed nonhomogeneous hyperintensity on T2-weighted images in the right basal ganglia without mass effect (Figure, B).
8. Atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere and right cerebral peduncle was observed (not shown).
9. A, T2-weighted axial brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at the basal ganglia level performed 16 months before the current hospitalization showing slight hyperintensity at the right putamen and posterior limb of the internal capsule (arrowhead).
10. B, T2-weighted axial MRI performed 13 months before the current hospitalization showing moderate hyperintensity at the right basal ganglia without mass effect (arrowhead).
11. C, T2-weighted axial MRI at the basal ganglia level showing remarkable progression of the lesions in the right basal ganglia and thalamus with heterogeneous high signal intensity and multicystic change (arrowhead).
12. There was no history of tumors elsewhere, and his family history was unremarkable.
13. Neurological examination revealed distal left hemiparesis, left facial palsy, and decreased pinprick sensation in his left face and extremities.
14. On MRI, the lesion appeared larger than before (Figure, C), with remarkable heterogeneous enhancement (not shown).
15. Human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) levels in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were normal.
16. A hormone assay disclosed normal pituitary function.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Glioma
B: Infarction
C: Germinoma
D: Demyelination

1. A 33-year-old white man presented with a 5-month history of a progressively necrotic plaque on the nose and scattered nodules on the extremities.
2. The plaque first appeared as a small inflammatory papule on the left nostril.
3. Shortly thereafter, the patient was hospitalized at an outside facility for multifocal pneumonia.
4. He was also treated for a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection of his nose.
5. Despite antibiotic therapy, the papule continued to grow and ulcerate and eventually became necrotic (Figure, A).
6. One month before presentation at our facility, the patient began developing erythematous papules on his arms and legs.
7. The papules enlarged and ulcerated.
8. Some of them healed spontaneously with poxlike scars.

13. Head computed tomography demonstrated a soft-tissue mass that encased the nasal bone and extended into the right maxillary sinus and left nasal cavity.
14. Chest computed tomography showed bilateral pulmonary nodules.
15. Physical examination revealed a necrotic plaque with surrounding erythema on the distal nose (Figure, A).
16. A 1 × 1-cm crateriform papule with central necrosis was present on the left malar cheek.
17. Multiple nodules with central, dry necrosis and areas of poxlike scarring were scattered across the extremities.
18. Slight contractures of his fingers were also noted.A, Clinical photograph.
19. B-D, Analyses of a shave biopsy specimen of the necrotic papule on the patient’s left cheek (B, hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400; C, original magnification ×400; D, original magnification ×200).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
B: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis
C: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis)
D: Histoplasmosis

question:
1. An 11-day-old girl presented with a worsening corneal opacity of the right eye.
2. The patient had received a diagnosis of conjunctivitis at 6 days of life but failed to respond to treatment with topical erythromycin ophthalmic ointment, 0.5%.
3. The baby was an otherwise healthy girl born at full term.
4. Her perinatal history was significant only for a positive maternal test for group B Streptococcus agalactiae, which was treated prior to delivery.
5. Results of the initial examination were significant for conjunctival hyperemia or vasodilation of the right eye, with a 3 × 4-mm central corneal ulcer.
6. Results of B-scan ultrasonography showed no posterior chamber involvement.
7. Corneal cultures for bacteria, fungi, and herpes simplex virus were obtained.
8. Owing to concern for systemic involvement of group B S agalactiae, herpes simplex virus, and other infectious causes, the patient was admitted to the children’s hospital for a full sepsis workup.
9. Treatment with topical polymyxin B sulfate-trimethoprim and intravenous ampicillin, cefepime hydrochloride, and acyclovir sodium was initiated.
10. Results of spinal ultrasonography demonstrated spinal cord tethering at L4, preventing lumbar puncture and collection of cerebrospinal fluid for culture.
11. Two days later, the patient’s right eye developed a hypopyon, and its intraocular pressure was elevated (Figure).
12. Anterior chamber fluid was sent for culture.
13. Results of another B-scan ultrasonography showed a normal posterior segment without inflammation.
14. The topical antibiotic eyedrops were changed to fortified vancomycin hydrochloride, 50 mg/mL, and tobramycin sulfate, 14 mg/mL, and topical timolol maleate, 0.5%, and dorzolamide hydrochloride, 2.0%, were added.
15. The following day, the hypopyon worsened.
16. Photograph of the right eye demonstrating a central corneal infiltrate and large temporal layered hypopyon.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform another anterior chamber paracentesis procedure and culture
B: Perform corneal biopsy
C: Inject intravitreal antibiotics
D: Start prednisolone eyedrops

question:
1. A woman in her 30s was referred for evaluation of corneal opacities.
2. Her medical history was notable for keratoconjunctivitis sicca, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and anti–interferon-γ autoantibody syndrome treated with 6 monthly rituximab infusions (375 mg/m2 with 100 mg of methylprednisolone acetate).
3. Infusions were given weekly for the first 3 weeks and then every 6 to 8 months based on a CD20 count.
4. She had previously been diagnosed with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection requiring 2 years of treatment with rifabutin, 300 mg/d; ethambutol hydrochloride, 1000 mg/d; and clarithromycin in a divided dose, 500 mg twice a day.
5. This treatment concluded 2½ years before presentation.
6. In addition, she had a long-standing history of arthralgias with intermittent arthritis treated with hydroxychloroquine, 300 mg/d, that was discontinued 2 years before presentation.
7. On examination, she had no visual concerns.
8. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU.
9. Conjunctivas were normal, lenses were clear, and anterior chambers were deep and quiet.
10. The results from the slitlamp examination showed numerous bilateral, peripheral light brown corneal opacities.
11. The opacities were located in the far posterior corneae and were present circumferentially (Figure, A).
12. There was no associated keratitis or corneal neovascularization.
13. Anterior segment optical coherence tomographic findings showed focal areas of hyperreflectivity anterior to the Descemet membrane.
14. Confocal microscopy revealed variably shaped, hyperreflective clusters of opacities just anterior to the endothelium (Figure, B).
15. Imaging of the right eye of a patient with rifabutin-related posterior corneal deposits.
16. A, Slitlamp photograph with arrowhead highlighting one of numerous bilateral peripheral, small corneal light brown opacities.
17. B, Confocal microscopic image captured at a slightly oblique angle illustrates normal endothelial cells (yellow arrowhead).
18. Just anterior to the endothelium, the drug deposit appears as variably shaped, hyperreflective clusters of opacities (white arrowhead).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start treatment with topical corticosteroids
B: Start treatment with topical antibiotics
C: Plan a descemetorhexis and posterior cornea biopsy
D: Reassure the patient and observe

2. She recalled having a small abrasion on her left leg before wading waist-deep in search of trout.
3. Prior to presentation, she was unsuccessfully treated by 3 different physicians for allergic contact dermatitis and cellulitis.

8. The left leg was tender to palpation.
9. The patient reported no history of cutaneous eruptions on her legs or feet, and there was no obvious thickening, yellowish discoloration, or subungual debris of the fingernails or toenails on examination.
10. A laboratory work-up, potassium hydroxide scraping (Figure, C), and punch biopsies for histopathologic analysis and fungal, bacterial, and atypical mycobacterial tissue cultures were performed.A, Erythematous, crusted, edematous plaques and pustules on the left leg prior to definitive treatment.
11. B, Near complete resolution of pustules and resultant postinflammatory hyperpigmentation after definitive treatment.
12. C, Potassium hydroxide scraping taken from the left leg.

A: Bacterial folliculitis
B: Mycobacterium marinum
C: Sporotrichosis
D: Majocchi granuloma

1. A previously healthy man in his 30s presented with spontaneous bruising, epistaxis, and haematuria.
2. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML) was diagnosed by bone marrow aspirate morphology, immunophenotyping, and detection of the bcr1 variant of the PML-RARα fusion transcript in peripheral blood.
3. He was commenced on treatment with the PETHEMA LPA 20051 protocol consisting of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and idarubicin, an anthracycline based chemotherapy.
4. Dexamethasone was prescribed to reduce the risk of ATRA syndrome, a potentially life threatening complication seen in these patients and characterized by fever, pulmonary infiltrates, hypotension, and leucocytosis.
5. After 12 days of treatment, the patient developed pyrexia and was started on empiric antibiotics.
6. Two days later he developed tender black spots on the scrotum that progressed to painful ulcers over 8 days (Figure, A).
7. Systemic antifungal and antiviral therapy were added with no improvement.
8. Peripheral blood cultures and skin swabs from the lesions did not identify bacterial or viral infection.
9. Scrotal ultrasonography showed a subcutaneous hypervascular lesion with no abscess.
10. The development and progression of scrotal ulceration coincided with recovery in neutrophil count from 0.3 × 109/L to 1.2 × 109/L and persistent pyrexia.
11. As scrotal ulceration progressed, they enlarged and became necrotic with a black eschar.
12. A specimen was obtained for histopathology.
13. A, Clinical photograph of scrotum and penis shows ulceration and necrosis of penile and scrotal skin with surrounding inflammation.
14. B, Scrotal biopsy histopathologic specimen (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×20).
15. Scrotal ulceration secondary to induction chemotherapy with ATRA

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Fournier gangrene (necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum)
B: Scrotal ulceration secondary to induction chemotherapy with ATRA
C: Deep fungal infection
D: Mycobacterial infection

1. A 21-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressive depression, bradyphrenia, dyscalculia, and fatigue, necessitating withdrawal from college.
2. She had an ovarian cyst, but her medical history was otherwise unremarkable.
3. There was no history of recreational drug use, tobacco or alcohol consumption, or sexually transmitted diseases.
4. Her mother had died at 32 years of age, after having a chronic neuropsychiatric illness, culminating in a rapidly progressive dementia.
5. A postmortem brain examination reported the presence of multitudinous corpora amylacea, but no specific neuropathological diagnosis was made.Neurologic examination of the patient during the initial consultation revealed a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 24 of 30 (points were missed on attention, calculation, and abstraction), and the patient was abulic, but it was otherwise unremarkable.
6. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed scattered small foci of T2 hyperintensity in the white matter affecting the corpus callosum, bifrontal, and biparietal regions, associated with bifrontal and bitemporal atrophy (Figure1A).
7. No lesions were identified in the cerebellum or brainstem.
8. There was no abnormal enhancement.
9. Laboratory investigations including complete blood cell count with differential; electrolytes; liver, renal, and thyroid function tests; vitamin B12 and folate levels; vitamin E; cholesterol and triglycerides; amino acids (serum and urine); syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serologies; a paraneoplastic panel; and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were unrevealing.
10. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a slight protein elevation, but no pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands, or elevated immunoglobulin G synthesis rate.
11. Arylsulfatase activity was normal.A, Axial T2 sequence showing bifrontal cerebral convexity sulcal enlargement greater than expected for patient's age, punctate bifrontal subcortical fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintense foci (right greater than left) are noted.
12. B, Brain magnetic resonance imaging axial and coronal T2 FLAIR sequence showing more pronounced global cerebral atrophy, progression of the subcortical FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the frontal predominant distribution, and also affecting the periventricular and deep white matter into the subcortical areas.

B: Adrenoleukodystrophy

2. Although previously healthy, he reported some hospitalizations for nonspecific abdominal pain during his infancy.
3. Colicky abdominal pain started after eating cornflakes in the morning, then regressed spontaneously during the day.
4. A relapse of the symptoms occurred the morning after and worsened during the day, with the onset of nausea as well.
5. For this reason, the patient autonomously took 2 tablets of hyoscine butyl bromide without any benefit.
6. His bowel was initially open to gas and normal stools but, afterward, only to gas.
7. A physical examination revealed a soft and nondistended abdomen, with localized tenderness and guarding in the epigastric region and in the right lower quadrant.
8. Hyperactive bowel sounds could be heard.
9. The results of a digital rectal examination were normal.
10. His vital signs were as follows: an axillary temperature of 37.3°C, a pulse rate of 71 beats per minute, and blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg.
11. The results of a urinalysis were negative; blood test results were within the normal limits, except for an elevated white blood cell count of 13 000/μL (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001), an unconjugated bilirubin level of 1.2 mg/dL (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 17.104), an increased aspartate aminotransferase level of 52 U/L (to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), and an alanine aminotransferase level of 136 U/L (to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167).
12. His C-reactive protein level was 10 mg/L (to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).
13. A plain radiograph of his abdomen was negative for air-fluid levels and for signs of perforation.
14. 1. A 75-year-old woman of white race/ethnicity was referred for bilateral choroidal lesions.
2. She described her vision as being blurred in the left eye, with areas of her vision being “blocked.” Her review of systems was unremarkable.

10. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated hyperechoic, plaquelike, solid lesions with posterior acoustic shadowing corresponding anatomically to the lesions seen on clinical examination (Figure, B).
11. Fluorescein and indocyanine angiography demonstrated leakage in the area of subretinal hemorrhage in the left eye (Figure, C).
12. A, A yellowish lesion is located in the superonasal quadrant with nasal subretinal hemorrhage (asterisk).
13. B, B-scan ultrasonography (transverse at the 11-o’clock equator) reveals a hyperechoic, plaquelike, solid lesion with posterior acoustic shadowing, consistent with calcification corresponding to the clinically visible lesion.
14. C, Superonasal leakage corresponding to the area of clinically visible subretinal hemorrhage.
15. Check parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and calcium levels

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform transvitreous biopsy
B: Begin oral corticosteroid therapy
C: Check parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and calcium levels
D: Treat with plaque brachytherapy

2. He received oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and 2 days of intravenous clindamycin phosphate and ceftriaxone sodium.

4. The patient was discharged with a tentative diagnosis of viral conjunctivitis.
5. Three days later, the patient returned with fever, prominent submandibular lymphadenopathy, and ipsilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis (Figure).
6. Results of the remainder of the anterior segment and dilated examination were unremarkable.

11. Perform conjunctival cultures on blood, chocolate, Löwenstein-Jensen, Sabouraud, and thioglycolate media before restarting antibiotic therapy.

13. Perform serologic testing for Bartonella henselae and Francisella tularensis

1. A 56-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma receiving ipilimumab and nivolumab every 3 weeks developed headaches during the course of her treatment.
2. In the week following her first treatment, the patient reported a few mild morning headaches that improved with acetaminophen.
3. After receiving 3 cycles of ipilimumab, 3 mg/kg, and nivolumab, 1 mg/kg, and 8 weeks after her first treatment, the patient reported experiencing daily headaches for at least the prior week and a half.
4. The location of her headaches varied, and there was no associated eye or temple pain.
5. At best, with taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, the headache decreased to pain rated 3 on a scale of 1 to 10.
6. Also at this time, the patient reported low energy levels and difficulty reading; however, physical examination showed no gross visual field defects.
7. Laboratory workup conducted 8 weeks after initiating treatment included adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol levels that were measured at 25 pg/mL (reference range, 10-60 pg/mL) and 16.8 μg/dL (reference range, 6-24 μg/dL), respectively.
8. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was 0.82 mIU/L (reference range, 0.5-5.0 mIU/L), which was gradually decreasing compared with 1.41 mIU/L 5 weeks earlier and 1.21 mIU/L 2 weeks earlier.
9. Her total triiodothyronine level was measured at 73 ng/dL (reference range, 80-200 ng/dL) and free thyroxine level was 1.0 ng/dL (reference range, 0.9-1.7 ng/dL).
10. Her serum sodium level was measured at 138 mEq/L; 1 week later it was measured at 135 mEq/L (reference range, 135-145 mEq/L).
11. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was performed for further assessment (Figure).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Brain metastasis
B: Immune-related hypophysitis
C: Pituitary adenoma
D: Mucocele

1. An infant boy, born to a nonconsanguineously wed couple, presented to the dermatology outpatient clinic with recurrent skin blisters since age 2 months.
2. The lesions initially started over the trunk and subsequently progressed to involve the face, hands, and feet.
3. The episodes of skin blisters were accompanied by pruritus and redness all over the body.
4. There was no history of oral erosions or difficulty in feeding.
5. Bowel and bladder movements were normal.
6. The child had an older sibling who had no skin ailments, and none of the other family members were affected.
7. On examination, multiple tense, angulated vesicles and bullae on a background of erythema were seen over the face, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A and B).
8. Few urticated papules and wheals were seen in isolation over the trunk.
9. The ruptured bullae were healing with hypopigmentation with accompanying scarring and discrete milia formation.
10. The mucosae and nails were normal.
11. No contractures or webbing of fingers was noted.
12. There was no organomegaly.
13. A punch biopsy from a vesicle was subsequently performed (Figure, C and D).
14. A, Multiple angulated vesicles and tense bullae over the forehead and chin.
15. Background erythema can be appreciated.
16. B, Tense bullae over the trunk with superficial erosions and postinflammatory hypopigmentation, which are healing with scarring and discrete milia formation.
17. Few urticated papules and plaques can also be appreciated.
18. C, Subepidermal bulla with bandlike mast cell infiltrate in the upper dermis (hematoxylin and eosin stain).
19. D, Higher magnification showing dense infiltrate of mast cells in the upper dermis.
20. Mast cells can be identified by ovoid to spindle-shaped nuclei (hematoxylin and eosin stain).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa
B: Chronic bullous disease of childhood
C: Bullous mastocytosis
D: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria

2. The numbness progressed over 10 months to involve his entire right arm, patches of his left arm, and his distal lower extremities.
3. He also developed right-hand incoordination and imbalance.
4. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain is shown in Figure 1A.
5. A complete blood cell count with a differential; liver function testing; tests for HIV, rapid plasma reagin, serum aquaporin-4 antibody, and antinuclear antibodies; and levels of sodium, calcium, creatinine, glucose, thyroxine, and vitamin B12 were unremarkable.
6. Examinations of the cerebrospinal fluid had normal results twice, including for white blood cell count with a differential, glucose level, total protein level, IgG index, oligoclonal bands, cultures, and cytology testing.A, A brain coronal T1 postgadolinium magnetic resonance image (MRI), showing a lobulated heterogeneously enhancing mass in the brainstem and dural enhancement.
7. B, A brain coronal T1 postgadolinium MRI from 10 months later with persistent yet evolving enhancement and mild size increase in brainstem lesion and ongoing dural enhancement.He sought neurological reconsultation 9 months later, reporting progressive blurred vision bilaterally, dysphagia, dysarthria, and urinary and bowel urgency.

A: Sarcoidosis
B: Erdheim-Chester disease
C: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
D: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis associated with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody

3. He was diagnosed as having glaucoma 6 months prior to presentation owing to optic nerve cupping and visual field deficits on automated perimetry and was taking latanoprost.
4. His medical history was significant for pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, and his family history was notable for glaucoma in his grandmother.
5. He was being treated by the neurology department for his pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency with thiamine, vitamin C, and oxaloacetate.
6. His systemic symptoms included hyperhidrosis and episodes of hand tremors, ataxia, and dysarthria that occur every 2 to 3 years.

8. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 16 mm Hg OU, and pachymetry was 611 μM OD and 592 μM OS (normal mean [SD], 542.4  [33.5] μM).
9. He identified 8/8 OD and 3/8 OS Ishihara color plates.
10. He had an exotropia with full range of motion in both eyes.
11. His nuclear sclerotic cataracts were not consistent with visual acuity in both eyes; his anterior segment examination was otherwise within normal limits.
12. His dilated examination was normal except for cupping and pallor in both eyes with a supratemporal optic nerve pit in the right eye.
13. The optic discs and automated perimetry are shown in the Figure.

15. A and B, Fundus photographs show cupping with optic nerve pallor in both eyes and a supratemporal optic nerve pit in the right eye (arrowhead).
16. C and D, Automated perimetry demonstrating temporal hemianopia respecting the vertical midline in the left eye with cecocentral scotoma in the right eye, consistent with a junctional scotoma.
17. Repeated visual fields with IOP check in 1 month

A: Observation
B: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain/orbits

D: Repeated visual fields with IOP check in 1 month

9. Her neurological and mental state examination had unremarkable results.

12. Back biopsy shows occlusion of dermal blood vessels, perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, and mucin deposition (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×40).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Pancreatitis panniculitis
B: Malignant atrophic papulosis
C: Systemic lupus erythematosus
D: Lymphomatoid papulosis

2. Her ocular history was notable for a previous uncomplicated cataract surgery in the left eye that had a good visual outcome.

7. A dilated examination revealed multiple spots of retinal whitening with tiny intraretinal hemorrhages concentrated in the posterior pole (Figure, A).
8. The patient was referred urgently for consultation by a retina specialist.
9. Optical coherence tomography revealed intraretinal cystoid abnormalities in the macula and hyperreflective patches in the nerve fiber layer and inner nuclear layer (Figure, B).
10. A, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrating multifocal patches of inner retinal whitening in the posterior pole.
11. B, Optical coherence tomography through the macula demonstrating mild intraretinal cystoid abnormalities and hyperreflective thickened areas in the nerve fiber and inner nuclear layer, corresponding to the white retinal patches.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start systemic steroids
B: Obtain more information on the patient’s history
C: Vitreous tap and injection of foscarnet
D: Infectious and autoimmune workup

1. A 16-year-old girl presented to our ataxia unit with a report of a peculiar finding in fundoscopy.
2. Her parents were nonconsanguineous, and her family history was unremarkable.
3. She had unsteadiness and frequent falls at gait initiation since age 16 months.
4. There was a progressive worsening of her gait difficulties, and she complained of loss of balance.
5. On examination, she had saccadic pursuit, subtle appendicular ataxia, and a spastic gait with a wide base.
6. She could not stand or walk with her feet in the tandem position.
7. Her muscle strength was normal.
8. Achilles tendon reflexes and plantar responses were absent, and vibration sense was decreased in her toes and ankles.
9. Visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields were normal.
10. Fundoscopy revealed increased visibility of retinal nerve fibers, hiding the contours of retinal vessels bilaterally.
11. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed increased thickness in the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) (Figure 1).
12. Ophthalmological findings include color fundus photograph of the right eye (A) with increased visibility of the retinal nerve fiber layer, which hides retinal vessel contour; an optical coherence tomographic vertical B-scan revealing a markedly thickened retinal nerve fiber layer (asterisks) (B), captured along the green line seen on a red-free image of fundus (C).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
B: Friedreich ataxia
C: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
D: Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia

2. He had initially developed rhinorrhea, cough, and low-grade fever 2 weeks prior.
3. The patient was treated with azithromycin and subsequently developed few small, pruritic blisters on the hands and feet.
4. He went to an urgent care facility and was diagnosed as having bronchitis and prescribed doxycycline and diphenhydramine.
5. Over the next several days, he developed worsening fever, chills, and blisters and bullae on the arms, legs, and face.
6. He was admitted to the hospital, and the dermatology service was consulted.
7. Physical examination revealed numerous pink to violaceous macules, papules, and patches on the palms, dorsal hands, forearms, elbows, feet, and distal lower extremities (Figure, A and B).
8. Fewer, scattered macules were on the face, neck, trunk, upper legs, upper arms, and scrotum.
9. Dusky bullae were seen on the bilateral dorsal aspect of the hands, fingers, toes, and heels.
10. In the oral cavity, there was 1 violaceous macule on the right buccal mucosa and a few linear, horizontal, white lines on the left buccal mucosa.
11. Laboratory findings revealed a white blood cell count of 25 600/μL (reference range, 3700-10 500/μL) and a platelet count of 12 400/μL (reference range, 15 000-40 000/μL).
12. Results from a Tzanck smear from the initial lesion on the right dorsal aspects of the third finger were negative for multinucleated giant cells.
13. A punch biopsy was performed on the anterior side of the thigh

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Atypical hand-foot-mouth disease
B: Disseminated zoster
C: Erythema multiforme
D: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis

10. B, Fluorescein angiography frame (2 minutes, 3 seconds) shows multiple microaneurysms in correspondence of the dot-blot retinal hemorrhages and a barely visible perifoveal vascular leakage.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observe
B: Perform panretinal photocoagulation
C: Obtain carotid Doppler
D: Refer to cardiology

8. Skin examination otherwise had unremarkable results, including normal scalp, palms, soles, and nails, as well as no palpable cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.

question:
1. A 2-year-old white boy was referred for evaluation of a choroidal mass.
2. He had mild periorbital edema and low-grade eye pain in the left eye over 2 weeks prior to presentation.
3. He had completed antibiotic treatment for presumed sinusitis with no improvement.
4. A recent flulike illness over the past 1.5 weeks responded minimally to ibuprofen.
5. Medical and family history were otherwise unremarkable.
6. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits revealed an intraocular mass, suspicious for retinoblastoma.
7. The patient was advised consultation by an ocular oncology service.
8. On examination, visual acuity was fix and follow OU.
9. The right eye showed normal findings anteriorly and posteriorly.
10. The left eye revealed mild conjunctival chemosis with periorbital edema.
11. There was trace eyelid edema and mild leukocoria.
12. Dilated ophthalmoscopic examination of the left eye displayed a solid gray mass in the macular region, deep to the retina and with surrounding subretinal fluid (Figure 1A).
13. A, Dilated ophthalmoscopic examination found a gray mass in the macular region of the left eye measuring 12 mm in diameter and 5.1 mm in thickness, with additional subretinal fluid inferiorly.
14. B, B-scan ultrasonography confirmed the fundus mass, dependent subretinal fluid, and echolucency outside the posterior wall of the eye.
15. Examination under anesthesia confirmed the solid mass, measuring 12 mm in diameter and 5.1 mm in thickness and demonstrating echodensity on ultrasonography (Figure 1B).
16. There were no tumor-feeding vessels, and tumor margins were ill defined.
17. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated slight hyperfluorescence of the disc and faint hyperfluorescence of the mass with overlying scattered pinpoint hyperfluorescent leakage.
18. Optical coherence tomography revealed shallow subretinal fluid extending within 3.2 mm of the foveola.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Treat with intra-arterial chemotherapy
B: Treat with plaque radiotherapy
C: Treat with oral corticosteroids
D: Perform fine-needle aspiration biopsy

C: Acquired palmoplantar keratoderma
D: Sclerotylosis (Huriez syndrome)

question:
1. A 25-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC) presented to the emergency department with lower abdominal pain.
2. She received a diagnosis of UC 6 years earlier and has taken mesalamine to control UC.
3. She was discharged a week before this admission for a UC flare that was managed with prednisone.
4. Review of systems was notable for diarrhea; however, she denied hematochezia, melena, emesis, fevers, or changes in urination.
5. Her last colonoscopy was 3 years ago, and UC without evidence of dysplasia was confirmed.
6. Otherwise, her medical history was unremarkable.
7. Family history was negative for inflammatory bowel diseases and gastrointestinal malignancies.
8. On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs.
9. Her abdomen was tender to palpation in the left lower quadrant, which was soft and nondistended.
10. The patient’s complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel results were unremarkable.
11. Computed tomographic scan of the abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a thickened colon from the middescending colon to the rectosigmoid.
12. There was also a 2.7-cm intramural abscess in the descending colon.
13. She started receiving piperacillin/tazobactam but began to have increased abdominal pain, emesis, and inability to tolerate oral intake.
14. A repeated computed tomographic scan performed 4 days after the original scan demonstrated that the intramural mass had increased to 3.5 cm and was partially obstructing the descending colon.
15. She underwent a colonoscopy, which demonstrated multiple areas of inflammation in the rectum through the descending colon (Figure 1).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Ulcerative colitis flare
B: Conversion to Crohn disease
C: Adenocarcinoma
D: Lymphoma

3. He was nonadherent with medications and denied drug and alcohol abuse.
4. On examination, he appeared comfortable.

9. Folic acid level was low (3 nmol/L [reference, ≥5 nmol/L]) and vitamin B12 level was normal (478 pg/mL [reference, 193-982 pg/mL]).
10. Results for iron panel, reticulocyte count, prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), international normalized ratio, liver function tests, and levels of indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin, fibrinogen, and creatine kinase were all within reference range.

1. A man in his 50s presented with an abdominal skin eruption of 2 days’ duration.
2. His medical history included hepatitis C, cirrhosis, and an orthotopic liver transplant (OLT) 3 years prior that was subsequently treated with tacrolimus, 5 mg, and mycophenolate, 750 mg, twice daily.
3. Approximately 2½ years after the transplant, the patient developed gastric outlet obstruction secondary to an infiltrative gastric wall mass.
4. The gastric wall mass was found to be associated with plasmablastic posttransplantation lymphoproliferative disorder (pPTLD).
5. He was subsequently instructed to stop use of mycophenolate and decrease use of tacrolimus to 0.25 mg daily, then treated with 1 cycle of CHOP chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin hydrochloride, vincristine sulfate, and prednisone) and lenalidomide, resulting in symptomatic and radiologic improvement.
6. Five weeks after treatment with CHOP chemotherapy, the patient presented with an acute-onset abdominal skin eruption without fever or pain.
7. A computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed possible abdominal wall cellulitis, so treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin was empirically started.
8. Physical examination revealed confluent indurated violaceous papules and plaques coalescing into an annular pattern encircling the healed OLT incisional scar with central sparing (Figure 1A).
9. A 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B and C) and bacterial and fungal cultures.A, Confluent, indurated, violaceous papules and plaques coalescing into an annular pattern encircling the well-healed orthotopic liver transplant incisional scar.
10. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the punch biopsy shows an atypical, hyperchromatic infiltrate present throughout the superficial and deep dermis.
11. C, High magnification reveals crushed but markedly atypical-appearing lymphoid cells with nuclear hyperchromasia and scant amounts of cytoplasm.
12. Multiple mitotic and apoptotic figures are easily identified.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Reactive granulomatous disorder
B: Posttransplantation lymphoproliferative disorder
C: Deep fungal infection
D: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma

question:
1. A 14-year-old girl was seen with progressive vision loss in both eyes.
2. Two years before our examination, her visual acuity had been 20/200 OD and 20/60 OS.
3. At our initial evaluation, her visual acuity was 20/300 OD and 20/250 OS.
4. Optic nerve atrophy was noted, with no optociliary collaterals.
5. Imaging of the retinal nerve fiber layer showed thinning in both eyes.
6. Automated perimetry demonstrated general constriction of visual fields and bilateral central scotomas.
7. Ocular motility was full, without pain, and orthotropic.
8. Two years prior, initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits with and without contrast was read as normal.
9. Retrospectively, those images were reviewed and noted to be limited due to artifact from dental braces and a lack of fat suppression.
10. Two years prior, lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure.
11. Complete blood cell count with differential was negative, as were test results for erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption, antinuclear antibody, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and serum neuromyelitis optica antibodies.
12. Whole-exome genome sequencing was negative for genes associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and type 2.
13. After removal of dental braces, MRI of the brain and orbits with and without contrast demonstrated thickening and nodular enhancement of bilateral perioptic nerve sheaths extending up to the orbital apex.
14. Patchy T2-weighted hyperintensity was noted within the bilateral optic nerves (Figure).
15. A, T1-weighted fat-suppressed image demonstrates thick, nodular, circumferential enhancement in the bilateral optic sheaths.
16. B, T1-weighted postcontrast image shows sparing of the optic chiasm.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Observation
B: Optic nerve sheath biopsy
C: Radiotherapy (fractionated external beam radiotherapy)
D: Optic nerve sheath biopsy and radiotherapy

4. The child’s parents denied any new topical exposures or medications.
5. The child was born via vaginal delivery at full term.

14. Serum zinc and alkaline phosphatase were within normal limits.
15. A punch biopsy of the edge of the ulcer was obtained and stained with hematoxylin-eosin (Figure, B and C).
16. Microbial stains were negative.
17. Tissue cultures for anaerobic and/or aerobic, mycobacterial, and fungal organisms were all negative, though wound cultures grew Escherichia coli, Klebsiella oxytoca, and Enterococcus faecalis.
18. Viral cultures were negative.
19. A, Clinical photograph shows a symmetric, well-defined ulcer with a cribriform base, central necrosis, and rolled, pink-to-violaceous, undermined border extending from the gluteal cleft to just inferior and medial to the scrotum.
20. B, Histopathology demonstrating an ulcer with surrounding mild epidermal hyperplasia and a neutrophil predominant perivascular and interstitial infiltrate.
21. C, Histopathology demonstrating an ulcer with surrounding mild epidermal hyperplasia and a neutrophil predominant perivascular and interstitial infiltrate.

A: Fournier gangrene
B: Pyoderma gangrenosum

D: Acquired acrodermatitis enteropathica

question:
1. A woman in her 30s with no significant medical history presented with a 1-month history of worsening “bulging,” redness, and mild pain in her right eye.
2. She also reported intermittent, binocular diplopia.
3. Results from a review of systems were otherwise negative, and she had not experienced recent trauma.
4. She was started on topical antihypertensive drugs for elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in the affected eye (30 mm Hg) and referred to our institution.
5. On examination, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes with subjective red desaturation OD.
6. Pupils were equal and without afferent pupillary defect.
7. Confrontation visual fields were full.
8. Intraocular pressures were 24 mm Hg OD and 12 mm Hg OS.
9. Hertel exophthalmometry showed 4.5 mm of relative proptosis OD.
10. She had limitation of her extraocular muscles in nearly all fields of gaze OD, with the most obvious limitation occurring in abduction.
11. She had decreased sensation to light touch in the right cheek (cranial nerve V2).
12. There were no orbital bruits.
13. Ocular examination revealed diffuse conjunctival injection OD with tortuous, dilated, corkscrew-shaped blood vessels (Figure, A).
14. Dilated fundus examination revealed mild optic nerve hyperemia and mild vascular tortuosity OD.
15. Vital signs and results from complete blood cell count and thyroid function tests were normal.
16. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, angiography, and venography of the brain and orbits revealed extraocular muscle enlargement and enhancement and a dilated superior ophthalmic vein OD.
17. There was no mass, abscess, or arteriovenous fistula (Figure, B).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Orbital biopsy
B: Start systemic corticosteroids
C: Start systemic antibiotics
D: Order catheter cerebral angiography
