question:
1. A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with diffuse oral lesions, fever, and nonproductive cough for 1 week.
2. He was diagnosed with herpes simplex virus (HSV) and discharged home with acyclovir.
3. Two days later, he returned with worsening oral lesions, painful phonation, poor oral intake, odynophagia, and new painful penile lesions.
4. He denied any abdominal pain, diarrhea, rectal bleeding, weight loss, arthralgia, fatigue, vision changes, or skin rashes.
5. He reported a similar episode of widespread oral lesions 18 months earlier that was less severe and self-resolving.
6. He had no other medical conditions, took no medications, and was sexually monogamous with his wife, who was asymptomatic.
7. The patient was hemodynamically stable and had a normal respiratory examination.
8. He had a fever (39.4°C) on presentation, but his temperature abated overnight and he remained afebrile for the rest of the admission.
9. His superior and inferior lips had extensive well-circumscribed erosions and ulcerations with erythematous edges, crusting, and a gray-white base.
10. Lesions extended into the buccal mucosa and soft palate.
11. His tongue was enlarged with fissures.
12. A genital examination showed similar lesions on the penis, with scalloped borders.
13. There were no skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.
14. Results of laboratory tests from the emergency department were normal, and a chest radiograph showed no evidence of pneumonia.
15. Results of further testing for antinuclear antibodies, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, HIV, HSV serology, syphilis, chlamydia, and gonorrhea were negative.
16. Bacterial and viral cultures of the oral and penile lesions were also negative.
17. Serum enzyme immunoassay for Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM was positive at 1280 U/mL.
18. The patient did not consent to a punch biopsy of the oral lesions.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform upper endoscopy and colonoscopy
B: Test for anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies
C: Prescribe oral azithromycin
D: Prescribe oral suspension nystatin

1. A man in his 50s with diagnoses of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, hepatitis B, and latent tuberculosis presented with a slow-growing nodule on the left foot.
2. The lesion started 1 year prior as a tender red nodule on the medial aspect of his first metatarsophalangeal joint, which would enlarge and become painful approximately once a month (Figure, A).

11. D, Gram staining of the biopsy supported the diagnosis.

question:
1. An African American woman in her 30s with no medical history presented with a 4-year history of diffuse progressive proliferation of dark papules.
2. The patient noted that the lesions initially began on her thighs and rapidly multiplied throughout her skin.
3. Some of the lesions were pruritic and when scratched could be removed, leaving behind a hyperpigmented macule.
4. The patient described a sunburn several weeks prior to the initial eruption.
5. She was taking no medications and these lesions were unchanged throughout an uncomplicated pregnancy.
6. There was no personal or family history of melanoma or eruptive nevi.
7. On physical examination, she had hundreds of 1- to 2-mm dark brown-black monomorphic papules throughout her trunk, extremities, palms, face, tongue, and sclera (Figure, A).
8. No lymphadenopathy was present.
9. Findings from laboratory tests, including a complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and computed tomography of the chest, were unremarkable.
10. A punch biopsy was performed for histopathologic examination (Figure, B-D).
11. A, Photograph of left thigh shows diffuse 1- to 2-mm dark brown-black macules and papules.
12. B and C, Punch biopsy of right arm shows a circumscribed proliferation of pigmented epithelioid melanocytic nests, located primarily at tips of rete ridges.
13. Moderate cytologic atypia is present.
14. Superficial papillary dermis shows prominent pigment incontinence.
15. No mitotic figures are seen.
16. Kamino bodies were not visualized.
17. D, Melan-A immunostain shows low pagetoid migration of melanocytes with a lack of melanocytic confluence at the dermal-epidermal junction.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Superficial spreading melanoma
B: Eruptive disseminated Spitz nevi
C: Dermatosis papulosa nigra
D: Metastatic melanoma

question:
1. A 70-year old man with a history of soft contact lens wear presented for a general eye examination.
2. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal intraocular pressure.
3. Several giant follicles were noted on the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva, and a few smaller follicles were noted in the left inferior fornix.
4. Papillae were also noted bilaterally on the superior palpebral conjunctiva.
5. He did not report any redness or discharge but did note mildly increased irritation mainly from soft contact lens wear.
6. He had endorsed proper contact lens care and hygiene.
7. He also noted an upper respiratory tract illness 4 weeks before presentation.
8. Initially, he received a giant papillary conjunctivitis diagnosis because of soft contact lens intolerance and a recommendation to take a contact lens break.
9. Because of the papillary reaction, prednisolone acetate, 1%, twice a day for 2 weeks was prescribed.
10. After 3 months, the symptoms had improved in the left eye, but conjunctival follicles were still present in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva (Figure 1).
11. The patient subsequently underwent testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea, and the result was negative.
12. At the 1-year follow-up, the examination findings were unchanged.
13. During this follow-up, Lyme disease and Epstein-Barr virus serologic tests were performed in addition to repeated chlamydia testing.
14. The results were negative, except for a positive Epstein-Barr virus IgG.
15. Slitlamp photograph showing prominent large follicles (arrowhead) in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start an empirical trial of oral azithromycin
B: Start a longer trial of topical steroid with topical antihistamine
C: Proceed with conjunctival biopsy
D: Order chest radiography and an angiotensin-converting enzyme serum level test

1. A girl in her teens with a history of postconcussion syndrome was referred for retinal evaluation after failing her vision examination for her learner's permit for driving.
2. She complained of progressively declining, blurred vision for 2 years.
3. She denied floaters, flashes of light, headaches, and eye pain.
4. The patient had a concussion 1 year prior after becoming dehydrated during marching band practice, fainting, and hitting her head on pavement.
5. Her postconcussion symptoms included headaches, dizziness, and dysarthria.
6. The headaches and dizziness resolved but the dysarthria remained.
7. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within the last year was normal.
8. She denied acute vision changes after the concussion.
9. Family history was unremarkable for vision loss, glaucoma, inherited retinal degeneration, and autoimmune disease.Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OU.
10. Ishihara testing revealed red-green color deficiency bilaterally.
11. Intraocular pressures, extraocular motility, confrontational visual fields, and pupils were normal.
12. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable.
13. Ophthalmoscopic examination demonstrated mild mottled retinal pigment epithelial abnormalities bilaterally (Figure, A).Right eye multicolor fundus image and retinal spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT).
14. A, Multicolor fundus image demonstrates mild macular mottling.

16. B, Retinal SD-OCT shows normal foveal contour with disruption and loss of the interdigitation and ellipsoid zones subfoveally.Fundus autofluorescence showed bilateral mild macular hyperautofluorescence likely within normal range without evidence of flecks.
17. Retinal spectral-domain optical coherence tomography demonstrated bilateral disruption of the interdigitation and ellipsoid zones subfoveally (Figure, B).
18. Electroretinogram (ERG) revealed delayed and decreased amplitude responses to 30-Hz flicker with normal dark-adapted responses.
19. Goldmann visual field testing showed mild bilateral nasal constriction.Two months after presentation, the patient returned with new balance difficulties and worsening dysarthria.
20. Horizontal and vertical saccades were markedly slowed bilaterally.

What Would You Do Next?

A: MRI of the brain/orbits with contrast
B: Genetic testing
C: Lumbar puncture
D: Audiogram

7. He was also noted to have right-sided subconjunctival hyperemia with a 7.2 mm × 2.5 mm corneal erosion and 2 mm of pannus on the right eye.
8. A photograph of the patient demonstrating asymmetric clinical findings and scarring of the medial canthal area from previous biopsy.
9. A, Fullness of the right upper eyelid with ptosis.
10. B, Severe right-sided meibomian gland dysfunction, thickening of the medial lower eyelid, and subconjunctival hyperemia.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Initiate treatment with doxycycline
B: Increase the frequency of tobramycin-dexamethasone ointment
C: Biopsy the eyelid
D: Repair his ptosis

question:
1. A pregnant woman in her late 30s had normal findings on anatomic ultrasonography at 19 weeks’ gestation.
2. Follow-up ultrasonography at 32 weeks’ gestation identified fetal hydrops.
3. The fetal ultrasonogram showed a large left-sided hydrothorax, mediastinal shift, and ascites.
4. After ruling out infectious causes, an ultrasonography-guided thoracoamniotic shunt was placed successfully at 32 weeks’ gestation.
5. Results of follow-up ultrasonography on postoperative day 3 showed improvement in the fetal hydrothorax and resolution of hydrops and identified a feeding vessel originating from the descending aorta supplying a lung mass (Figure 1A).
6. A, Feeding vessel (arrowhead) from descending aorta identified on ultrasonography at 32 weeks’ gestation.
7. B, Feeding vessel (arrowhead) to lung mass (outlined) over left hemidiaphragm on computed tomography at age 9 months.
8. Owing to premature rupture of membranes, the mother delivered at 33 weeks.
9. The neonate showed no respiratory distress after birth, and the shunt was removed.
10. On the day of birth, radiographic findings showed a left-sided pleural effusion.
11. Ongoing pleural effusion caused respiratory distress, and on day 3 of life, a temporary thoracostomy tube was placed.
12. During the following weeks, the thoracostomy tube output decreased, the tube was removed, and the patient was discharged home.
13. At 9 months of age, follow-up computed tomography confirmed a lung mass with a feeding vessel (Figure 1B), and the patient returned for elective thoracoscopic resection.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Teratoma
B: Bronchopulmonary sequestration
C: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation
D: Carcinoma

4. Previous treatment included antihistamines and oral corticosteroids for several months without improvement.
5. Dysesthesia was recorded on her lesions.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Borderline-borderline leprosy
B: Mycosis fungoides
C: Disseminated annular granuloma
D: Sarcoidosis

9. B, Biopsy from the left elbow.

A: Acquired epidermolysis bullosa
B: Pseudoporphyria
C: Photoallergic drug reaction
D: Graft-vs-host disease

12. A, Low-powered slitlamp examination of the right eye showing irregularity of the posterior light reflection inferotemporally, indicating iris elevation.

15. Attempt lesion rupture with neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet laser

3. Prior to this admission, he was working in a restaurant, did not ingest any drugs or mushrooms, and had no operations and no family history of similar problems.
4. He was found to have hyperammonemia to 239.5 µg/dL and respiratory alkalosis (pH level, 7.482; partial pressure of carbon dioxide, 27.3 mm Hg, and partial pressure of oxygen, 109 mm Hg [to convert to kPa, multiply by 0.133]; and bicarbonate, 20.2 mEq/L [to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 1]).
5. 6. His mental status rapidly declined despite treatment with lactulose, necessitating intubation.
7. Head computed tomography and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unrevealing.
8. Ammonia levels progressively increased to 1120.5 µg/dL, requiring hemodialysis and sodium phenylbutyrate, which did not lead to significant clinical improvement.

10. Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids were requested.
11. Continuous venovenous filtration hemodialysis and carnitine treatment were started because of concern for inborn errors of metabolism.
12. Within a few hours of transfer, his ammonia level peaked to 1960 µg/dL and he lost all brainstem activity due to diffuse cerebral edema (Figure 1B).
13. A, Electroencephalography (EEG) showing diffuse polyspike complexes consistent with myoclonic seizures.
14. B, Head computed tomography showing diffuse cerebral edema, obliteration of basal cisterns, and transtentorial and tonsillar herniation.

B: Urea cycle disorder
C: Fatty acid oxidation disorder
D: Organic acidemia

1. A Hispanic woman in her 60s presented to the oculoplastics clinic with a 1-week history of pain, redness, and swelling in the medial aspect of the right periorbital region.
2. Her medical history included sarcoidosis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease.
3. Her ocular history included pseudophakia and proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes; she had also undergone pars plana vitrectomy and panretinal photocoagulation in both eyes.

6. She reported increasing swelling and pain in the affected region.
7. She denied changes in vision, eye pain, or pain with eye movements.
8. The patient’s best-corrected visual acuity was 20/60 OD and 20/50 OS, her pupils were reactive, extraocular motility was full and painless, and intraocular pressures were 18 mm Hg in both eyes.
9. External examination revealed an erythematous, tender, firm mass in the medial periorbital area (Figure, A).
10. Results of anterior slitlamp examination and dilated fundus examination were unremarkable.
11. Contrast-enhanced computed tomographic imaging of the maxillofacial region was performed and showed a peripherally enhancing mass in the affected area (Figure, B).
12. A, External photograph demonstrating a firm, tender, erythematous mass located in the medial periorbital area.
13. B, Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomographic scan showing a peripherally enhancing mass (arrowhead) in the medial aspect of the right periorbital region.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform a biopsy of the mass
B: Perform magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits and maxillofacial region
C: Perform endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy and prescribe antibiotics
D: Prescribe topical and systemic antibiotics and recommend use of warm compresses without planned surgical or procedural intervention

8. The conjunctival lesion had vascular and papilliform elements (Figure) and had not been noted on a routine examination 6 months prior.
9. Clinical photograph showing a soft-tissue lesion on the palpebral conjunctiva of the left lower eyelid, accompanied by inferior bulbar conjunctival injection.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform time-domain anterior segment optical coherence tomography
B: Observe the patient
C: Perform a biopsy of the lesion
D: Obtain a culture of the lesion

1. A 6-year-old girl presented to the ophthalmology emergency service with 4 days of double vision associated with headache and fever.
2. She had a history of upper respiratory tract infection with nasal congestion and discharge being treated with oral antibiotics.
3. She also recently received a diagnosis of migraines.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Continue oral antibiotics
B: Refer to neurology department
C: Continue neuroimaging
D: Proceed with strabismus surgery

1. A 30-year-old woman presented with widespread, erythematous, purpuric macules and papules on the abdomen and extremities.
2. The eruption had been present for approximately 8 months and consisted of asymptomatic, self-resolving, and continuously appearing macules and papules.
3. Her medical history was significant for chronic hepatitis B infection, for which tenofovir was initiated 4 months ago.
4. Review of systems was positive only for occasional arthralgias in her knees and ankles.
5. She was not taking any other medications.
6. The patient was in no acute distress, and her vital signs were within normal limits.
7. On physical examination, there were purpuric, erythematous macules coalescing into patches on the upper extremities, abdomen, and lower extremities (Figure).
8. She had no oral or genital involvement and no joint effusions or deformities.
9. A skin punch biopsy showed extravasated erythrocytes, a neutrophilic infiltrate, fibrinoid necrosis, and broken-down neutrophils releasing nuclear debris, consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis (Figure).
10. A second skin punch biopsy was performed for direct immunofluorescence, which was negative.
11. Results of a complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel were unremarkable.
12. Physical examination of the lower extremities.
13. Dotted areas indicate areas of the skin that were biopsied.
14. Inset, Photomicrograph from first skin punch biopsy (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×200).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Prescribe prednisone
B: Evaluate for systemic vasculitis
C: Prescribe a topical glucocorticoid
D: Provide reassurance and observe patient

question:
1. A man in his 30s with no medical history reported a 2-year history of waxing and waning pruritic papules involving his left popliteus, contralateral popliteus, groin, and penis with each lesion occurring at different time points.
2. He was initially evaluated by an infectious disease physician and a local dermatologist, who had intermittently prescribed empirical antibiotics (clindamycin hydrochloride and doxycycline calcium) for a presumptive clinical diagnosis of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection for more than 1 year with minimal response.
3. Because no objective data including wound culture or biopsy were obtained during his prior evaluations, he sought an alternate clinical consultation given the appearance of new violaceous ulcerated lesions over his right lateral proximal calf (Figure, A) despite his actively taking doxycycline.
4. He endorsed spontaneous healing of previously involved sites despite the absence of antibiotic exposure but denied constitutional complaints, recent travel, or high-risk behavior.
5. His physical examination was unremarkable for hepatosplenomegaly or systemic adenopathy.
6. Laboratory evaluation including complete blood cell count, peripheral blood cultures, MRSA swab, human immunodeficiency virus/human T-cell lymphotropic virus testing, flow cytometry, and Lyme disease titers had unremarkable results.
7. Pathologic sampling of the lesions revealed V-shaped perifascicular infiltrative large lymphocytes with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli (Figure, B and C).
8. Lesional cells exclusively involving the dermis stained positive for CD30, leukocyte common antigen, CD2, TIA-1, and CD4 and negative for CD7, CD8, CD43, CD56, and programmed cell death protein 1.
9. Scattered B lymphocytes were PAX5 positive and CD20 positive.
10. Ki-67 level was 87%.
11. Scattered dermal dendritic and Langerhans cells were S100 positive.
12. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement testing had negative results.
13. Systemic imaging did not reveal extracutaneous involvement, and screening endoscopy for upper and lower gastrointestinal involvement had unremarkable results.A, Photograph of right lateral proximal calf shows violaceous ulcerated nodule.
14. B and C, Biopsy of the lesion revealed V-shaped perifascicular infiltrative large lymphocytes with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli hematoxlyn-eosin, original magnification ×2 and ×20, respectively).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma
B: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
C: Lymphomatoid papulosis
D: Transformed mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome

question:
1. A healthy 43-year-old woman presented with weight loss, heartburn, and progressively worsening dysphagia to solid food.
2. Intriguingly, the heartburn was most severe while she was sitting up but lying supine relieved the symptoms.
3. Paradoxically, dysphagia was worse while she was reclining and partially resolved in the upright position.
4. The physical examination was normal while laboratory workup revealed mild anemia.
5. She was administered a trial of acid-suppression therapy for 6 weeks, which transiently alleviated heartburn but the dysphagia persisted.
6. Subsequently, further workup with an esophagram revealed a 2.7-cm filling defect at the gastroesophageal junction, suggestive of extrinsic compression.
7. Computed tomography demonstrated a 2.5-cm low-attenuation ovoid lesion at the gastroesophageal junction (Figure 1A).
8. Considering a diagnosis of gastric tumor, she then underwent upper endoscopy that showed a mobile smooth-surfaced polypoid subepithelial lesion at the posterolateral wall of the gastroesophageal junction.
9. The mass flopped back and forth into the gastroesophageal junction.
10. Mucosal biopsies were performed, which were consistent with normal squamous mucosal epithelium.
11. Following this, endoscopic ultrasonography was performed, which demonstrated an anechoic, loculated, subepithelial lesion located within the submucosa of the distal esophagus (Figure 1B).
12. The endosonographic borders were well defined without invasion into the nearby structures.
13. Manometry and 24-hour pH testing revealed preserved motility but abnormal acid exposure of the distal esophagus.
14. Ultrasonography of the liver, gallbladder, and pancreas revealed no abnormalities.Diagnostic imaging for the patient.
15. A, Contrast computed tomogram (CT) revealing a mass at the gastroesophageal junction protruding into the cardia of the stomach.
16. B, Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a cystic lesion originating and localized to the wall of the esophagus but not invading local structures.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
B: Esophageal carcinoma
C: Inclusion cyst
D: Bronchogenic cyst

16. Search for nematodes under a high-magnification fundus contact lens examination

2. This was associated with diarrhea, vomiting, fevers, and chills.
3. He reported some relief of symptoms with loperamide.

1. A woman in her 80s with a history of recurrent oral cancer presented with a new, biopsy-confirmed, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
2. Her oncologic history began 16 years ago with diagnosis and local resection of a lesion on the palate.
3. Cancer recurrence at the left buccal mucosa was identified and excised 10 years later.
4. She then was diagnosed with 3 recurrences of SCC in rapid succession.
5. Each malignant neoplasm was locally resected and the patient was also treated with adjuvant radiotherapy for the last episode.
6. She remained asymptomatic, and a routine surveillance clinical examination uncovered a sixth lesion at the margin of a palatal graft.
7. The patient’s medical history was also noted for a total thyroidectomy in the 1950s, complicated by recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
8. She had a history of tobacco use and stopped smoking cigarettes in the 1970s.
9. Physical examination and laryngoscopy findings confirmed a painless lesion on the left side of the palate and immobility of the left vocal cord.
10. No other mucosal lesion was identified.
11. Positron emission tomography (PET) was performed to assess extent of disease and to plan treatment.
12. The PET scan results showed focal fludeoxyglucose F 18 localization within the known oral cavity SCC (Figure 1A) and in a small, level IIA lymph node, located lateral to the upper right internal jugular vein.
13. There was unexpected, prominent, metabolic activity in the medial and asymmetrically enlarged left vocal cord (Figure 1B).
14. A, Positron emission tomography reveals focal fludeoxyglucose F 18 uptake in biopsy-confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the left palatal graft margin (arrowhead).
15. B, Increased metabolic activity in the left vocal cord (arrowhead).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma
B: Primary laryngeal carcinoma in the setting of extensive, recurrent head and neck SCC
C: Inflammatory reaction
D: Postradiation change

1. A white woman in her 50s presented to an oral medicine clinic for evaluation of asymptomatic pigmented lesions affecting the maxillary and mandibular gingiva of 6 years’ duration.
2. The patient reported previous orolabial melanotic macules.
3. Her medical history was significant for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, asthma, and breast cancer.
4. Medications included levalbuterol, nadolol, and cetirizine.
5. Family medical history was significant for breast cancer and social history was unremarkable.
6. Review of systems was positive for cutaneous ephelides.
7. Physical examination revealed a 7 mm × 6 mm asymmetric, heterogeneously pigmented lesion without indurated borders on the gingiva associated with the left maxillary central incisor tooth (number 9) (Figure, A).
8. A lesion similar in clinical appearance, although smaller, was observed on the gingiva associated with the right mandibular first premolar tooth (number 28) (Figure, B).
9. Biopsy specimens were obtained with a 3 mm punch instrument from both lesions for routine histology which demonstrated similar microscopic findings (Figure, C and D).
10. A, Heterogeneously pigmented lesion of the gingiva associated with the left maxillary central incisor.
11. B, Heterogeneously pigmented lesion of the gingiva associated with the right mandibular first premolar.
12. C, Mucosal epithelium exhibiting spongiosis and a diffuse proliferation of heavily pigmented dendritic melanocytes that extend the full thickness of the epithelium (arrowheads).
13. Melanin incontinence is also noted (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×100).
14. D, Squamous mucosa exhibiting spongiosis with diffuse pigmentation in the basal cell layer and dendritic melanocytes (arrowheads) in the stratum spinosum (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×200).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Oral melanotic macule
B: Oral malignant melanoma
C: Oral melanocytic nevus
D: Oral melanoacanthoma

question:
1. An adolescent girl presented with a 3-month history of a growing, painless mass in the right thigh.
2. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan showed an inhomogeneous nodule in the subcutaneous layer with a largest diameter of approximately 5 cm.
3. No enlarged lymph nodes were detectable in the groin.
4. Results of a complete blood cell count and levels of alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase, and C-reactive protein were unremarkable.
5. An ultrasonography-guided core needle biopsy was performed, and histopathologic evaluation showed the aspects of a small round-cell tumor, which was confirmed to be a Ewing sarcoma by immunohistochemical and molecular analysis (with positivity for the EWS-FLI1 fusion gene [OMIM 133450]).
6. The patient then underwent disease staging with computed tomography (CT) of the chest and whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET).
7. The CT findings were negative for secondary lesions; the FDG-PET scan demonstrated, as expected, high uptake in the right thigh (maximum standard uptake variable [SUVmax], 8.4) at the site of the subcutaneous tumor and at a second lesion in the left ankle joint (SUVmax, 12.0).
8. The patient reported vague pain around the left ankle but no functional limitations and no history of trauma at that site.
9. A radiograph of the ankle did not show calcifications within the soft-tissue lesion.
10. An MRI scan of the ankle showed a 1.5-cm soft tissue mass in the posterior recess of the ankle joint with a low to intermediate signal in T1- and T2-weighted sequences and moderate contrast enhancement throughout the lesion (Figure 1).Magnetic resonance imaging fast spin echo of the left ankle showing the soft-tissue mass in the posterior recess.
11. The sagittal T1-weighted image shows an isointense, bean-shaped mass (arrowhead) (1.5 × 0.7 cm) (A), whereas the sagittal T2-weighted image shows the isointense signal of the mass (arrowhead) (B).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Ganglion cyst of the ankle joint
B: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor
C: Ewing sarcoma (soft-tissue metastasis)
D: Synovial sarcoma

question:
1. A boy in his teens with no significant medical history, ocular history, or recent trauma was referred by an ophthalmologist for mild photophobia and an iris lesion.
2. The referring clinician initially suspected traumatic iridodialysis and vitreous prolapse.
3. On ophthalmic evaluation, visual acuity was 20/20 OS, intraocular pressure was 13 mm Hg OS, and slitlamp examination of the left eye demonstrated a clear, intrinsically vascularized, cystic lesion extending into the anterior chamber from the peripheral superonasal iris (Figure 1A).
4. The base of the lesion was surrounded by iris atrophy and corectopia was noted.
5. The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable.
6. Examination of the right eye was also unremarkable.
7. Ultrasonographic biomicroscopy of the anterior segment demonstrated a large, cystic lesion incorporated in the iris of the left eye with a thickness of 2.2 mm and a maximum radial extent of 6.1 mm (Figure 1B).
8. A, Slitlamp photograph of the iris cyst in the superonasal periphery of the left eye.
9. B, Ultrasonographic biomicroscopy of the anterior segment in the left eye with longitudinal orientation at the 10-o’clock position.
10. Given the patient’s excellent visual acuity and no documented evidence of growth, the lesion was initially monitored closely.
11. One month after presentation, the patient developed worsening photophobia, and his visual acuity declined to 20/50 OS.
12. The iris lesion was noted to have grown, with maximum thickness measuring 3.5 mm and with radial extension now involving the visual axis.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Aspiration with absolute alcohol injection
B: Surgical resection
C: Continued monitoring
D: Laser cystotomy

question:
1. A boy aged 17 years presented after noticing that his right pupil was off-center.
2. He had a high hyperopic refractive error, and the magnification of his spectacle lenses highlighted the eccentric pupil.
3. He had no associated symptoms of decreased vision, ocular pain, diplopia, glare, or haloes and had no history of ocular infection, surgical procedure, or trauma.
4. His mother, also hyperopic, previously underwent prophylactic laser iridotomy for anatomically narrow, occludable angles.
5. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU, with a manifest refraction of +7.75 −1.00 × 170 OD and +7.75 −1.25 × 010 OS.
6. Slitlamp examination confirmed mild corectopia in the right eye, along with 4 clock hours of iridocorneal touch nasally and a “hammered silver” appearance to the involved cornea (Figure 1).
7. On examination via gonioscopy, there were high peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) above the Schwalbe line in this area, while the remaining angle was deep without PAS.
8. The left eye was normal.
9. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS.
10. Pachymetry testing revealed symmetric central corneal thicknesses of 577 μm OD and 582 μm OS.
11. Both optic discs appeared healthy, with a cup-disc ratio of 0.2.
12. There were no visual field defects.
13. Slitlamp photography showed the right eye had mild corectopia and iridocorneal touch nasally.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start pilocarpine eyedrops
B: Test the aqueous fluid for Human herpesvirus 1
C: Obtain specular microscopy
D: Recommend genetic testing

question:
1. A teenaged male presented with a 2-week history of vegetating, bleeding plaques and pustules on his face, scalp, trunk, and extremities.
2. He reported that lesions began as pustules and developed into painful, itchy plaques.
3. Before evaluation at a referral hospital in Kenya, the patient was treated with prednisolone tablet 5 mg twice daily, clindamycin hydrochloride 300 mg daily, and fluconazole 200 mg daily, but he continued to develop new lesions.
4. A complete review of systems was notable for the patient’s difficulty with walking because of skin lesions.
5. On examination, pustules and hemorrhagic-crusted plaques were seen on the scalp, legs, arms, and trunk along with keloidal plaques on the face (Figure, A and B).
6. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay testing for HIV was negative.
7. A punch biopsy specimen from the arm was obtained for histopathologic study (Figure, C and D).
8. Extensive vegetative plaques with bleeding and ulceration on extremities (A), and pustules and ulcerated plaques on extremities and trunk (B).
9. Histopathologic examination of a biopsy specimen taken from the arm demonstrates pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×100) (C) and dermal neutrophilia and microabscesses with eosinophilia (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×400) (D).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Pyoderma gangrenosum
B: Blastomycosis
C: Pyoderma vegetans
D: Halogenoderma

question:
1. A 76-year-old white woman with a history of left corneal stem-cell deficiency and cataract presented for a second opinion of recurrent left upper eyelid blepharedema, ptosis, erythema, photophobia, mucopurulent discharge, and a feeling she described as a “knife in my left eye” over the past 4 years (Figure 1).
2. Previous treatment included topical steroids, antibiotics, and serum tears, with temporary relief.
3. However, she experienced recurrences of symptoms after therapy discontinuation.
4. Additional treatment included weekly bandage contact lenses for many months, which made the left eye pain tolerable.
5. A dacryocystogram of the left lacrimal system indicated partial dacryostenosis, but compression of the canaliculi and lacrimal sac did not exacerbate discharge.
6. A prior computed tomography scan of the orbits and sinuses showed no abnormalities.
7. Her visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS.
8. Deep superior conjunctival fornices were noted in both eyes (Figure 1), and eversion of the left upper eyelid revealed a pseudomembrane of the tarsal conjunctiva.
9. Cultures of the copious discharge demonstrated many gram-negative Serratia marcescens.
10. She subsequently started treatment with topical prednisolone acetate, moxifloxacin, and systemic azithromycin.
11. Patient presented with recurrent left eye ptosis, erythema, blepharedema, chronic discharge, and knifelike pain over the past 4 years (arrowhead).
12. Two weeks after the initial consultation, the patient reported persistent but improved symptoms in the left eye.
13. At this follow-up visit, her visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/200 OS.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Start treatment with systemic steroids
B: Perform a dacryocystorhinostomy
C: Sweep the superior fornix
D: Perform a canaliculotomy

1. A 59-year-old man presented to the vitreoretinal service with a 2-week history of acute-onset, progressively worsening decreased vision and central scotomas in both eyes.
2. He had no systemic symptoms and denied having eye redness, pain, and photophobia.
3. His medical and surgical history included prostate cancer, status postcryotherapy, osteoarthritis, and migraines.
4. His social history was significant for active cigarette smoking and immigration from a Middle Eastern country.
5. His medications included naproxen at 500 mg as needed, tamsulosin at 0.4 mg daily, and aspirin at 81 mg daily.
6. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuities were 20/40 OD and 20/25 OS.
7. His pupils were reactive, his extraocular motility was full, and the intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg in both eyes.
8. The results of the external examination and anterior slitlamp examinations were unremarkable, and there was no anterior chamber or anterior vitreous cell or flare.
9. The dilated fundus photography examination revealed yellow-gray, curvilinear, and puzzle piece–shaped subretinal macular lesions in both eyes (Figure).
10. The lesions were hyperfluorescent with hypofluorescent borders on fundus autofluorescence testing results (Figure).
11. Optical coherence tomography revealed that the involved areas exhibited a disruption of the outer retinal layers (including and deep to the outer nuclear layer) along with hyperreflectivity of the outer retina, retinal pigment epithelium, and choroid.
12. There was no involvement of the inner retina.
13. The patient underwent laboratory testing for syphilis and tuberculosis, which yielded negative results.
14. Fundus photographs showing yellowish, puzzle piece–shaped, curvilinear lesions in the maculae of the right eye (A) and left eye (B).
15. Fundus autofluorescence (insets) exhibits hyperfluorescent lesions with hypofluorescent borders.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Recommend multivitamin supplementation
B: Give an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection
C: Discuss the potential risks and benefits of initiating oral corticosteroid therapy
D: Insist on observation for spontaneous resolution

D: Perform adrenal magnetic resonance imaging

1. A 60-year-old woman with a history of Lyme disease presented with polydipsia and polyuria and received a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus.
2. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) results revealed a thickening and enhancement of the pituitary gland, stalk, and hypothalamus.
3. The abnormal imaging findings improved on subsequent MRIs without treatment.
4. Surveillance pituitary MRIs remained stable.
5. Four years later, MRI results (Figure) revealed bilateral T1 and T2 low-intensity intraconal soft tissue masses with avid enhancement on postcontrast images.
6. The optic nerves were encased with no evidence of infiltration of the nerves, vascular structures, or extraocular muscles.
7. She reported the sensation of eye fullness and denied pain.
8. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU.
9. Her pupils were symmetric and responded to light and near effort; there was no relative afferent pupillary defect.
10. The results of testing with an Amsler grid and Ishihara color plates were normal.
11. Her visual fields were full to confrontation.
12. The optic nerves and retina were normal bilaterally.
13. There was bilateral periorbital swelling and proptosis.
14. Exophthalmometry measurements on a base of 92 were 17 mm on the right and 19 mm on the left.
15. Applanation tonometry results were 12 mm Hg on the right and 15 mm Hg on the left.
16. Extraocular motility examination results revealed substantial (−3) deficits in both eyes.
17. The remainder of the neurologic examination results were normal.Coronal (A) and axial T1 postcontrast (B) shows avid homogeneous enhancement of intraorbital lesions.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain thyroid function test results or obtain endocrine evaluation results
B: Obtain Doppler ultrasonography results with and without Valsalva
C: Chest computed tomography
D: Obtain biopsy results

1. A woman in her 80s presented with a 1-year history of pruritic erythema on the trunk and extremities.
2. The erythema did not respond to topical corticosteroid, oral roxithromycin (300 mg/d), or narrow-band UV-B phototherapy.
3. The patient had a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension and was treated with glimepiride, sitagliptin phosphate hydrate, and amlodipine besylate.
4. The patient also had polymyalgia, which was treated with a low dose of prednisolone.
5. The prednisolone therapy had been discontinued 2 months before her visit to the dermatology clinic when she had been hospitalized with pneumonia.
6. Multiple tense blisters had subsequently appeared on the palms.
7. Physical examination at the first visit revealed scaly erythematous plaques on the whole body and tense blisters on the arms, hands, soles, and buttocks.
8. Neither scar formation or mucosal involvement was observed.
9. A skin biopsy specimen was obtained from a bulla on the forearm.
10. Histopathologic analysis revealed a subepidermal bulla with inflammatory infiltrates of neutrophils.
11. The results of an IgG chemiluminescence enzyme immunoassay for bullous pemphigoid (BP) 180 noncollagenous (NC) 16A were negative.
12. After treatment with oral prednisolone, 20 mg/d, the lesions healed without scar or milia formation (Figure 1).
13. Clinical features before (A) and after (B) treatment with oral prednisolone, showing no scar formation.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Bullous pemphigoid
B: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
C: Anti–laminin γ1 pemphigoid
D: Linear IgA dermatosis

1. A woman in her 60s presented with numerous whitish papules on the back of more than 10 years’ duration.
2. The lesions previously resolved with topical corticosteroids but flared soon after treatment discontinuation.
3. Some papules became pruritic and extended to the waist and anterior trunk in the past month.
4. No family history of similar lesions was recorded.
5. Physical examination revealed multiple hypopigmented, flat-topped papules on the back, waist, and inframammary area without genital involvement (Figure, A).
6. Most lesions were folliculocentric under close inspection.
7. Dermoscopy revealed central keratin plugs and some foci of structureless, whitish, and homogenous areas with surrounding erythema (Figure, B).
8. The results of laboratory tests for antinuclear antibody and hyperglobulinemia were negative.
9. A biopsy specimen was obtained from the back for histologic analysis (Figure, C).
10. A, Multiple hypopigmented, atrophic, keratotic, and folliculocentric papules are seen on the trunk.
11. B, Dermascopic findings included 2 foci of central keratin plugs and another ill-defined, whitish, and homogenous area with surrounding erythema.
12. Scale bar corresponds to 1 mm.
13. C, Histopathologic examination of a biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Lichen amyloidosis
B: Folliculocentric lichen sclerosus et atrophicus
C: Guttate vitiligo
D: Eruptive tumors of the follicular infundibulum

12. B, yellowish nodules located on the left labia majora.

A: Atypical mycobacterial infection
B: Cutaneous malakoplakia
C: Cryptococcosis
D: Calcinosis cutis

D: Cutaneous angiosarcoma

2. He was previously healthy and had no prior abdominal operations.
3. The patient noted pencil-thin stools that occurred during the past several months but had not had a colonoscopy in more than a decade.
4. The rest of his history was noncontributory.
5. He was mildly tachycardic but normotensive and afebrile.
6. Physical examination revealed a lethargic patient with a distended abdomen, diffuse rebound tenderness, and involuntary guarding.
7. No surgical scars or inguinal hernias were apparent on examination.
8. The only abnormal laboratory values were as follows: sodium concentration, 126 mEq/L (reference range, 135-145 mEq/L) (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); lactate concentration, 58.6 mg/dL (reference range, 0-18.0 mg/dL) (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.111); and white blood cell count, 18 500/μL (reference range, 3400-10 000/μL) (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001).
9. He was resuscitated with 2 L of lactated Ringer solution and underwent computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast.
10. Computed tomography revealed diffuse free fluid but without free air and several loops of dilated small bowel with thickened, hypoenhancing bowel walls.
11. The mesentery was markedly edematous (Figure).
12. The rest of the small bowel were dilated and air and fluid filled but had normal bowel wall enhancement.
13. The colon was normal.Axial computed tomography image of the abdomen and pelvis.
14. Blue arrowhead indicates intravenous contrast demonstrating mesenteric edema; yellow arrowhead, hypoenhancing bowel walls; and white arrowhead, a contrast filling defect.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Inflammatory bowel disease
B: Small-bowel neoplasm

D: Superior mesenteric artery thromboembolism

1. A 66-year-old man with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma underwent autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).
2. On posttransplant day 10, he developed fever (38.4°C).
3. He was started on empirical treatment with cefepime; however, his fevers persisted despite antibiotic therapy.
4. On posttransplant day 14 he developed new-onset pruritic, confluent, erythematous, blanching morbilliform macules and papules on his trunk and extremities (Figure, left).
5. Review of systems was notable for diarrhea and a 6-pound weight gain since transplantation and negative for headache, cough, shortness of breath, or abdominal pain.Left, Macules and papules on the trunk of the patient.
6. Right, Axial chest computed tomography of the patient.On examination, there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
7. The patient’s heart rate was 100/min, blood pressure was 106/68 mm Hg, and he occasionally experienced mild hypoxia to 94% on ambient air.
8. Results of a basic metabolic panel were normal, with a blood urea nitrogen level of 10 mg/dL (3.57 mmol/L) and creatinine level of 0.7 mg/dL (61.88 μmol/L).
9. White blood cell (WBC) count was 7300/μL, and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was 5480/μL.
10. Neutrophil recovery occurred beginning on posttransplant day 10, with WBC count of 700/μL and ANC of 532/μL on posttransplant day 10, correlating with the onset of the patient’s fevers.
11. Platelet count was 48 × 103/μL, and hemoglobin was 8.2 g/dL.
12. Results of liver function tests were normal.
13. Blood, urine, sputum, and respiratory viral cultures were negative.

15. Chest computed tomography demonstrated multifocal ground-glass and consolidative pulmonary opacities (Figure, right).
16. Computed tomography of the abdomen was unremarkable.
17. A skin punch biopsy demonstrated subtle vacuolar change; rare epidermal dyskeratosis, including within a hair follicle; and superficial perivascular mononuclear cell infiltrate with occasional eosinophils.

A: Initiate empirical antiviral and antifungal therapy
B: Discontinue antibiotic therapy and consider systemic corticosteroids
C: Obtain ferritin and soluble IL2Rα testing
D: Perform bronchoscopy and biopsy of the pulmonary lesions

10. Right, Histopathologic findings under low-power magnification (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20).

B: Perform immunohistochemical analysis on the biopsy specimen
C: Perform tissue culture for bacterial and fungal organisms
D: Provide reassurance

3. She did not have diplopia, facial numbness, or paresthesias.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was reported to have normal results, but on review, we noted thickening and enhancement of both optic nerves (with the right eye larger than the left eye), cranial nerve III in the right eye, cranial nerve V bilaterally, the pituitary infundibulum, and the hypothalamus, as well as adjacent cavernous sinuses.
9. Leptomeningeal thickening over the convexities of the anterior frontal lobes was also evident.
10. The patient’s cerebrospinal fluid contained a small population of polyclonal CD19+ B cells and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
11. An extensive laboratory workup, including tests for HIV, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, serum protein electrophoresis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, complete blood cell count, antiganglioside antibodies, anti–myelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies, and angiotensin-converting enzyme, gave normal results.
12. A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the thorax and a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)/CT scan revealed no abnormalities.

14. Over the ensuing 5 years, she had multiple similar presentations that also included facial pain and paresthesias.

1. A healthy 10-year-old girl with a recent history of blunt trauma to the left eye presented to the emergency department with acute-onset blurry vision and pain.
2. On her initial ophthalmic examination 3 weeks earlier, she was diagnosed with commotio retinae and traumatic iritis in the left eye after being struck with the brim of a hat.
3. She was treated with a topical corticosteroid, with rapid resolution of iritis and commotio.
4. However, she developed ipsilateral, asymptomatic grade 2 optic disc edema.
5. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU with a 2-diopter myopic shift in the left eye.
6. There was no afferent pupillary defect, color vision was normal, and intraocular pressure (IOP) was 10 mm Hg OD and 8 mm Hg OS.

8. The results of examination and testing of the right eye were unremarkable.

10. Ophthalmic examination in the emergency department revealed diminished visual acuity to counting fingers, an IOP of 59 mm Hg, and a relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye.
11. Additional findings included corneal microcystic edema, formed anterior chamber without hyphema, and stable grade 2 optic disc edema.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Order magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with venography
B: Perform gonioscopy
C: Instill a miotic agent
D: Perform peripheral iridotomy

13. Finally, magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffuse pachymeningeal (dural-arachnoid) enhancement (Figure) without leptomeningeal (pial) enhancement, left-sided mastoiditis, and subtle optic nerve enhancement.

2. He has no relevant medical history and does not take any medications.
3. No family members have similar symptoms.
4. Apart from the lesions, the physical examination is unremarkable.
5. Skin examination reveals disseminated sharply demarcated, dome-shaped, red-brown papules and nodules with a shiny, waxy surface.
6. These 0.1- to 0.8-cm lesions are on his face, scalp, ears, neck, trunk, shoulder (Figure 1A), upper extremities (Figure 1B), lower extremities including the palms and soles, and scrotum.
7. The mucous membranes and periorbital area are spared.
8. A shave biopsy reveals a yellow appearance of the base of the papule.
9. Hematoxylin-eosin stains reveal a diffuse inflammatory infiltration of the upper and middle dermis with lymphocytes, plasma cells, numerous foamy histiocytoid cells, and a large number of multinucleated cells.
10. Emperipolesis (engulfed lymphocytes) is present within the histiocyte cytoplasm.
11. There is rare nuclear atypia.
12. Electron microscopy shows indented nuclei and emperipolesis in histiocytes.
13. Birbeck granules are not seen.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Acid-fast staining
B: Immunoelectron microscopy
C: Immunohistochemical testing
D: PAS (periodic acid–Schiff) staining

1. A 44-year-old man with a 3-year history of postprandial chest pain and odynophagia presents with a severe exacerbation of symptoms over 2 months and a weight loss of 8.1 kg.
2. His history included lumbar spine surgery and chronic back pain leading to continued requirement for opiate analgesia.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Treat with analgesia and nutritional support
B: Treat with calcium channel antagonists
C: Recommend an extended esophageal myotomy
D: Recommend esophageal resection

1. A 64-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-day temperature of 38.9°C (102°F).
2. The patient had some accompanying cough, nausea, and arthralgias but denied having dyspnea, emesis, and chest or abdominal pain.
3. She had a complicated medical history that was significant for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic diarrhea, myelodysplastic syndrome treated with chemotherapy, and Behçet syndrome treated with prednisone acetate (6 mg daily).
4. Her surgical history was significant for a previous right-sided hemicolectomy due to recurrent right-sided diverticulitis.
5. On examination, she was alert and awake with appropriate mental status.
6. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure of 150/59 mm Hg, heart rate of 127 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, temperature of 38.5°C (101.3°F) (oral), and an oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry of 99% in room air.
7. The physical examination was unremarkable.
8. Significant laboratory data included a white blood cell count of 2700/μL (reference range, 4800-10 800/μL; to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001), a lactic acid level of 19.8 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.111), and a platelet count of 72×103/μL (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 1.0).
9. Urinalysis showed trace blood, positive nitrite, +1 leukocyte esterase, and a white blood cell count of 2000/μL to 5000/μL.
10. A urine culture came back positive for Klebsiella pneumonia, and a blood culture came back positive for Enterobacter sakazakii (now know as Cronobacter sakazakii).
11. There was concern about the source of the bacteremia, so an infectious disease consult was ordered, and a computed tomographic scan of the abdomen/pelvis with contrast was performed.
12. Figure 1 shows a coronal, reformatted image of the scan.
13. The patient was scheduled for surgery, and the findings are shown in Figure 2.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Perforated bowel
B: Crohn disease
C: Cholecystocolonic fistula
D: Gallstone ileus

What Would You Do Next?

A: Locally explore the mandibular wound
B: Perform angiography
C: Perform a thoracotomy to remove the foreign body
D: Perform flexible bronchoscopy

question:
1. A 28-year-old previously healthy man developed constant mid-epigastric and supraumbilical abdominal pain.
2. One day after the onset of pain, he presented to the emergency department.
3. The patient described his pain intensity as 8 on a scale of 1 to 10.
4. He also described having some nausea but no anorexia, and he experienced a single episode of emesis in the emergency department.
5. He was afebrile, and his heart rate was 86 beats/min; blood pressure, 128/86 mm Hg; and body mass index, 28 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared).
6. Bilateral lower abdominal and supraumbilical tenderness was present, as was lower abdominal voluntary guarding to palpation.
7. Deep palpation of the left lower quadrant did not elicit pain over the right lower quadrant (ie, negative Rovsing sign).
8. Internal and external rotation of the flexed right leg did not elicit pain (ie, negative obturator sign).
9. Dorsiflexion of the right thigh against the examiner’s hand resulted in right lower quadrant pain (ie, positive psoas sign).
10. Rectal examination was unrevealing.
11. Levels of liver function enzymes, amylase, and bilirubin were normal, as was a complete blood cell count, except for leukocytosis of 14 000 cells/mm3.
12. Urinalysis was unremarkable.
13. A computed tomography (CT) scan was obtained (Figure 1).Computed tomography scan in the case patient.
14. A, Axial view.
15. B, Coronal view.
16. C, Sagittal view.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Admit the patient for observation
B: Initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics and serial abdominal examinations
C: Perform laparoscopic appendectomy
D: Obtain an abdominal ultrasound

1. A 30-year-old woman with a history of migraine headaches presented to our emergency department with the sudden onset of blurred vision and a frontal headache.
2. She reported a normal eye examination by an optometrist 6 months prior and no history of corrective lens wear.
3. Her visual acuity without correction in each eye was count fingers at 5 ft with pinhole improvement to 20/200.
4. The pupils were 4 mm OU and unreactive.
5. On slitlamp examination, the anterior chambers were shallow and the angles on gonioscopy were closed in each eye (Figure).
6. The undilated fundus examination revealed normal-appearing optic nerves with cup-to-disc ratios of 0.2.
7. Intraocular pressures were 48 mm Hg OD and 49 mm Hg OS.
8. When given a −6.50 D sphere trial lens, her visual acuity improved to 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS.
9. When asked about her medications, she reported that she recently discontinued a medication for migraine headaches.Patient at presentation with shallow anterior chambers (A) and closed angles on gonioscopy (B).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Administer a miotic agent (ie, pilocarpine)
B: Proceed directly to choroidal drainage sclerotomy
C: Perform laser peripheral iridotomy
D: Obtain a detailed list of the patient’s medications

2. She had no significant medical history or prior ocular problems.
3. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS, with eccentric fixation and trace exophoria in the left eye.
4. Pupils were equally round and reactive.
5. Anterior segment examination revealed an enlarged right corneal nerve.
6. The left macula had a fibrotic-appearing epiretinal membrane (Figure 1A).
7. There were 2 small, flat, pigmented lesions along the arcades of the right fundus (Figure 1B), likely atypical congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) lesions, or pigmented ocular fundus lesions (POFLs).
8. Observation was elected.
9. On follow-up, optical coherence tomography showed focal macular thickening in the left eye, most likely a retinal hamartoma (Figure 1C), and intraretinal abnormalities between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor layer in the right eye, consistent with POFLs and likely representing combined retina-RPE hamartomas (Figure 1D).
10. B-scan ultrasonography and biometric A-scan showed bilaterally clear vitreous without retinal detachment.
11. Fluorescein angiography showed hyperfluorescence around the macula lesion without leakage, consistent with staining (Figure 1E), in the left eye.
12. There was no leakage or hyperfluorescence of the POFLs in the right eye (Figure 1F).
13. Fundus lesions near the macular in the patient’s left eye (A), pigmented ocular fundus lesions (asterisks) in the right eye (B), optical coherence tomography of the left (C) and right (D) eyes, and fluorescein angiography of the left (E) and right (F) eyes.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Inquire about family cancer history and order genetic testing
B: Pars plana vitrectomy and retinal biopsy
C: Diode laser treatment to lesions
D: Metastatic workup

1. A man in his 50s presented with blurred vision in his right eye greater than in the left.
2. His medical history included squamous cell carcinoma of the lung diagnosed 1 year prior, which was resected.
3. On examination, his visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/25 OS and he had mutton fat keratic precipitates and 1+ cells in both eyes.
4. The vitreous and retina revealed no signs of inflammation.
5. The day before, he had undergone a positron emission tomography scan to look for evidence of metastatic lung cancer.
6. The result revealed mild to moderate diffuse lymphadenopathy in the neck, axillae, mediastinal, and inguinal regions.
7. The symmetric pattern favored a diagnosis of sarcoidosis; metastatic disease was less likely.
8. Because the scan was consistent with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis in this patient with granulomatous anterior iritis, no further laboratory testing was pursued.
9. The patient started treatment with prednisolone acetate, 1%, 4 times daily in both eyes.
10. A lymph-node biopsy showed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation, consistent with sarcoidosis.
11. There was no evidence of lymphoma.
12. The results of special stains were negative for bartonella, fungal organisms, and mycobacterial infection (Figure 1A).
13. A, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of the lymph-node biopsy, low (top) and high (bottom) power (original magnification ×2).
14. B, Fundus photograph of the right eye with 3+ vitreous haze and retinitis.
15. C, Fundus photograph of the left eye with retinitis, serous retinal detachment, and disc hyperemia.
16. The patient returned with loss of vision in his right eye.
17. On examination, his visual acuity was counting fingers OD and 20/30 OS.
18. He had 2+ cells in the anterior chamber and 3+ vitreous haze (Figure 1B).
19. He was treated with prednisone, 60 mg daily, for sarcoid panuveitis.
20. One week later, he had vision loss in both eyes.
21. His visual acuity was hand motions OD and counting fingers OS.
22. He had panuveitis in the right eye and uveitis with subretinal fluid and mild disc swelling in the left (Figure 1C).
23. Urgent immunology consultation for treatment of steroid-resistant sarcoidosis

A: Increase the dose of prednisone
B: Add an immunomodulatory agent
C: Further laboratory and imaging studies
D: Urgent immunology consultation for treatment of steroid-resistant sarcoidosis

1. A 53-year-old man presented with progressively worsening blurry vision of the left eye.
2. The patient reported redness in his eye for 2 days.
3. He denied pain, itchiness, or recent ocular trauma.
4. He had a distant history of contact lens wear but terminated use owing to recurrent corneal abrasions.
5. His medical history was significant for uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus, leading to bilateral below-the-knee amputations, and osteomyelitis.
6. The patient was unemployed and denied cigarette smoking, alcohol use, or drug use.
7. Current medications included insulin, nasal spray, and aspirin.
8. Review of systems was positive for stiff joints of the hands and back pain.
9. The patient reported that results from a workup for Crohn disease were negative.
10. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye.
11. Findings from Schirmer testing without anesthesia for 2 minutes were 20 mm OD and 15 mm OS.
12. Corneal sensation was bilaterally decreased to a level of 2/4.
13. There were inferior corneal epithelial defects, with significant corneal thinning bilaterally, and an inferonasal Descemetocele of the right eye.
14. The anterior chambers possessed 3 to 4+ cells, with bilateral hypopyons (Figure).
15. Serology was sent owing to concern regarding the patient’s joint pain, need for a Crohn disease workup, and presence of bilateral corneal thinning with anterior uveitis.
16. Significant results included an elevated rheumatoid factor of 27 IU/mL (normal, 0-14 IU/mL), while all other laboratory results were within normal limits.
17. Results from corneal cultures were positive for pansensitive coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, which was likely a contaminant from the eyelids.A, Slitlamp photograph of the right eye demonstrating a paracentral neurotrophic ulcer with anterior uveitis and a hypopyon.
18. B, Slitlamp photograph of the left eye demonstrating fluorescein staining of the corneal persistent epithelial defect.
19. Of note, the left eye also has reactive anterior chamber uveitis with a hypopyon.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Prescribe oral prednisone
B: Place bandage contact lenses
C: Perform tarsorrhaphy
D: Prescribe lubrication with autologous serum tears

14. Results from antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody tests were negative.

B: Initiate treatment with rituximab

2. He was seen by 2 dermatologists, a family physician, and an otolaryngologist in Venezuela as well as 2 dermatologists, 2 family physicians, a nurse practitioner, and an infectious diseases specialist in the United States.
3. These 10 clinicians collectively prescribed oral amoxicillin, cefadroxil, cephalexin, azithromycin, clindamycin, and cefdinir as well as intramuscular ceftriaxone and topical bacitracin, mupirocin, and polymyxin B.
4. None of these therapies was of benefit.
5. The patient reported no significant medical history and was not taking other medications.
6. He reported nasal congestion and pain, bleeding, and minor sloughing of nasal mucosal tissue.
7. On examination he had an erythematous plaque without ulceration on the right side of the neck (Figure, left).
8. Examination also revealed erythema and swelling of the left nasal ala extending to the infratip lobule (lowermost portion of the nasal tip directly above the nostril openings) and left alar rim as well as disruption of the nasal architecture with crusting of the left nare (Figure, right).
9. Cervical lymphadenopathy was present and most pronounced on the right side.
10. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.
11. A biopsy of the nasal tissue revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, a lymphoplasmocytic inflammation, with no organisms found using special staining.
12. Left, Erythematous plaque with crusting on the right side of the neck.
13. No ulceration was noted.
14. Right, Pronounced erythema, swelling, and crusting of the left nasal ala, extending to the infratip lobule and left alar rim.
15. Perform leishmaniasis polymerase chain reaction testing of biopsied tissue Prescribe intravenous vancomycin for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain immunofluorescence of biopsied tissue
B: Perform biopsy with oncology consultation
C: Perform leishmaniasis polymerase chain reaction testing of biopsied tissue
D: Prescribe intravenous vancomycin for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection

question:
1. A previously healthy woman in her early 20s presented with bilateral decreased vision of 2 weeks’ duration in the left eye and 5 days’ duration in the right eye.
2. She denied any medication use and had no history of ocular surgery or known ophthalmic disorders.
3. Best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 ft OD and 20/300 OS.
4. There was no afferent pupillary defect.
5. Slitlamp examination revealed fine keratic precipitates bilaterally, with 2+ anterior chamber cells in her right eye and 0.5+ cells in her left eye.
6. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye demonstrated a creamy white lesion emanating superiorly from the optic nerve associated with areas of intraretinal hemorrhage and extensive perivascular sheathing along the vascular arcades into the midperiphery (Figure 1A).
7. Ophthalmoscopic examination of the left eye showed a peripapillary preretinal gliotic lesion exerting mild traction on the macula with fine retinal striae and a macular star configuration of exudates (Figure 1B).
8. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography revealed significant cystoid macular edema with associated subretinal fluid in the right eye and hard exudates without evidence of cystoid macular edema in the left eye.Baseline montage color fundus photographs.
9. A, Right eye demonstrates retinal whitening superior to the optic nerve adjacent to several pigmented chorioretinal scars.
10. B, Left eye demonstrates a preretinal gliotic lesion with a macular star.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy
B: Neuroimaging of brain and orbits
C: Anterior chamber paracentesis for polymerase chain reaction
D: Blood cultures

12. Posterior segment examination was within normal limits.A, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrates whitening of the macula with a central red spot.
13. Flame-shaped hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are present in the nasal macula and surrounding the superior arcade.
14. B, Optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrates subfoveal debris with distortion of the normal foveal architecture.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Reassure and observe
B: OCT imaging

D: Electroretinogram

2. They had first appeared on her lower legs 15 years ago and were slowly increasing in number and spreading to involve her feet and bilateral upper extremities.
3. The patient denied tenderness, pruritus, and edema.
4. She reported no family history of this problem and denied any personal history of anemia, epistaxis, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, or hemoptysis.
5. She had a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco abuse, requiring treatment with losartan and atorvastatin.

question:
1. An 85-year-old man with a history of occupational exposure to asbestos presented with 1 week of nausea and vomiting without any bowel function.
2. He reported only mild abdominal pain.
3. The patient denied any history of abdominal surgery.
4. On examination, he was mildly distended and tender focally on the right side.
5. In the emergency department, a nasogastric tube was placed, yielding a moderate amount of dark, foul-smelling output.
6. Laboratory results were significant for a white blood cell count of 13 300/μL (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001) (bands 20%).
7. A contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated dilated small intestine (measuring up to 4.7 cm), with air-fluid levels extending to the terminal ileum (Figure 1A and B).
8. The entire colon was collapsed.
9. There were several loops of normal-caliber bowel proximal to the area of concern.
10. The decision was made to take him to the operating room for exploration given the lack of any previous abdominal surgical procedures and no other explanation for his symptoms.
11. Intraoperatively, a large portion of the small intestine was involved in dense adhesions.
12. After performing careful lysis on the distal involved bowel, a tightly coiled and twisted segment was encountered (Figure 1C).
13. At this point, further attempts to separate loops of small intestine would have been difficult, and the decision was made to resect this segment (approximately 110 cm) and perform a primary anastomosis.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Peritoneal mesothelioma
B: Sclerosing encapsulated peritonitis
C: Malrotation with Ladd bands
D: Peritoneal encapsulation

1. A 50-year-old healthy woman underwent an uncomplicated elective clipping of a right middle cerebral artery aneurysm via pterional craniotomy.
2. Ophthalmology was consulted urgently in the recovery room because of complaints of vision loss and ophthalmoplegia in the right eye.
3. On examination, visual acuity was no light perception (NLP) OD and 20/20 OS.
4. Pupils were equal and round, with a 3+ relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye.
5. Intraocular pressure was within normal limits in both eyes.
6. There was complete ophthalmoplegia in the right eye with no signs of restriction on forced ductions and normal motility in the left eye.
7. Visual field was full to confrontation in the left eye.
8. The right eye also demonstrated mild fullness of the orbit, right cheek skin erythema, trace proptosis, and trace conjunctival chemosis.
9. Posterior examination was significant for diffuse retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot in the macula in the right eye (Figure 1A).
10. There were no other neurologic deficits identified on examination.Case presentation.
11. A, Fundus photograph of right eye showing diffuse retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot.
12. B, Immediate postoperative magnetic resonance imaging showing enlarged extraocular muscles on the right side (arrowheads).A computed tomography scan without contrast did not show an acute intracranial hemorrhage and demonstrated diffuse enlargement of the right extraocular muscles.
13. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits with contrast again showed enlargement and abnormal signal of the extraocular muscles on the right (Figure 1B); there was no evidence of cavernous sinus pathology.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Immediate surgical re-exploration
B: Emergent angiography
C: Immediate anticoagulation
D: Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis

1. A woman in her early 60s with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia was transferred to our hospital after multiple transient ischemic attacks and left internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis during the past several months.
2. Her most recent presentation was 1 week prior for a minor stroke with amaurosis fugax, slurred speech, right-sided weakness, and facial droop lasting longer than 24 hours.
3. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated subacute infarctions involving the left frontal and parietal hemispheres.
4. She was a current smoker and was taking aspirin and statin medication at the time of presentation.
5. Workup at another facility prior to transfer included computed tomographic angiography of the neck, which showed chronic occlusion of the right ICA and 95% stenosis of the left ICA.
6. On examination, the patient was afebrile with a heart rate of 69 beats/min and blood pressure of 134/69 mm Hg.
7. Pertinent findings included no carotid bruit, a regular cardiac rhythm, and equally palpable upper extremity pulses bilaterally.
8. The patient was neurologically intact, save for 4/5 motor strength in her right upper extremity.
9. Computed tomographic angiography of the head and neck was performed (Figure 1).
10. Sagittal view demonstrates the left internal carotid stenosis (A indicates anterior; P, posterior) (A) and the distal extent of the findings (arrowhead) (B).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Trapped air embolus
B: Free-floating arterial thrombus
C: Ruptured arterial plaque
D: Radiographic artifact

1. A woman in her 60s presented to the hospital because she felt abdominal pain and increasing asthenia during the previous 4 months.
2. She reported a weight loss of 40 kg during the previous 12 months concomitant with depression.
3. The patient had a history of cardiac arrhythmia, hypertension, and sigmoidectomy for diverticulitis.
4. Medications included lasilix, amlodipine, amiodarone, and atenolol.
5. On examination, the patient appeared well.
6. Her vital signs were normal.
7. The abdomen was soft without distension.
8. A positive Murphy sign was observed.

11. The results of renal and liver function, coagulation, blood level of electrolytes, total protein, albumin, antigen carcino embryonnaire, carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carbohydrate antigen 125, and β2 microglobulin tests were normal.
12. The patient had a normal esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy.
13. Ultrasonography revealed a 10 × 8-m mass in the right hypochondrium.
14. Abdominal computed tomography scan revealed a thickened gallbladder wall infiltrating the liver parenchyma.
15. There were 3 perihepatic lymph nodes.

B: Acute cholecystitis

D: Lymphoma

2. She was diagnosed with depression and began treatment with antidepressant medication.
3. After 8 months, she had worsening complaints.
4. At that time, a family member reported that her memory problems had progressed.
5. She was no longer able to find misplaced objects, remember appointments, or handle financial affairs.
6. She was often subdued, her mood depressed, and her sleeping time increased.
7. Clinical examination at that time revealed a flattened affect and a 22 of 30 Mini-Mental State Examination score.
8. Findings were otherwise normal, and there were no focal neurologic deficits.
9. Basic laboratory workup results were unremarkable.
10. She was referred to a neurologist, who ordered contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain.
11. The MRI (Figure) revealed extensive ill-defined areas of FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) and T2 signal abnormalities with additional enhancing nodular foci located within deep white matter structures, the basal ganglia, the caudate, the pons, and the midbrain.

13. Magnetic resonance images (MRIs) of the head obtained 8 months after patient’s first clinical visit.
14. A, Axial T2-weighted MRI of the head at the level of the lateral ventricles demonstrates extensive ill-defined areas of increasing signal with only minimal associated mass effect involving the frontal lobe white matter, greater on the left than on the right.
15. B, Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI at the same level demonstrates abnormal patchy enhancement of the head of the left caudate nucleus and the deep anterior left frontal lobe white matter.
16. Neoplasms such as multicentric glioma, glioblastoma multiforme, and metastases

A: Inflammatory demyelinating processes such as multiple sclerosis
B: Neoplasms such as multicentric glioma, glioblastoma multiforme, and metastases

1. A 56-year-old man with systemic lupus erythematosus was taking chloroquine for 7 years (2.6 mg/kg daily; cumulative dose, 332 g).
2. He was diagnosed as having nephropathy 5 years ago.
3. He presented with a history of bilateral, painless, progressive visual diminution for 2 years.
4. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/200 in both eyes.
5. He had bilateral posterior subcapsular cataracts.
6. Both the corneas were clear.
7. Intraocular pressures were 14 and 16 mm Hg in the right and left eyes, respectively, by Goldmann applanation tonometry.
8. Dilated ophthalmoscopy revealed a hypopigmented zone in the parafoveal macula (Figure).
9. Color vision testing revealed red-green deficiencies in both eyes.Advanced chloroquine retinopathy.
10. Fundus photographs of the right (A) and left (B) eyes showing hypopigmented zones concentric to the fovea consistent with chloroquine retinopathy.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Discontinue treatment with chloroquine
B: Reassure and observe
C: Treat with intravitreous corticosteroids
D: Examine family members for macular dystrophy

1. A woman in her 70s was referred for treatment of a choroidal melanoma of the left eye approximately 4 years ago.
2. At presentation, she reported occasional photopsias, floaters, and blurred vision but no pain.
3. Visual acuity was 20/25−2 OD and 20/40 OS.
4. Her choroidal melanoma was located at the 11- to 1-o’clock position, anterior to the equator but posterior to the ciliary body.
5. Low internal reflectivity and a mass measuring 8.4 mm in height by 12.9 mm across the base (Figure, A and B) were revealed on B-scan ultrasonography.
6. A complete blood cell count and results of liver function tests were within reference limits; a computed tomographic scan of the abdomen, chest, brain, and orbits showed no evidence of metastasis.A and B, B-scan ultrasonography of the left eye.
7. A, Original scan shows a mass with a height of 8.4 mm and a base dimension of 12.9 mm.
8. B, Follow-up scan shows the mass in a transverse 12-o’clock position with a decrease in tumor height to 1.4 mm 4½ years after iodine 125 plaque brachytherapy.
9. C, An external slitlamp photograph of the left eye shows a bluish black pigmented lesion on the sclera measures 4.5 × 3.0 mm (anterior-posterior by horizontal orientation).
10. This lesion corresponds to the site of the choroidal melanoma and plaque placement.A radioactive episcleral iodine 125 (125I) plaque was surgically placed over the lesion and removed 1 week later.
11. The tumor decreased in height, and visual acuity remained stable at 20/30 OS.
12. The tumor height decreased to 2.3 mm by 1 year and remained at less than 2 mm in years 2 through 4½ on B-scan ultrasonography (Figure, B).At her last follow-up, the patient had a 4.5 × 3.0-mm bluish black flat lesion on the sclera (Figure, C).
13. Results of a dilated fundus examination showed a grayish black, minimally elevated choroidal lesion with surrounding retinal pigment epithelial atrophy but without subretinal fluid, hemorrhage, or hard exudates.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Repeat iodine 125 plaque brachytherapy
B: External beam radiotherapy
C: Enucleation
D: Observation
