question:
1. A woman in her 50s was referred to a neurologist for a history of gait, balance, personality, and judgment changes over 4 years.
2. Her family noted that her first symptoms appeared at age 55, with subtle gait dysfunction and then evident imbalance.
3. By age 57, there was concern over progressive withdrawal from social interchange, personality changes, and impairment of judgment.
4. By age 59, she was experiencing bouts of inappropriate out-of-context laughter and tears, inattention, daytime fatigue, and frank memory impairment.
5. She developed visuoperceptive changes and difficulties using the television remote control device.
6. She developed obsessive checking behaviors.
7. She started having swallowing difficulties but nonetheless had unexpected weight gain.
8. She developed progressively worse motoric problems, with stiffness, abnormal posturing, a left toe pointing upward, and falls.
9. Her medical history was significant only for restless legs syndrome, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, myopia, and a deviated nasal septum.
10. Her family history revealed that her father was alive and well at approximately age 90 years, and her mother had died at approximately age 80 years with a history of neuropsychiatric disease and gait change.
11. There was no history of tobacco, excess alcohol, or recreational drug use.
12. General examination findings were noncontributory.
13. Neurological examination revealed abnormal mental status, with full orientation and good registration, concentration, digit span, and language function but with poor calculations and constructions (Figure 1A) and decreased short-term memory.
14. Nonetheless, her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 28 of 30.
15. Cranial nerve examination revealed some decreased upgaze and mild facial masking.
16. Motor examination revealed rigidity and dystonic posturing in the left arm and leg, imbalance on gait, decreased arm swing, and retropulsion but no significant tremor.
17. Sensory examination findings were normal.
18. Reflex examination showed mild left hyperreflexia with an upgoing left toe.
19. Blood and urine laboratory study results were within normal limits.
20. Cerebrospinal fluid was unremarkable except for biomarkers that showed a mid-range β-amyloid 42 level of 530 pg/mL and normal total tau and phosphotau levels of 182 and 25 pg/mL, respectively.
21. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was reported as unremarkable (Figure 1B).
22. Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of the brain revealed right frontotemporoparietal hypometabolism with some sensorimotor sparing (Figure 1C), which was neither typical nor atypical of Alzheimer disease.
23. Electroencephalography showed left frontotemporal sharp waves and slowing.
24. She had continued progressive decline in cognition and motor function and died almost mute and bedridden in her early 60s after a 9-year course of illness.
25. A, Patient testing.
26. Constructional apraxia is seen in her copying of the top row template figures, with preserved writing in script.
27. B, Brain magnetic resonance imaging at the time of presentation.
28. The top panel shows selected sagittal T1-weighted images, and the bottom panel shows selected axial T1-weighted images.
29. C, Brain positron emission tomography using fluorodeoxyglucose F 18 tracer in the axial plane.
30. Frontal and temporal hypometabolism is seen, more marked on the right, with some apparent sensorimotor sparing bilaterally.

What is your diagnosis?

A: Alzheimer disease, frontal variant
B: Frontotemporal dementia
C: Progressive supranuclear palsy
D: Corticobasal degeneration

10. A punch biopsy for histopathologic examination was performed (Figure, B and C).A, Retiform purpura on the right helix.
11. B, Abundant red blood cell extravasation and fibrin thrombi (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×10).
12. C, Leukocytoclastic vasculitis and fibrin thrombi (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40).

A: Levamisole-induced vasculopathy
B: Mixed cryoglobulinemia

D: Septic vasculitis

1. A white man in his 30s with a remote history of right eye enucleation following globe trauma presented to our clinic in July 2014 with decreased visual acuity in the left eye.
2. He described a history of initially intermittent (lasting hours to days) then constant (for the past 6-8 weeks) central and peripheral blurred vision in the left eye.
3. He reported no headaches, numbness, weakness, eye pain, hearing loss, or other neurologic issues.
4. Eight years earlier, he had sustained a fireworks injury to his right eye followed by globe repair and enucleation within 3 days.
5. He had no other significant medical or ocular history.
6. His right eye’s external appearance was normal, and the prosthesis fit well.
7. Uncorrected visual acuity was Snellen 20/70−1 OS (no improvement with pinhole); intraocular pressure was 13 mm Hg.
8. Slitlamp examination results of the anterior segment were normal.
9. Ophthalmoscopy demonstrated 1+ cells in the anterior vitreous and a serous retinal detachment involving the macula and extending from the 2-o’clock to the 10-o’clock position with pigmentary and atrophic changes in the macula.
10. No breaks were noted on scleral depressed examination.
11. Fluorescein angiography showed multifocal areas of early hyperfluorescence with late leakage and diffuse retinal vascular leakage predominantly in the inferior retina (Figure 1A).
12. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed a thickened choroid and subretinal fluid throughout the macula (Figure 1B).
13. Enhanced depth imaging showed an enlarged choroid throughout the posterior pole, and ultrasonography confirmed extensive inferior retinal detachment (not shown).
14. A, Fluorescein late-phase angiogram shows multifocal areas of posterior choroidal leakage and diffuse retinal vascular leakage in the inferior (detached) retina.
15. B, Optical coherence tomographic en face infrared image (left) and vertical line scan (right) through the fovea show subretinal fluid extending inferiorly with hyperreflective subretinal deposits.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Systemic corticosteroid therapy
B: Observation
C: Photodynamic therapy
D: Antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy (anti-VEGF)

2. She was initially admitted for altered mental status in the setting of an unwitnessed fall and was noted to have “bruises” on her lower extremities.
3. Dermatology was consulted after the development of new lesions on her nose, ear, and the extensor surfaces of her arms bilaterally.
4. Admission laboratory test results showed hypercalcemia (calcium level, 11.5 mg/dL) and acute kidney injury (creatinine level, 5.6 mg/dL).
5. On physical examination, the patient’s nose, bilateral cheeks, forehead, and left ear (helical rim and antihelix [Figure, A]) were found to have dusky purpuric macules and patches.
6. Her knees, feet, and the extensor surfaces of her arms had reticulated purpuric macules and patches.
7. There was skin sloughing off the lesions on her elbows (Figure, B) and knees.
8. Four-millimeter punch biopsy specimens were taken from the left ear, right arm, and forehead (Figure, C and D).
9. Clinical and histopathologic images from a case of acral retiform purpura.
10. A, Dusky purpuric macules on the helical rim and antihelix of the ear.
11. B, Reticulated purpuric patches with focal areas of necrosis on the extensor surfaces of the arms.
12. C and D, In specimens from the forehead, multifocal intravascular fibrinoid material consisting of a mix of cryoglobulins and fibrin thrombi with relatively little vessel wall inflammation was seen (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×4 [C] and ×10 [D]).

What is your diagnosis?

A: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
B: Antiphospholipid syndrome
C: Type I cryoglobulinemia associated with multiple myeloma
D: Purpura fulminans

1. A man in his 60s presented with a painless rapidly enlarging ulcer on his left leg 1 week after the onset of diverticulitis, a neutropenic fever, and severe sepsis due to multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection that necessitated admission to the intensive care unit.
2. His medical history included a heart transplant for ischemic cardiomyopathy in his early 50s, and he was receiving long-term immunosuppressive therapy with cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, and deflazacort.
3. He had received a diagnosis of plasmablastic lymphoma 6 months earlier and was being treated with polychemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin hydrochloride, vincristine sulfate, and prednisone [CHOP] regimen).
4. Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated 5 × 5-cm round ulcer with raised border, surrounding erythema, and a base with purulent debris (Figure 1A).
5. A superficial swab culture sample grew P aeruginosa.
6. A punch biopsy specimen from the edge of the ulcer was obtained and sent for histopathologic evaluation (Figure 1B).
7. A, Cutaneous ulcer on the patient’s left leg with a raised erythematous border and a base with purulent debris.
8. B, Diagnostic biopsy shows enlarged endothelial cells with intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo, and some cytoplasmic inclusions.
9. Similar findings are detected in some macrophages (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Ecthyma gangrenosum
B: Cytomegalovirus ulcer
C: Mucormycosis ulcer
D: Pyoderma gangrenosum

1. A newborn girl with a nodular lesion on the scalp present since birth was seen at the dermatology clinic.
2. The parents reported occasional erosions and crusting that resolved with topical mupirocin, 2%, cream, but with no continued growth.
3. The mother had had a normal pregnancy.
4. Physical examination revealed a firm, exophytic, and flat-topped nodule, with superficial erosion and crust on the right parietal side of the scalp measuring 3 cm in diameter and 1 cm thick (Figure, A).
5. No other skin lesions were found.
6. A 4-mm punch skin biopsy was performed, and tissue was sent for pathologic analysis (Figure, B and C).
7. Cerebral and abdominal ultrasonography revealed no evidence of visceral involvement.
8. The lesion regressed without treatment over a period of 8 months.
9. Close follow-up every 3 months was scheduled, and complete involution of the tumor was noted at 10 months of age (Figure, D).
10. A, Nodular lesion on the right parietal scalp at initial presentation.
11. B, Histopathologic image of a biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×200).
12. C, Immunohistochemical image of a biopsy specimen (actin stain, original magnification ×100).
13. D, Complete regression of tumor at 10 months of age.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Giant cell fibroblastoma
B: Infantile myofibromatosis
C: Dermoid cyst
D: Keratoacanthoma

1. A 36-year-old woman reported experiencing shortness of breath for 1 month.
2. She reported a 6.3-kg weight loss, tremor, diaphoresis, and palpitations over the course of 2 months.
3. She denied eye symptoms or muscle weakness.
4. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, tongue and hand tremors, no exophthalmos, a 2-fold diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, and brisk reflexes.
5. Laboratory results showed a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level of 0.005 mIU/L (normal, 0.45-4.50 mIU/L), free thyroxine level greater than 7.77 ng/dL (100.01 pmol/L) (normal, 0.82-1.77 ng/dL [10.55-22.78 pmol/L]), free triiodothyronine level of 30.6 pg/mL (47.1 pmol/L) (normal, 2.0-3.9 pg/mL [3.08-6.01 pmol/L]), and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin index of 5.5 (normal, <1.3).
6. The patient began treatment with methimazole, 20 mg twice daily.
7. A noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest (Figure, left) and an 18F-fludeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography (FDG-PET)/CT scan (Figure, right) were completed to evaluate her dyspnea.
8. Left, Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the upper chest shown in cross section.
9. Right, 18F-fludeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography/CT scan of the whole body.
10. Note the increased uptake in the thymus indicating increased metabolic activity.
11. Refer to surgery for removal of the thymus.
12. Do nothing now but repeat CT scan in 3 to 6 months

What Would You Do Next?

A: Refer to medical oncology
B: Perform biopsy of the thymus
C: Refer to surgery for removal of the thymus
D: Do nothing now but repeat CT scan in 3 to 6 months

question:
1. A 5-year-old boy with a 1-year history of intermittent abdominal pain presented to the emergency department with 2 days of nausea, nonbilious emesis, and diffuse abdominal pain.
2. He was afebrile and had normal vital signs.
3. Physical examination findings were notable for mild abdominal distension and tenderness without guarding or rebound sign.
4. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal appendix.
5. Abdominal radiography (Figure 1A) revealed multiple polygonal calcified lesions in the pelvis and a nonobstructive bowel gas pattern.
6. Computed tomography (Figure 1B) revealed a 5.6 × 5.3 × 4.6-cm midline cystic pelvic mass adjacent to the anterior rectal wall that contained several irregularly shaped ossifications.
7. Laboratory study results were significant for normal levels of α-fetoprotein and chorionic gonadotropin and a white blood cell count of 19 700/μL (reference range, 5500-15 500/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001).
8. The patient was taken to the operating room for an exploratory laparotomy.A, Supine abdominal radiograph reveals multiple polygonal calcified lesions in the pelvis (black arrowhead).
9. B, Computed tomographic sagittal image of the abdomen reveals a midline cystic pelvic mass that contains several irregularly shaped ossifications (white arrowhead).
10. L indicates left.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Pelvic teratoma
B: Meckel diverticulum
C: Enteric duplication cyst
D: Carcinoid tumor

7. There was no evidence of recurrent disease after this treatment.
8. External examination revealed mild edema, erythema, and ptosis of the left upper lid (Figure 1).
9. Left cervical lymphadenopathy was present.
10. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25, and left ocular motility was full.
11. Photographs of the upper face show the ocular prosthesis (black arrowheads) and asymmetric enlargement, erythema, and ptosis of the left upper eyelid (white arrowheads).
12. A, Front view.
13. B, Left side.

1. Two brothers in their late teens presented with bilateral eyelid swelling and irritation that had lasted 1 year.
2. There was no history of associated eyelid pain or bleeding.
3. The older brother had an extensive medical history, including dysphonia, oral mucosal lesions, alopecia, recurrent parotitis, vocal cord swelling, and recurrent vesicular eruptions on his face, trunk, and perineum.

7. Focal trichiasis was associated with superficial punctate keratitis.
8. There were no other corneal findings.
9. There were no lesions on the conjunctiva or iris bilaterally.
10. The lenses were clear and no abnormalities were visualized using funduscopy.
11. Findings from the remainder of the ocular examination were unremarkable.
12. Clinical appearance of eyelid margin nodules in the older brother.
13. Waxy nodular lesions are present along the upper and lower eyelids of the patient’s left eye.
14. The younger brother had similar, although less severe, ocular and systemic findings, including eyelid nodules, facial scarring, hyperkeratosis, oral mucosal lesions, and dysphonia.
15. The patients’ parents denied consanguinity.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Administer hyperfocal cryotherapy to the eyelid nodules
B: Start D-penicillamine therapy
C: Perform an eyelid nodule biopsy
D: Assess for enlarged tongue with decreased motility

3. He applied ice to alleviate the burning, but this worsened the condition.
4. A heating pad provided some measure of relief, as did a brief course of systemic corticosteroids.
5. Physical examination revealed that some papular lesions were associated with slight purpura and hemorrhagic crust (Figure, A).

9. C, Biopsy specimen from the left ear under direct immunofluorescence and stained for anti-IgM highlights thrombi within vessels (original magnification ×200).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Relapsing polychondritis
B: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis)
C: Cold agglutinin disease
D: Chilblain

B: Secondary syphilis

question:
1. A woman in her 70s with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and venous thromboembolism presented to the hospital with 2 months of progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion.
2. Her medical history was significant for a single episode of lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis during a prior hospitalization, complicated by multiple subsegmental pulmonary emboli.
3. At that time, she underwent inferior vena cava filter placement, followed by initiation of anticoagulation therapy.
4. Her current medications included metoprolol tartrate, simvastatin, and warfarin sodium.
5. She denied any substantial tobacco or alcohol use, and her family history was negative for venous thromboembolic disease.
6. Her initial physical examination had unremarkable results, with laboratory evaluation of prothrombin time significant for an international normalized ratio of 2.8.
7. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed a large filling defect within the main pulmonary artery, flattening of the interventricular septum, and multiple pulmonary nodules.
8. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated evidence of severely increased right ventricular systolic pressure, with moderate right ventricular dilation.
9. She was referred for urgent pharmacomechanical interventions, including catheter-directed embolectomy and thrombolysis, for a presumed diagnosis of submassive pulmonary embolism.
10. Following the procedure, she experienced no substantial clinical or radiographic improvement.
11. She underwent a repeated CT scan of the chest (Figure).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Venous thromboembolic disease
B: Pulmonary artery sarcoma
C: Locally advanced lung cancer
D: Pulmonary tumor embolism

10. Case presentation.

12. B, Enlarged fundus photograph shows nummular macular lesions with mild retina striae and optic disc edema.

B: Perform electroretinography
C: Perform fluorescein angiography
D: Perform magnetic resonance angiography

question:
1. An 11-month-old boy presented to the clinic with a papule on his right lower eyelid that had doubled in size since it first appeared 3 months earlier (Figure 1).
2. He had been born at full term and was otherwise healthy.
3. His medication regimen included a pediatric multivitamin.
4. There was no history of trauma to the area.
5. On examination, the patient’s pupils were equal in diameter and reactive to light, his ocular motility was full, and the lesion did not obstruct his vision.
6. Findings from external examination were significant for a single 3 × 2 × 2–mm, red-brown, raised, solid, fixed papule at the center of the lower eyelid margin.
7. There was no madarosis and no evidence of epiphora or conjunctivitis.
8. The lesion was initially diagnosed as a hemangioma and the decision was made to monitor it.
9. On examination 1 month later, the papule had grown slightly, with a 1 × 1–mm area of ulceration.
10. It also appeared to encroach on the visual axis in the downgaze position.
11. The parents reported that the patient had started to rub his eyelid intermittently, causing irritation and a minimal amount of associated bleeding.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Continue observation
B: Prescribe propranolol hydrochloride
C: Excise the lesion
D: Perform curettage of the lesion

1. A 52-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus and cigarette smoking who had a prior laparoscopic cholecystectomy was referred to our institution for severe postprandial epigastric abdominal pain that had been ongoing for several months and unintentional weight loss.
2. She had been prescribed total parenteral nutrition prior to referral.
3. On presentation, her physical examination was remarkable for mild epigastric tenderness.
4. The results of laboratory testing, including a complete blood cell count, chemistry values, liver function tests, and amylase and lipase levels, were unremarkable.
5. Computed tomography demonstrated focal gastric thickening.
6. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic ultrasonography was performed that confirmed a submucosal gastric mass (Figure, A).
7. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy revealed benign and reactive glandular cells and debris.
8. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a 2.4-cm hypervascular and exophytic mass in the gastric antrum and locoregional lymphadenopathy (Figure, B).
9. A, Endoscopic ultrasonography of the gastric antrum mass reveals an area of gastric thickening (arrowheads) corresponding to computed tomographic findings.
10. During endoscopy, this area was visualized grossly as a bulge in the atrium along the incisura.
11. A fine-needle aspiration biopsy was nondiagnostic, showing gastric antral-type mucosa without pathologic changes (inset).
12. B, The coronal image in T2 phase reveals a 1.8 × 2.4 × 1.5-cm hypotense lesion (arrowhead) in the gastric antrum.
13. The lesion was also enhanced on T1 arterial phase sequencing.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
B: Gastric cancer
C: Peptic ulcer disease
D: Ectopic pancreas

2. He noted a childhood history of plantar warts and believed these lesions to be identical in appearance.
3. He did not recall any injury or unusual exposure.
4. He had received his third cycle of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin hydrochloride, vincristine sulfate, prednisone) 2 weeks prior to presentation as well as an injection of granulocyte-colony stimulating factor.
5. He was anticipating his fourth cycle of treatment the day of his presentation.

7. The patient was afebrile, and his vital signs were within normal limits.
8. Physical examination revealed grouped, brown, flat-topped papules on his distal plantar left foot (Figure).

11. A few areas had shallow erosions.
12. Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia, with a white blood cell count of 2800/μL, hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dL, and a platelet count of 81 × 103/μL.
13. His lactate dehydrogenase level was elevated at 914 U/L, and results of his comprehensive metabolic panel were unremarkable. 1. A 64-year-old man with coronary artery disease and an 80 pack-year smoking habit presented with 2 weeks of gait instability leading to frequent falls and 8 weeks of vertigo and double vision.
2. He reported unintentional weight loss without fevers or decreased appetite.
3. He denied any history of alcohol abuse.
4. Medications included metoprolol and aspirin.
5. On examination, he was alert and oriented and vital signs were normal; body mass index was 24.
6. Neurologic examination revealed right eye heterotropia and nasal upshoot indicative of a fourth cranial nerve palsy (Figure 1A), left ptosis, flattening of the right nasolabial fold (Figure 1B), and bilateral restricted upgaze and ataxia (Video).
7. Strength and reflexes were preserved.
8. Results of a basic metabolic panel and complete blood cell count were normal.
9. Screening for human immunodeficiency virus, Lyme disease, and drug use was negative.
10. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was unremarkable.
11. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sampling revealed elevated protein (75 mg/dL [reference range, 10-42]), lymphocyte predominant pleocytosis (21-66 cells/uL [reference range, 0-11]), and oligoclonal bands (OCBs).
12. Pleural thickening was seen on routine chest radiography; chest computed tomography (CT) revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy, subcentimeter pulmonary nodules, and calcified pleural plaques.A, Right fourth cranial nerve palsy.
13. On adduction, the right eye turns upward.
14. This finding (nasal upshoot) suggests the presence of a fourth nerve palsy.
15. B, Mild left ptosis and flattening of the right nasolabial fold.

A: Obtain evoked potentials
B: Obtain electromyography (EMG)
C: Check thiamine levels and start oral supplementation
D: Obtain a whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET)/CT scan and paraneoplastic antibody evaluation

question:
1. A woman in her 50s presented for evaluation of a growing, painful scar on the right side of her abdomen.
2. She reported having a rectangular area of discolored skin for the past 10 years that developed as a result of a complication during an interventional radiology procedure for treatment of a splenic aneurysm.
3. Two months prior to presentation this lesion became painful and enlarged, without improvement with triamcinolone cream or oral antibiotics.
4. She also reported recent fevers, night sweats, nausea, and fatigue.
5. She denied international travel, drug use, incarceration, and high-risk sexual behavior.
6. The patient had a history of uterine cancer at age 25, for which she underwent hysterectomy and chemotherapy.
7. She also had a history of breast cancer in her 40s, for which she underwent lumpectomy and tamoxifen therapy.

13. Inferior to the plaque there was an approximately 3-cm, tender, orange-to-yellow patch.
14. No lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were noted.

A: Obtain bacterial and mycobacterial cultures of ulcerated area and pursue treatment with a longer course of antibiotics
B: Perform a skin biopsy for histopathologic examination
C: Obtain a computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest and abdomen
D: Check the patient’s human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) status

4. He was randomized to experimental drug CPX-351 for induction, but treatment was discontinued as a result of renal failure.

12. Slitlamp examination of the right eye revealed a 0.5-mm hypopyon with small hemorrhages on the iris surface (Figure 1A).
13. In the left eye, examination demonstrated a 1.5-mm hypopyon mixed with hemorrhage, 1+ cells in the anterior chamber, and small hemorrhages on the iris surface (Figure 1B).
14. Bilaterally, gonioscopy revealed open angles with few hemorrhages in the angle but no neovascularization.
15. Dilated fundoscopic examination had unremarkable results bilaterally, with no retinal hemorrhages or optic disc swelling.

B: HLA-B27 uveitis

D: Leukemia relapse

question:
1. A man in his 30s presented with a 5-day history of bilateral redness, blurred vision, and photophobia.
2. The patient had received a diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection 4 months before, with a nadir in his CD4 count of 11/μL.
3. He started highly active antiretroviral therapy, with improvement in his CD4 count to 101/μL most recently.
4. During the past few months, he had reported increasing fatigue and intermittent fevers thought to be owing to immune reactivation syndrome.
5. In addition to highly active antiretroviral therapy, he received combined sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim and azithromycin prophylaxis.
6. His visual acuity was 20/150 OD and 20/100 OS, and intraocular pressures were 6 and 10 mm Hg, respectively.
7. On slitlamp examination, both eyes were injected with diffuse mutton-fat keratic precipitates and had more than 50 cells per 1×1-mm slitlamp high-power beam in the anterior chamber.
8. Results of a dilated ophthalmoscopic examination revealed bilateral vitritis, hyperemic optic nerves, and extensive whitening likely involving all layers of the retina (Figure 1).
9. He was hospitalized and started therapy consisting of intravenous (IV) acyclovir sodium, 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, and prednisone, 30 mg/d.
10. Samples for a laboratory workup for infectious causes were obtained.
11. After 48 hours of treatment, his condition did not improve.
12. Marked vitritis, hyperemia of the optic nerve, and coalescent areas of retinal whitening involving the posterior pole are seen in the left eye.
13. Visual acuity is 20/100.
14. Check laboratory results and add IV penicillin G

What Would You Do Next?

A: Continue the same treatment
B: Increase the dose of the corticosteroids
C: Check laboratory results and add IV penicillin G
D: Vitreous tap/biopsy

question:
1. An 80-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, gastric ulcers, celiac artery occlusion, and transient ischemic attacks presented with a painful rash on her flank of 2 days’ duration.
2. She denied any history of trauma and had not applied anything topically in this area of skin.
3. She denied fevers, systemic symptoms, joint pain, and skin thickening.
4. Her medications included metformin, lansoprazole, venlafaxine, diltiazem, atorvastatin, oxycodone/acetaminophen, ramopril, reglan, zolpidem, and clopidogrel.
5. Physical examination revealed an 8-cm solitary, erythematous plaque with vesiculation and central erosion on the right lateral area of her abdomen (Figure, A).
6. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.
7. A punch biopsy showed a vacuolar interface dermatitis pattern, but a definitive clinical diagnosis was not established.
8. She was treated with clobetasol cream (0.05%), and the plaque resolved in 4 weeks with postinflammatory hypopigmentation.
9. Ten months later, the patient developed a tender, pink, indurated 7-cm plaque with telangiectasias and central ulceration in the same location, with no other cutaneous findings (Figure, B).
10. No precipitating factors could be identified.
11. A punch biopsy showed minimal inflammation, atrophy and hyperkeratosis of the epidermis, and edema, sclerosis, and absence of hair follicles in the dermis (Figure, C).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Order laboratory studies for antinuclear, anti-Scl-70, and anti-centromere antibodies
B: Obtain a detailed procedural history
C: Perform patch testing for a possible contact allergen
D: Obtain skin swab for varicella zoster virus direct fluorescent antibody level

1. A woman in her 40s was referred to our service owing to unusual findings detected on routine abdominal ultrasonography ordered by her gynecologist.
2. The ultrasonographic scan showed a hepatic mass in the right lobe composing approximately 50% of the liver parenchyma.
3. The patient was asymptomatic, and there were no significant findings on abdominal physical examination— the liver was not palpable.
4. Results of whole blood analyses, including α-fetoprotein, were within the reference ranges.
5. She had not received any medication, including contraceptive pills or hormones, for more than 10 years.

11. Cross-sectional computed tomographic image of the abdomen shows a large, intrahepatic, 20-cm solid mass.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Hepatocellular carcinoma
B: Fibrolamellar carcinoma
C: Hepatic metastasis
D: Gossypiboma

question:
1. A 65-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a painful anal mass and fecal incontinence.
2. The anal lesion appeared 1 year earlier and grew slowly to the current size.
3. The patient reported bleeding from the rectum after defecation and denied weight loss or fever.
4. The patient noted no other symptoms.
5. His medical history included atopic dermatitis and pulmonary tuberculosis.
6. There was no family history of gastrointestinal pathology.
7. He had not undergone any previous abdominal surgery, except inguinal hernia repair.
8. He claimed to be a heavy smoker.
9. No history of sexually transmitted diseases was found.
10. Physical examination revealed a 12 × 10-cm hard mass on the left side of the anus (Figure 1A).
11. It was ulcerated, covered by purulent exudate, and very painful.
12. The scrotum was mildly tender to palpation.
13. Digital rectal examination and rectoscopy were not performed because of the pain and fecal incontinence.
14. The abdomen was soft and nontender.
15. Routine blood, liver, and renal function test results were normal, as were results for carcinoembryonic antigen and cancer antigen 19-9.
16. Chest radiography showed no abnormalities.
17. Computed tomographic scan of the pelvis showed a hypodense 12 × 7 × 3-cm mass extending to the anus, anal canal, and lower perirectal space (Figure 1B).
18. Abdominal computed tomography showed no pathology.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Giant perianal abscess
B: Giant condyloma
C: Anal adenocarcinoma
D: Anal squamous cell carcinoma

1. A 60-year-old man with advanced melanoma presented with headaches and increasing fatigue during treatment with ipilimumab.
2. Several months earlier, he presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath.
3. Imaging revealed pulmonary emboli and incidental groin lymphadenopathy.
4. Biopsy of a lymph node showed melanoma.
5. He then underwent inguinal lymph node dissection and was found to have 9 lymph nodes involved with melanoma (stage IIIC melanoma).He was then treated with ipilimumab (3 mg/kg), a monoclonal antibody to cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4), every 3 weeks, as part of an investigational adjuvant therapy clinical trial.
6. When presenting for his fourth and final dose of ipilimumab, he reported central headaches, severe fatigue, poor appetite, intermittent nausea, and a mild rash.
7. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits.
8. Physical examination had largely unremarkable results except for a slightly red, raised rash over his chest and proximal extremities.Laboratory testing showed the following: thyrotropin, 0.02 mIU/L (reference range, 0.3-5.0 mIU/L), and free thyroxine, less than 0.25 ng/dL (reference range, 0.5-1.2 ng/dL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 12.871).
9. Cosyntropin stimulation test showed a cortisol peak level of 0.9 µg/dL (reference range, >20 µg/dL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 27.588).
10. He had low corticotropin (<5 pg/mL; reference range, 7-51 pg/mL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 0.22) and testosterone levels (<0.1 ng/mL; reference range, 2-11 ng/mL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 0.0347).
11. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is shown in the Figure.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Neurosarcoid
B: Melanoma metastasis
C: Hypophysitis
D: Pituitary macroadenoma

question:
1. A man in his 40s with a history of chronic blurry vision in both eyes (worse in the right eye) had latent extrapulmonary tuberculosis that had been treated with antitubercular therapy 1 year earlier.
2. Oral prednisone provided visual improvement.
3. However, the therapy was complicated by avascular hip necrosis that required total hip arthroplasty, and his visual symptoms recurred with corticosteroid tapering.
4. At presentation, his visual acuity was 20/150 OD and 20/15 OS.
5. The anterior segment was normal in both eyes.
6. Dilated ophthalmoscopic examination of the right eye revealed a diffuse subretinal yellow mass and an exudative retinal detachment temporal to the fovea (Figure 1).
7. Ophthalmoscopic examination of the left eye was normal.
8. B-scan of the right eye showed a dome-shaped choroidal lesion with an apical height of 3.4 mm and medium to high internal reflectivity.
9. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated heterogeneous leakage, and optical coherence tomography of the macula showed subretinal fluid with irregular retinal and choroidal thickening.
10. Results from extensive workup for infectious and autoimmune etiologies (including serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, lumbar puncture, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits, and computed tomography of the chest) were negative, except for positive purified protein derivative skin testing and positive interferon-γ release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold; Cellestis, Inc).
11. Large choroidal tuberculoma at presentation.
12. In a fundus view of the right eye, a moderate amount of subretinal fluid is seen adjacent to the lesion, involving the fovea center.
13. B-scan (not shown) measured an apical height of 3.4 mm.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Consult infectious diseases for alternative antitubercular therapy
B: Initiate corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppressive therapy
C: Inject intravitreous triamcinolone acetonide
D: Perform pars plana vitrectomy with intravitreous methotrexate

15. Results of human immunodeficiency virus screen and urine drug screen were normal.

18. Right, Bullae and erosions on the upper back.

1. A healthy white man in his late 70s was referred to the retina clinic for evaluation of nerve fiber layer infarcts (cotton-wool spots).
2. He had been experiencing nonprogressive diminished vision in his left eye for 6 weeks.
3. He denied any history of diabetes or past ocular problems and reported having mild hypertension for which he was taking lisinopril.
4. Review of systems was positive for fatigue of his tongue while eating but he denied any jaw claudication, fevers, malaise, joint pain, or weight loss.
5. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/30 OS.
6. Pupillary and anterior segment examination in both eyes were unremarkable with the exception of bilateral nuclear sclerotic cataracts.
7. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye showed a nerve fiber layer infarct (NFLI) inferior to the optic nerve (Figure 1A).
8. In the left eye, there were several scattered NFLIs in the peripapillary region (Figure 1B).
9. Fluorescein angiography (FA) showed relatively normal flow without evidence of occlusion or vasculitis.
10. An extensive inflammatory and infectious laboratory workup revealed a hemoglobin level of 12.6 g/dL and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level of 54 mm/h and 6.16 mg/L, respectively (to convert hemoglobin to grams per liter, multiply by 10, and C-reactive protein to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).
11. Antinuclear antibody testing was positive (1:80 with homogenous pattern).
12. Further workup including human immunodeficiency virus testing was nonrevealing.Fundus photographs of the right and left eye demonstrating nerve fiber layer infarcts in the peripapillary region.
13. Media clarity is affected by nuclear sclerotic cataracts in both eyes.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Proceed with temporal artery biopsy
B: Refer patient to primary care physician for management of his hypertension
C: Refer for rheumatologic workup
D: Observe and reevaluate in 2 months

15. B-D, Histopathologic images.

1. A man in his 70s presented for evaluation of a nonhealing lesion of his left cheek.
2. Examination of the head and neck revealed the incidental finding of bilateral auricular rigidity and immobility.
3. Both ears appeared normal and were nontender and asymptomatic (Figure, A).
4. The patient recalled that his barber had noted an increase in difficulty trimming hair in the areas around his auricles owing to their inflexibility.
5. The only other notable finding was increased rigidity of his nasal cartilage.
6. The patient denied any decrease in auditory acuity, frostbite, or any previous trauma to his ears.
7. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension and secondary chronic renal insufficiency, cardiovascular disease, and gout.
8. His long-term medications included lisinopril, glipizide, terazosin, insulin glargine, labetalol, allopurinol, hydrochlorothiazide, and erythropoietin.
9. An incisional biopsy of his left auricle was performed.
10. Hematoxylin-eosin staining of the biopsy specimen showed regions of ossification and calcification (Figure, B).
11. A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the head was performed within 2 weeks of his original biopsy and showed extensive calcification in the area of the auricles (Figure, C).
12. The patient’s laboratory workup showed an elevated creatinine level of 1.8 mg/dL (reference range, 0.6-1.2 mg/dL), which had been his baseline level for the past 2 years.
13. He had a hemoglobin level of 11.1 g/dL (reference range, 14-18 g/dL), which was felt to be secondary to his chronic renal failure.
14. His serum calcium level had been normal with the exception of an elevated value noted of 10.4 mg/dL noted 1 year ago (reference range, 8.7-10.2 mg/dL).
15. His phosphorus, alkaline phosphorus, electrolyte, and AM cortisol levels; parathyroid function; and thyroid function were within normal limits.A, Photograph of ear.
16. B, Photomicrograph of biopsy sample.
17. C, Head computed tomographic image.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Chondrodermatitis nodularis helicis chronicus
B: Relapsing polychondritis
C: Petrified ear
D: Scleroderma

2. Acetaminophen and meloxicam provided only partial relief.
3. He also noted progressive thickening of skin in the nape of his neck.
4. He denied any prior history of Raynaud phenomenon; heart, kidney, or liver disease; diabetic retinopathy; nephropathy; or neuropathy.
5. He had quit smoking 24 years ago and reported currently drinking 3 glasses of wine per week.
6. His medications included rosiglitazone, glimepiride, and levothyroxine.
7. On examination, he weighed 131.5 kg (body mass index, 40.57); his heart rate was 82/min and blood pressure was 161/89 mm Hg.
8. He had facial swelling and brawny periorbital edema (Figure 1A).
9. He also had a large area of diffuse, slightly erythematous, nonpitting woody induration extending from the nape of his neck (Figure 1B), to the upper back, shoulders, and upper arms.
10. This resulted in limitation of range of motion of his neck.
11. Examination of his heart, lungs, abdomen, and lower extremities was unremarkable.
12. A, Facial swelling and periorbital edema.
13. B, Woody induration involving the nape of neck and upper back.
14. Laboratory testing showed a fasting blood glucose level of 178 mg/dL (9.9 mmol/L).
15. Complete blood cell count, levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone and albumin, and the remainder of his comprehensive metabolic panel were normal.
16. Urinalysis showed trace protein without blood.
17. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 34 mm/h, C-reactive protein level was 0.3 mg/dL (2.9 nmol/L), and hemoglobin A1C level was 7.5%.

A: Measure 24-hour urine protein
B: Obtain a 2D echocardiogram
C: Obtain a skin biopsy from the upper back
D: Obtain a thoracic computed tomography scan

question:
1. A man in his 70s with a history of rheumatoid arthritis and a 50-pack-year smoking history presented with a worsening unproductive cough.
2. Chest radiography identified a right lung nodule, with complete workup revealing a T2aN0M0 right upper lobe non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) measuring 4.3 × 2.9 cm.
3. A clinically significant cardiac history precluded the option of surgery.
4. He was treated with a definitive accelerated hypofractionated course of radiotherapy to a total of dose 60 Gy in 8 fractions.
5. Acute toxic effects were not observed, with the exception of minor fatigue that resolved 1 month after treatment.
6. A surveillance computed tomographic (CT) scan obtained at 3 months demonstrated that the right upper lobe tumor had decreased by 1 cm in all dimensions, and at this time the patient denied any new symptoms, including pain.
7. Approximately 5 months after treatment, he awakened with abrupt onset of severe right shoulder pain.
8. The pain was sharp, constant, and localized to his right scapula and ultimately progressed to the point of radiating down the extensor surface of his arm ending at his elbow.
9. He denied paresthesias, weakness, or any inciting events that could have led to its onset.
10. His primary care physician obtained a CT scan, followed 2 days later by a magnetic resonance image (MRI) of his right shoulder (Figure 1).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Metastatic non–small-cell lung cancer
B: Rib fracture
C: Radiation-induced myositis
D: Polymyalgia rheumatica

11. 12. B, Spectral-domain optical coherence tomographic (SD-OCT) image of the right eye shows outer retinal foveoschisis and outer retinal thinning with interruptions of the ellipsoid in the peripheral macula (seen in both eyes).

question:
1. A male neonate born prematurely at 27 weeks’ gestational age was noted to have a erythematous eruption at birth.
2. The neonate was the product of a dichorionic, diamniotic twin pregnancy.
3. The other twin did not have any dermatalogic abnormalities.
4. They were born to a previously healthy woman who had been hospitalized 12 days prior for tocolytic therapy.
5. One day prior to delivery, the mother was noted to have yeast on urinalysis.
6. The presence of epithelial cells in the sample suggested vaginal contamination.
7. Despite tocolytic therapy, labor ultimately progressed the following day and cesarean delivery was performed owing to breech presentation of the unaffected twin.
8. Physical examination of the affected twin revealed an afebrile, 1200 g preterm infant.
9. Skin examination showed 100 to 200 pink papules, 0.05 to 0.2 cm in size, distributed on the trunk, extensor upper arms, and upper legs (Figure, A and B).
10. A subset of the lesions appeared vesiculopustular, but no fluid was evident after attempted unroofing.
11. The diaper area, hands, feet, nails, and oral mucosa were unaffected.
12. The second twin had normal cutaneous examination findings.
13. Laboratory analysis revealed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 6000/μL, which was composed of 21% neutrophils, 38% lymphocytes, 24% monocytes, and 5% eosinophils.
14. Gram stain of lesional scrapings did not reveal bacteria nor WBCs, though potassium hydroxide staining showed numerous yeast forms.
15. Lesional polymerase chain reaction was negative for herpes simplex virus.
16. Bacterial cultures from the skin and the blood were ultimately negative.
17. The placentas from both neonates were sent for pathologic analysis (Figure, C and D).
18. A, Pink papules and vesicopustules were noted on the trunk, arms, and extensor thighs, but spared the diaper area; B, morphology of lesions; C and D, histopathologic images of umbilical cord section.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Neonatal candidiasis
B: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
C: Congenital dermatophytosis
D: Congenital cutaneous candidiasis

1. A 49-year-old woman with no relevant medical history presented with a 2-day history of headache and facial swelling.
2. She was found to have severely elevated blood pressure at an urgent care center, prompting her transfer to the hospital.
3. On review of systems, she endorsed anorexia and malaise for the past several days.
4. She was in no acute distress but appeared languid.
5. Her blood pressure was 210/110 mm Hg.
6. Physical examination demonstrated periorbital and 1+ bipedal pitting edema.
7. She had mild tenderness to percussion of both flanks.
8. Serum studies revealed a creatinine level of 13 mg/dL (to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4), potassium level of 6.6 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1.0), and bicarbonate level of 16 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1.0).
9. Her serum calcium level was 8.5 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.25) and her serum phosphate level was elevated at 5 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.323).
10. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed severe bilateral hydronephrosis with renal cortical thinning and obstructing calculi at both ureteropelvic junctions (Figure 1).
11. The patient underwent emergent dialysis followed by placement of bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy tubes.
12. Subsequently, her blood pressure normalized, edema improved, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis resolved, and serum creatinine level decreased to 1.6 mg/dL.
13. Interestingly, her serum calcium level elevated to 12 mg/dL and her serum phosphate level became low at 2.4 mg/dL.
14. Computed tomographic scans of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast, showing obstructing calculi bilaterally at the ureteropelvic junctions (arrowheads) with resultant severe hydronephrosis and renal cortical thinning (A) and significant renal stone burden in the lower pole of the left kidney (B).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Hypervitaminosis D
B: Malignant neoplasm
C: Primary hyperparathyroidism
D: Sarcoidosis

question:
1. A woman in her 60s with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), status post–nonallogenic bone marrow transplant and subsequent relapse, was admitted to the hospital with blast crisis (white blood cell count, 72 500/μL; 72% blasts) and tumor lysis syndrome.
2. Flow cytometry showed myeloid blasts, most of which (≥90%) expressed CD13, CD33, CD117, and partial CD11b (≥50%).
3. Blasts were also “highly positive” for myeloperoxidase.
4. Stains were weak for CD4 and were negative for CD34 and HLA-DR.
5. Cytogenetic studies revealed a normal karyotype with NPM1 and FLT3-ITD mutations.
6. Dermatology was consulted for evaluation of 5-day history of new tender lesions on the scalp.
7. The patient did not have a history of recent travel or trauma.
8. Physical examination revealed several tender purpuric papules and plaques with central necrosis and hemorrhagic crusting on the scalp (Figure, A).
9. Similar lesions were present on the right dorsal hand and left lower leg.
10. On the right forearm, there was a tender erythematous plaque with overlying vesicles and mild hemorrhagic crusting.
11. On the left medial thigh, there was a large indurated, tender red-brown plaque.
12. Wound cultures and polymerase chain reaction studies from the right forearm were negative for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus infections.
13. Punch biopsy specimens from lesions on the scalp, right forearm, and left thigh were sent for histopathological and immunohistochemical assessment and tissue culture (Figure, B-D).
14. A, Clinical image of tender purpuric papules and plaques with central necrosis on the scalp.
15. B-D, Histologic images of a punch biopsy specimen from a scalp lesion.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
B: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
C: Leukemia cutis with leukemic vasculitis
D: Cutaneous mucormycosis

10. A, Indurated papules and plaques are present on the lateral cheeks and behind the ears and neck along with a red-brown hue.

12. D, Papule specimen under IgG4 immunohistochemical stain.

B: IgG4-related skin disease
C: Cutaneous lymphoma
D: Sjögren syndrome

2. Angiography demonstrated widely patent grafts to the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries and a totally occluded graft to the obtuse marginal branch, which was known from a prior cardiac catheterization.
3. Disease in the obtuse marginal branch appeared stable, but there was worsening of disease in the ramus branch, where 2 serial lesions were identified.
4. Intravenous adenosine was administered at 140 µg/kg/min to induce maximal hyperemia, and fractional flow reserve (FFR) was measured in the ramus, revealing a nadir value of 0.43 across both lesions (Figure 1).
5. A slow, pull-back maneuver across the distal lesion demonstrated that the proximal lesion had an FFR value of 0.82.A, Angiography shows 2 serial lesions of intermediate severity in the ramus intermedius (red arrowheads).
6. B, Fractional flow reserve (FFR) measurement was performed after induction of maximal hyperemia, demonstrating a nadir value of 0.43.
7. HR indicates heart rate; iPa, instantaneous proximal (aortic) pressure; iPd, instantaneous distal (coronary) pressure; Pa, proximal (aortic) pressure; and Pd, distal (intracoronary) pressure.The proximal lesion is ischemic while the distal lesion is nonischemic.
8. Only the proximal lesion should have a stent placed.The distal lesion is ischemic while the proximal lesion is nonischemic.
9. Only the distal lesion should have a stent placed.Both lesions are ischemic and should have a stent placed.FFR with adenosine should be remeasured after placing a stent in the distal lesion to better assess the proximal lesion.

What Would You Do Next?

A: The proximal lesion is ischemic while the distal lesion is nonischemic. Only the proximal lesion should have a stent placed.
B: The distal lesion is ischemic while the proximal lesion is nonischemic. Only the distal lesion should have a stent placed.
C: Both lesions are ischemic and should have a stent placed.
D: FFR with adenosine should be remeasured after placing a stent in the distal lesion to better assess the proximal lesion.

1. A healthy man in his 20s presented to the emergency department with decreased vision in the left eye that was associated with intermittent left orbital pain progressing from a dull ache to throbbing pain over 2 days.
2. Findings from the examination were remarkable for reduced visual acuity in the left eye (20/80), proptosis with hypoglobus in the left eye, S-shaped left blepharoptosis, and left retinochoroidal folds (Figure 1A).
3. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits with contrast demonstrated a well-defined superotemporal mass with homogeneous enhancement (Figure 1B).
4. The patient was admitted for a trial of intravenous methylprednisolone, 1000 mg, for presumed inflammatory dacryoadenitis.
5. Results of a complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, antinuclear antibody, Lyme titer and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels, chest radiograph, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein levels, urinalysis, and IgG4 index were normal.
6. The patient’s pain nearly resolved after 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone treatment, and he was discharged with a regimen of 80 mg/d of oral prednisone.A, Left eye at initial presentation showed proptosis with hypoglobus, S-shaped blepharoptosis, and retinochoroidal folds.
7. B, Results of coronal, T1-weighted, postcontrast, fat-suppressed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits showing a 2 × 3 x 2.8-cm well-defined lesion of the lacrimal gland with inferior displacement of the globe and lateral rectus muscle.When the patient was reevaluated 2 weeks later, the pain at rest had resolved, but pain on palpation of the superotemporal left orbit persisted.
8. Results of the examination were otherwise unchanged.
9. Results of additional MRI of the orbits with contrast were unchanged.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Order a gallium scan
B: Perform incisional biopsy of the left lacrimal gland
C: Initiate antiviral therapy with acyclovir
D: Increase the dosage of oral prednisone

1. A man in his 60s had decreased visual acuity in the right eye.
2. He had a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with a CD4 count of 25 and retinal detachment of the left eye secondary to cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis.
3. He was taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for prophylaxis of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (formerly Pneumocystis carinii).
4. On examination, visual acuity was 20/30 OD and no light perception OS, which was phthisical with no view of the fundus.
5. In the right eye, the anterior segment was quiet, and there was 1+ nuclear sclerosis.
6. Dilated fundus examination showed no vitritis, multiple discrete hyperpigmented scars (Figure, A, black arrowhead), and an area of inferotemporal retinal whitening (Figure, A, white arrowhead) with associated hemorrhage.
7. The patient was presumptively diagnosed as having CMV retinitis based on the history of CMV retinitis in the contralateral eye, and the findings of hemorrhagic retinitis adjacent to chorioretinal scars suggestive of prior, healed CMV retinitis.
8. He was treated with oral valgancyclovir, but 3 weeks later, the lesions had progressed, prompting admission for intravenous ganciclovir before being lost to follow-up for 1 month.
9. On his return, his visual acuity had declined to 20/50 OD, there was mild vitritis, and there were new areas of retinitis along the inferior arcade (Figure, B, white arrowheads) and vascular sheathing (Figure, B, black arrowhead).
10. Fundus photographs of the right eye.
11. A, Inferotemporal area of retinal whitening (white arrowhead) with intraretinal hemorrhage adjacent to chorioretinal scars (black arrowhead).
12. There is retinal vascular sheathing within the area of retinitis.
13. B, Eight weeks after presentation, the retinitis has progressed with multiple new lesions along the inferior arcade (white arrowheads) threatening the macula and retinal vascular sheathing along the inferotemporal arcade (black arrowhead).
14. Obtain aqueous and vitreous samples for polymerase chain reaction/culture/cytology Check serology results for exposure to infectious agents

What Would You Do Next?

A: Add steroids
B: Obtain aqueous and vitreous samples for polymerase chain reaction/culture/cytology
C: Inject intravitreous voriconazole
D: Check serology results for exposure to infectious agents

question:
1. An adolescent boy was referred to the emergency department for suspected herpes zoster infection by his pediatrician.
2. He presented with a 2-day history of painful, left-sided vesicular rash around his eyelid and forehead.
3. Medical history was significant for a heart murmur with no known history of chickenpox.
4. His pediatrician prescribed oral acyclovir and ibuprofen as needed for pain.
5. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25-2 OS.
6. On examination, clear vesicles on erythematous bases were noted in the V1 distribution with left upper eyelid edema and erythema.
7. Pupils were equally reactive with no relative afferent pupillary defect.
8. Visual fields were full in both eyes.
9. Anterior examination was significant for left-sided conjunctivitis, dendritic keratitis (Figure), and anterior uveitis.
10. The findings of the remainder of the examination, including the anterior segment of the right eye and the dilated fundus examination of both eyes, were unremarkable.
11. Slitlamp photograph showing branching corneal pseudodendrites with minimal fluorescein uptake.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Obtain a corneal culture
B: Human immunodeficiency virus testing and lymphocyte analysis
C: Discontinue oral acyclovir and start topical trifluridine
D: Perform corneal topography

question:
1. An otherwise healthy adult man presented with left upper eyelid swelling for 2 days.
2. This was accompanied by foreign-body sensation and discomfort of the left eye and was preceded by a week of general malaise without fevers or chills.
3. He denied vision changes, light sensitivity, or drainage from the eye.
4. He denied previous similar episodes of eyelid swelling or recurrent chalazia.
5. He had no relevant medical history and his family history was negative for malignancy.
6. Clinical examination revealed an area of ulceration centrally along the left upper eyelid margin, measuring approximately 8 mm × 2 mm (Figure 1A).
7. The eyelid demonstrated mild boggy edema; however, there were no associated nodules, vesicles, or plaques on the surrounding skin or face.
8. There was mild madarosis in the area of ulceration.
9. There was also a tender and enlarged preauricular lymph node on the ipsilateral side.
10. The remainder of the clinical examination was unremarkable, including visual acuity, intraocular pressure, slitlamp biomicroscopy, and dilated fundus examination.
11. A photomicrograph of a hematoxylin-eosin–stained section from an incisional biopsy specimen is shown in Figure 1B.
12. A, External photograph of the left eye demonstrating central upper eyelid margin ulceration with sparse lashes and surrounding edema.
13. B, Incisional biopsy reveals a necrotic epithelium with multinucleated keratinocytes and cytoplasmic inclusions (hematoxylin-eosin, ×200).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Perform wide local excision with map biopsies
B: Initiate treatment with oral valacyclovir
C: Proceed with cryotherapy
D: Perform Mohs micrographic surgery followed by reconstruction with flap

1. A 72-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of a dull, epigastric pain, 10-kg weight loss (from 52 kg to 42 kg), and a 6- to 8-week history of nausea and vomiting.
2. Physical examination showed no notable abnormalities.
3. Blood test results revealed anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) but were otherwise unremarkable.
4. Upper gastrointestinal series showed subtotal occlusion in the second part of the duodenum (Figure 1 A).
5. Computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed intraluminal narrowing of the duodenum without signs of a mass (Figure 1 B, arrowhead).
6. Gastroduodenoscopy revealed a duodenal ulcer with pinpoint stenosis that could not be passed or dilated.
7. Multiple biopsies were negative for cancer.
8. Total parenteral nutrition was started and the patient was scheduled for surgery.
9. A, Coronal upper gastrointestinal series demonstrate subtotal occlusion in the second part of the duodenum.
10. B, Axial computed tomography image shows intraluminal narrowing of the duodenum without signs of a mass (arrowhead).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Fibrosis owing to chronic peptic ulceration
B: Duodenal carcinoma
C: Duodenal web
D: Annular pancreas

1. A young girl presented to establish care for skin lesions on her trunk and extremities that had been present since birth.
2. Her mother described an intermittent inflammatory reaction localized only to the patient’s abnormal skin lesions that was reproducible in febrile states and was concerned about asymptomatic, stable, dark brown lesions that had developed in areas of prior blistering and scarring on the patient’s right arm, left knee, and right upper back.
3. There was no history of developmental delay, eye abnormalities, or seizures.
4. Examination revealed irregular, dark brown, well-demarcated macules with regular pigment networks on dermoscopy within prominent soft, yellow, papular protrusions in a Blaschkolinear arrangement on her upper arms, particularly her right arm.
5. The right flank demonstrated linear, atrophic pink plaques with focal erosions and crusting, evidencing recent inflammation described by the patient’s mother (Figure, A).
6. Additional irregular, well-demarcated, evenly pigmented dark brown macules were present within pink, atrophic scars located on the right side of the trunk, the right upper back, and the left knee.
7. She had well-healed surgical scars on the hands, syndactyly of the toes, and ventral pterygium and dystrophy of the fingernails and toenails (Figure, B).
8. A, Irregular, dark brown, well-demarcated macules within prominent soft, yellow, papular protrusions in a Blaschkolinear arrangement on the upper arms; linear, atrophic pink plaques with focal erosions and crusting are seen on the right flank.
9. B, Extracutaneous features show syndactyly of the toes and ventral pterygium and dystrophy of the toe nails.
10. C, Hematoxylin-eosin staining of skin biopsy demonstrates close proximity of subcutaneous fat to the epidermis with attenuated collagen (original magnification × 20).
11. Previous treatment had included surgical excision of a frequently symptomatic focus of affected skin with subsequent adjacent tissue transfer.
12. Additionally, she had received dental implantation of frontal upper incisors.
13. Histopathologic slides from the prior excision of affected skin were reviewed (Figure, C).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Epidermolysis bullosa with mottled pigmentation
B: Focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome)
C: Incontinentia pigmenti
D: Nevus lipomatosus superficialis

1. A man in his mid-50s was referred to our hospital because he had a cystic mass in his spleen that was discovered incidentally during a routine physical examination.
2. He had no history of abdominal trauma, infection, or surgery.
3. A physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the posterior left upper quadrant.
4. A precontrast computed tomographic scan revealed a large, well-defined, cystic mass (7 by 6 cm) with mural calcification in the spleen (Figure 1A), and the cyst was not enhanced in the arterial phase.
5. The laboratory test results, including carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels, were all within normal ranges, except for a mild increase in the carbohydrate antigen 72-4 level, which was 11.89 U/mL (normal range, 0-6.9 U/mL).
6. A, Computed tomography (CT) revealed a large, well-defined, cystic mass with mural calcification in the spleen.
7. B, The surface of the cyst was extremely dense and appeared to have an eggshell-like calcification; the cyst was filled with about 300 mL of yellowish opalescent fluid containing numerous cholesterol-like crystals (arrowhead).
8. During a laparotomy, a huge hard mass, which was partially covered by fibrous and necrotic tissue, was found emerging from the lower pole of the spleen.
9. A total splenectomy was performed, and a gross pathologic examination revealed that the lower end of the spleen was occupied by a cyst, the surface of which was extremely dense and appeared to have an eggshell-like calcification (Figure 1B).
10. The cyst was filled with about 300 mL of yellowish opalescent fluid containing numerous cholesterol-like crystals (Figure 1B).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Echinococcal disease
B: Congenital splenic cyst
C: Secondary splenic cyst
D: Splenic abscess

1. A 57-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of upper abdominal pain.
2. The pain was localized to the epigastrium and had acute onset that prevented her from working for the rest of the day.
3. There was no association between the pain and eating.
4. No history of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, melena, hematochezia, constipation, or fevers was reported.
5. She had no alcohol abuse or smoking history.
6. Dyslipidemia and a transient ischemic attack 3 years before were her only medical history.
7. She had never had a colonoscopy or a gastroscopy.
8. Her medication included atorvastatin and acetylsalicylic acid.
9. The only past operation she reported was for treating carpal tunnel syndrome.
10. She was a sheep breeder and was in close contact with animals for 8 to 12 hours every day.
11. During physical examination, the heart and the lungs were normal.
12. Her abdomen was soft with tenderness in the epigastrium.
13. The laboratory evaluation results revealed normocytic anemia (hematocrit level of 28.1% [to convert to proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01] and hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) including a normal white blood cell count of 7600/µL (to convert to ×109 per liter, multiply by 0.001).
14. Results from a complete metabolic panel were normal.
15. An abdominal radiography was performed (Figure 1).
16. Anteroposterior abdominal x-ray film in erect position.
17. In the right side of the mid to lower quadrant, at the level of L5 vertebral body, there is a rounded radio-opaque lesion (arrowhead) that seems to contain a second smaller sclerotic lesion within its central part (a lesion-in-lesion appearance).

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Calcified hydatid cyst
B: Gallstone
C: Calcified bowel mass
D: Swallowed foreign body

2. The eruption presented abruptly over a 2-week course, and the patient attributed it to contact with plants while working in his yard.
3. He denied having similar lesions in the past.
4. He had used over-the-counter topical antibiotic and antihistamine creams, which alleviated the pruritus.
5. He denied recent sexual intercourse, penile discharge, fevers, chills, nausea, or vomiting.

8. There was also a 1-cm ulceration on the left lower lip.
9. The palms and soles were spared.
10. There was no lymphadenopathy noted.
11. One 4-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained from a nodule on the left medial cheek, bisectioned, and sent for both hematoxylin–eosin staining and tissue cultures for bacteria, fungi, and atypical mycobacteria (Figure, C and D).
12. A, Multiple crusted and ulcerative papules and nodules on the face.
13. B, Multiple ulcerated healing papules on the scrotum and umbilicated papules on the left inner thigh.
14. C, Low-power image (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40).
15. D, A Warthin-Starry silver impregnation stain (original magnification ×40).

A: Atypical mycobacterium infection
B: Cryptococcal infection
C: Eruptive keratoacanthomas
D: Secondary syphilis

question:
1. An Asian woman in her 50s with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with ptosis and intermittent esotropia of the right eye.
2. Fourteen years earlier, the patient underwent a pituitary adenoma resection and external beam radiation.
3. Immediately after the resection, she developed slight ptosis and an adduction deficit of the right eye, presumed to be secondary to partial oculomotor nerve III (CNIII) damage.
4. Four years earlier, she developed intermittent esotropia of the right eye, presumed secondary to cranial nerve VI palsy.
5. At the present clinic visit, the patient reported the persistence of intermittent diplopia, which had remained unchanged for years, and denied other ocular or systemic complaints.
6. Visual acuity measured 20/20 OU.
7. We noted 3 mm of relative right upper eyelid ptosis and anisocoria (3 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS in ambient lighting).
8. Pupils were round and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect.
9. The degree of anisocoria was the same in ambient and dim lighting.
10. Extraocular movements were initially intact; however, a few minutes later, the patient developed an intermittent esotropia of the right eye, with episodes of sustained adduction lasting up to 30 seconds followed by normalization of ductions and alignment (Video; Figure, A).
11. These episodes occurred more commonly following voluntary adduction.
12. On infraduction, the right upper eyelid simultaneously retracted, exposing 3 mm of superior sclera (Figure, B).
13. On adduction, the right pupil constricted slightly.
14. The remainder of the examination was within normal limits.
15. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) from 1 year prior showed a small amount of residual tumor within the right cavernous sinus, stable over years (Figure, C).

What Would You Do Next?

A: Topical apraclonidine test
B: Urgent MRI
C: Offer carbamazepine and routine MRI
D: Extraocular muscle surgery

question:
1. A woman in her 60s was referred for a chronic progressive left homonymous visual field defect.
2. Three years prior to presentation, she reported difficulties with her vision.
3. She had difficulty comprehending some words while reading and also reported the feeling of a “blind spot” in her vision and a “part of her vision” that she could not see.
4. She was found to have a left homonymous visual field defect.
5. She underwent repeated visual field examination every 6 months, showing progression of the visual field defect along with an increase in false-negative results.
6. She underwent 3 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the brain, showing no neoplasm or stroke, and also underwent a stroke workup with negative results.
7. Review of the most recent MRI showed profound cortical atrophy of the parieto-occipital lobes with a slight predilection to the right side compared with the left.
8. On further questioning, she had developed some recent difficulties with short-term memory and reported easily getting lost when driving.
9. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU, and color plate results were severely reduced in both eyes.
10. Dilated fundus examination findings were unremarkable.
11. Automated visual fields again showed a left homonymous visual field defect with high false-negative results (Figure, A).
12. She was unable to draw a clock and had simultanagnosia (Figure, B).
13. A, Automated visual field testing (Swedish interactive thresholding algorithm [SITA]) showed a dense left homonymous visual field defect with high false-negative results.
14. B, Abnormal clock drawing.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Lumbar puncture
B: Repeat MRI
C: Neuropsychological testing
D: Fluorescein angiography

question:
1. A man in his 50s with a history of ‎poorly controlled type 2 diabetes reported decreased vision in both eyes.
2. On examination, visual acuity was counting fingers OD and 20/200 OS.
3. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable.
4. Dense vitreous hemorrhage precluded fundus examination of the right eye, and B-scan ultrasonography did not reveal any additional pathology.
5. The left fundus examination exhibited diabetic macular edema with central subfield thickness of 425 μm on optical coherence tomography and severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, for which he had laser surgery for diabetic macular edema and panretinal photocoagulation.
6. He subsequently underwent vitrectomy in the right eye for nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage with an uneventful postoperative course and improvement of his visual acuity to 20/100.
7. The patient was lost to follow-up and returned 4 months later with visual acuity 20/125 OD and counting fingers OS, with a vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye for which he underwent vitrectomy with thorough panretinal photocoagulation (1200 spots).
8. On postoperative day 1, visual acuity was 20/200 and intraocular pressure was elevated to 35 mm Hg.
9. The conjunctiva had mild hyperemia with foci of subconjunctival hemorrhage, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet, the anterior vitreous contained no cells, and a few cobweblike, tan strands were present throughout the vitreous cavity.
10. Topical timolol/acetazolamide and brimonidine were started twice daily, together with prednisolone acetate and moxifloxacin every 6 hours.
11. On postoperative day 3, the patient noted decreased visual acuity OS but he denied pain or discharge.
12. Visual acuity was hand motion, and intraocular pressure was 17 mm Hg.
13. The anterior chamber had minimal inflammation.
14. Extensive strands and veils were noted throughout the vitreous cavity (Figure 1).
15. Anterior vitreous cavity (A) and wide-field fundus photograph (B) of the left eye demonstrating extensive transvitreal strands and sheets.

What Would You Do Next?

A: Increase topical steroids
B: Inject intravitreal antibiotics
C: Perform vitrectomy
D: Inject antifungal drug

1. A 32-year-old male with a history of end-stage liver disease secondary to alcoholic cirrhosis was transferred to our hospital with a 2-week history of a skin rash that developed at an outside facility where he was being treated for hepatic encephalopathy.
2. He reported that the lesions began on his face, then spread to his thighs and were mildly pruritic.
3. He did not have any other involvement and was in no pain.
4. On physical exam, multiple 1 to 3 cm purple papules with central black and hemorrhagic crusting were noted on his forehead, bilateral cheeks, and anterior thighs (Figure 1, A and B).
5. On his left flank, he had a large polycyclic, atrophic hyperpigmented plaque with a slightly erythematous and scaly border (Figure 1C).
6. The scalp, oral mucosa, back, chest, abdomen, arms, palms and soles were all spared.
7. Multiple toenails were noted to be dystrophic with hyperkeratotic subungual debris.
8. Over the next few days, the crusted papules and nodules eroded leaving smooth erythematous plaques with punched-out centers.
9. Testing for the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis was negative.
10. Punch biopsy specimens from the left anterior thigh were taken for histopathologic analysis and fungal, bacterial, and atypical mycobacterial tissue cultures.
11. A skin culture was obtained of the polycyclic plaque on his left flank.

What Is Your Diagnosis?

A: Kaposi sarcoma
B: Disseminated tinea infection
C: Bacillary angiomatosis
D: Leukemia cutis

A. Clozapine
B. Thioridazine
C. Chlorpromazine
D. Fluphenazine

1. #### **OBJECTIVE****:**
We compared the effect of clopidogrel plus aspirin vs aspirin alone on functional outcome and quality of life in the Clopidogrel in High-risk Patients with Acute Non-disabling Cerebrovascular Events (CHANCE) trial of aspirin-clopidogrel vs aspirin alone after acute minor stroke or TIA.
2. #### **METHODS****:**
Participants were assessed at 90 days for functional outcome using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and quality of life using the EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D).
3. Poor functional outcome was defined as mRS score of 2-6 at 90 days and poor quality of life as EQ-5D index score of 0.5 or less.
4. #### **RESULTS****:**
Poor functional outcome occurred in 254 patients (9.9%) in the clopidogrel-aspirin group, as compared with 299 (11.6%) in the aspirin group (p = 0.046).
5. Poor quality of life occurred in 142 (5.5%) in the clopidogrel-aspirin group and in 175 (6.8%) in the aspirin group (p = 0.06).
6. Disabling stroke at 90 days occurred in 166 (6.5%) in the clopidogrel-aspirin group and in 219 (8.5%) in the aspirin group (p = 0.01).
7. In stratified analysis by subsequent stroke, there was no difference in 90-day functional outcome and quality of life between the 2 groups.
8. #### **CONCLUSIONS****:**
In patients with minor stroke or TIA, the combination of clopidogrel and aspirin appears to be superior to aspirin alone in improving the 90-day functional outcome, and this is consistent with a reduction in the rate of disabling stroke in the dual antiplatelet arm.
9. #### **CLASSIFICATION** **OF** **EVIDENCE****:**
This study provides Class II evidence that for patients with acute minor stroke or TIA, clopidogrel plus aspirin compared to aspirin alone improves 90-day functional outcome (absolute reduction of poor outcome 1.70%, 95% confidence interval 0.03%-3.42%).

Given the original research abstract above, which of the following would be true if the authors had inadvertently encountered a type 1 error?

A. A type 1 error implies that the study's findings are due to chance rather than a true effect.
B. A type 1 error means the study is not significantly powered to detect a true difference between study groups.
C. A type 1 error is dependent on the statistical significance of a study.
D. A type 1 error is unrelated to the p-value used in hypothesis testing.
E. A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is true, but is rejected inappropriately.
F. A type 1 error can be reduced by increasing the study’s alpha threshold.
G. A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is false, but is rejected in error.
H. A type 1 error occurs when the alternative hypothesis is true but is not supported by the data.
I. A type 1 error is synonymous with a failure to reject the null hypothesis.
J. A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is false, yet is accepted in error.

3. The patient reports feeling tired and experiencing occasional headaches, which she attributes to school stress and lack of sleep.
4. She reports no breast pain, redness, itching, fever, visual changes, nausea, abdominal pain, or bowel/bladder issues.
5. She is sexually active and has been using combined oral contraceptive pills for 6 months with regular 28-day menstrual cycles.

7. She occasionally drinks alcohol and smokes marijuana monthly but denies tobacco or other drug use.

9. A few drops of milky discharge are expressed from multiple ducts of both breasts without visible or palpable abnormalities or axillary lymphadenopathy.
10. Ophthalmologic and neurologic exams are normal.

12. Serum prolactin is elevated at 50 ng/mL (reference range: 0–30).

What is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

A. Order CT scan of the head
B. Perform breast biopsy
C. Repeat prolactin level in macroprolactin-free sample
D. Perform mammography and breast ultrasound
E. Switch the fluoxetine to sertraline, and then recheck prolactin
F. Order magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
G. Measure serum estradiol levels
H. Discontinue oral contraceptive pills and reassess in 4 weeks
I. Measure follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone levels
J. Order genetic testing for BRCA mutations

Randomized clinical trial conducted among 315 patients with emphysema and severe air trapping recruited from 21 North American and 5 European sites from December 2012 through November 2015.
